We demonstrate that. such transi t.ions must. indeed exist. in analogous infinite array models. paragraphs: The paper investigates abrupt qualitative changes observed in simulations of cortical subnetworks as important parameters vary. Such changes resemble phase transitions: crossing a critical parameter value changes the kind of collective behavior a network exhibits. The authors ask how this observation should be understood mathematically.

For analogous models built from infinite arrays, they demonstrate that phase transitions must exist. This gives a theoretical basis for transition-like behavior rather than relying solely on simulation observations. The infinite-array setting is central to that result because it supports the classical description of changes in steady-state behavior.

Related finite arrays require a different interpretation. They may lack classical steady-state phase transitions, yet still show distinct changes in metastable transient behavior as parameters cross critical values. In other words, the behavior before final settling can change qualitatively even without a classical transition in the steady state. The paper's contribution is to separate these two possibilities and show why transition-like dynamics can matter in finite neural models.
summary.tldr: Infinite neural arrays exhibit phase transitions, while finite counterparts can show critical changes in metastable transient behavior.

abstract: The dendritic trees of cortical pyramidal neurons seem ideally suited to perfonn local processing on inputs. To explore some of the implications of this complexity for the computational power of neurons, we simulated a realistic biophysical model of a hippocampal pyramidal cell in which a "cold spot"-a high density patch of inhibitory Ca-dependent K channels and a colocalized patch of Ca channels-was present at a dendritic branch point. The cold spot induced a non monotonic relationship be(cid:173) tween the strength of the synaptic input and the probability of neuronal fIring. This effect could also be interpreted as an analog stochastic XOR.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how local processing within a neuron's dendritic branches can contribute to its computational abilities. The authors simulate a realistic biophysical model of a hippocampal pyramidal cell. Their model includes a specialized patch at a dendritic branch point, called a cold spot, where two types of ion channels are concentrated together.

This patch contains calcium channels and a high density of inhibitory calcium-dependent potassium channels. In the simulation, the cold spot makes the relationship between synaptic input strength and firing probability nonmonotonic. Consequently, increasing input strength does not simply produce a steadily increasing probability that the neuron will fire.

The authors interpret this behavior as an analog, stochastic form of XOR. That interpretation describes a nonlinear input-output relationship expressed through graded inputs and firing probabilities. The finding shows how a localized membrane feature can alter the computation of a whole cell. Within the modeled setup, dendritic channel organization provides a mechanism for nonlinear pattern separation at the level of a single neuron.
summary.tldr: A simulated dendritic ion-channel patch creates nonmonotonic firing responses that can be interpreted as an analog stochastic XOR.

title: Nonlinear Pattern Separation in Single Hippocampal Neurons with Active Dendritic Membrane

abstract: The bootstrap algorithm is a computational intensive procedure to derive nonparametric confidence intervals of statistical estimators in situations where an analytic solution is intractable. It is ap(cid:173) plied to neural networks to estimate the predictive distribution for unseen inputs. The consistency of different bootstrap procedures and their convergence speed is discussed. A small scale simulation experiment shows the applicability of the bootstrap to practical problems and its potential use.
originalAbstract: The bootstrap algorithm is a computational intensive procedure to derive nonparametric confidence intervals of statistical estimators in situations where an analytic solution is intractable. It is ap(cid:173) plied to neural networks to estimate the predictive distribution for unseen inputs. The consistency of different bootstrap procedures and their convergence speed is discussed. A small scale simulation experiment shows the applicability of the bootstrap to practical problems and its potential use.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to assess a neural network's predictions for inputs it has not seen. Its focus is the predictive distribution, which expresses uncertainty around a prediction rather than supplying only a single answer. Obtaining such information analytically can be difficult, motivating a computational approach.

The authors apply the bootstrap, a procedure for deriving nonparametric confidence intervals for statistical estimators. Here, it is used to estimate predictive distributions for neural networks. The approach matters because it offers a way to investigate prediction uncertainty when a tractable analytic solution is unavailable, although the procedure itself requires substantial computation.

The paper discusses whether different bootstrap procedures are consistent and how quickly they converge. These issues concern whether the estimation approach behaves appropriately and how much computation may be needed. A small simulation demonstrates practical applicability and potential usefulness. The stated evidence therefore supports bootstrap-based assessment as a promising way to examine neural predictions, with attention to both statistical behavior and computational effort.
summary.tldr: The paper applies bootstrap methods to estimate uncertainty in neural-network predictions and examines their consistency and convergence.

title: Assessing and Improving Neural Network Predictions by the Bootstrap Algorithm

abstract: Recent research on reinforcement learning has focused on algo(cid:173) rithms based on the principles of Dynamic Programming (DP). One of the most promising areas of application for these algo(cid:173) rithms is the control of dynamical systems, and some impressive results have been achieved. However, there are significant gaps between practice and theory. In particular, there are no con ver(cid:173) gence proofs for problems with continuous state and action spaces, or for systems involving non-linear function approximators (such as multilayer perceptrons). This paper presents research applying DP-based reinforcement learning theory to Linear Quadratic Reg(cid:173) ulation (LQR), an important class of control problems involving continuous state and action spaces and requiring a simple type of non-linear function approximator. We describe an algorithm based on Q-Iearning that is proven to converge to the optimal controller for a large class of LQR problems. We also describe a slightly different algorithm that is only locally convergent to the optimal Q-function, demonstrating one of the possible pitfalls of using a non-linear function approximator with DP-based learning.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a gap between successful reinforcement-learning applications and guarantees that learning will converge. It focuses on methods based on dynamic programming when states and actions are continuous and function approximation is involved. Linear quadratic regulation provides a control setting in which these theoretical questions can be examined.

The authors describe a Q-learning-based algorithm and prove that it converges to the optimal controller for a large class of these regulation problems. The setting requires a simple form of nonlinear function approximation. This makes the result relevant to learning beyond discrete state-and-action tables while retaining a concrete mathematical control problem.

A slightly different algorithm receives a weaker guarantee: it converges to the optimal Q-function only locally. The contrast shows that apparently related learning procedures can have substantially different convergence properties. The paper therefore supplies both a positive result and a specific example of a difficulty introduced by nonlinear approximation, clarifying why success in continuous control depends on the learning algorithm's precise form.
summary.tldr: A Q-learning algorithm provably reaches optimal controllers for a broad LQR class, while a nearby variant has only local convergence.

title: Reinforcement Learning Applied to Linear Quadratic Regulation

paragraphs: The paper addresses fault monitoring when training data cover only some of the situations a system may encounter. A classifier built from those data has an incomplete set of classes. Monitoring must therefore account for observations from unknown sources, rather than assuming every input belongs to a familiar category.

The proposed probabilistic approach combines an input-density model with a discriminative model of the known classes. These provide complementary information about the observations and their classification. Bayes' rule brings them together with prior estimates of how likely data are to come from known or unknown origins, producing classification equations that explicitly allow novelty.

The authors apply this approach with hidden Markov models to online monitoring of large ground antennas used for spacecraft tracking. The application particularly concerns transient behavior of unknown origin. Its significance is that recognizing known faults and detecting unfamiliar behavior become parts of the same probabilistic treatment. The stated need for prior known-versus-unknown likelihood estimates is part of that formulation.
summary.tldr: The paper combines density and class models to detect unfamiliar behavior during probabilistic fault monitoring of dynamic systems.

title: Probabilistic Anomaly Detection in Dynamic Systems

abstract: We present a silicon model of an axon which shows promise as a building block for pulse-based neural computations involving cor(cid:173) relations of pulses across both space and time. The circuit shares a number of features with its biological counterpart including an excitation threshold, a brief refractory period after pulse comple(cid:173) tion, pulse amplitude restoration, and pulse width restoration. We provide a simple explanation of circuit operation and present data from a chip fabricated in a standard 2Jlm CMOS process through the MOS Implementation Service (MOSIS). We emphasize the ne(cid:173) cessity of the restoration of the width of the pulse in time for stable propagation in axons.

paragraphs: The paper presents an electronic model of an axon, the part of a neuron that carries pulses. The intended role is as a building block for neural computations that depend on relationships among pulses across locations and times. For that purpose, the circuit needs to transmit pulses while preserving the features that make their timing meaningful.

The design reproduces several properties of its biological counterpart. It has a threshold for excitation and a brief refractory interval after a pulse, during which its response is restricted. It also restores both pulse amplitude and pulse width. These restoration mechanisms address two separate aspects of the signal: how strong the pulse is and how long it lasts.

The authors explain the circuit's operation and present measurements from a chip fabricated in a standard CMOS process. They particularly emphasize pulse-width restoration as necessary for stable propagation. This makes temporal shape a central engineering requirement: carrying a pulse reliably involves maintaining its duration as well as its amplitude. The hardware therefore addresses a concrete prerequisite for computations built around pulse correlations.
summary.tldr: A silicon axon preserves pulse amplitude and duration while reproducing excitation thresholds and refractory behavior.

title: A Silicon Axon

abstract: An adaptive back-propagation algorithm is studied and compared with gradient descent (standard back-propagation) for on-line learning in two-layer neural networks with an arbitrary number of hidden units. Within a statistical mechanics framework , both numerical studies and a rigorous analysis show that the adaptive back-propagation method results in faster training by breaking the symmetry between hidden units more efficiently and by providing faster convergence to optimal generalization than gradient descent.
originalAbstract: An adaptive back-propagation algorithm is studied and compared with gradient descent (standard back-propagation) for on-line learning in two-layer neural networks with an arbitrary number of hidden units. Within a statistical mechanics framework , both numerical studies and a rigorous analysis show that the adaptive back-propagation method results in faster training by breaking the symmetry between hidden units more efficiently and by providing faster convergence to optimal generalization than gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether an adaptive version of back-propagation can train a network faster than ordinary gradient descent. The setting is online learning in two-layer neural networks, with the analysis allowing an arbitrary number of hidden units. The comparison concerns both the progress of training and the approach to optimal generalization.

The authors use a statistical mechanics framework and support their conclusions with numerical studies and rigorous analysis. A central finding concerns symmetry between hidden units. When units behave similarly, learning must differentiate their roles; the adaptive method breaks this symmetry more efficiently than standard back-propagation. This gives a specific explanation for its faster training.

The adaptive method also reaches optimal generalization more quickly in the studied setting. That result connects the speed of internal differentiation to performance beyond the training examples. The paper's contribution is therefore both comparative and explanatory: it identifies an advantage of the adaptive rule and links that advantage to how hidden units become distinct during learning.
summary.tldr: Adaptive back-propagation speeds online learning by differentiating hidden units more efficiently and converging faster to optimal generalization.

title: Adaptive Back-Propagation in On-Line Learning of Multilayer Networks

abstract: Stochastic fluctuations of voltage-gated ion channels generate current and voltage noise in neuronal membranes. This noise may be a criti(cid:173) cal determinant of the efficacy of information processing within neural systems. Using Monte-Carlo simulations, we carry out a systematic in(cid:173) vestigation of the relationship between channel kinetics and the result(cid:173) ing membrane voltage noise using a stochastic Markov version of the Mainen-Sejnowski model of dendritic excitability in cortical neurons. Our simulations show that kinetic parameters which lead to an increase in membrane excitability (increasing channel densities, decreasing tem(cid:173) perature) also lead to an increase in the magnitude of the sub-threshold voltage noise. Noise also increases as the membrane is depolarized from rest towards threshold. This suggests that channel fluctuations may in(cid:173) terfere with a neuron's ability to function as an integrator of its synaptic inputs and may limit the reliability and precision of neural information processing.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how random changes in voltage-gated ion channels produce fluctuations in a neuron's membrane voltage. These channels contribute to the electrical behavior of neural membranes, so their randomness may affect how reliably neurons process information. The study focuses on the relationship between channel kinetics and voltage noise below the threshold for a spike.

The authors use Monte Carlo simulations of a stochastic Markov version of the Mainen-Sejnowski model of dendritic excitability in cortical neurons. Within these simulations, changes that increase excitability, including higher channel densities and lower temperature, also increase the magnitude of subthreshold voltage noise. Noise grows as the membrane moves from its resting voltage toward the firing threshold.

These findings connect increased responsiveness with increased electrical variability in the modeled membrane. The authors suggest that channel fluctuations may interfere with a neuron's ability to integrate synaptic inputs and may constrain the precision and reliability of information processing. That functional consequence is presented as an implication of the simulations, rather than a directly established universal limit.
summary.tldr: Simulations link greater membrane excitability to stronger channel-driven voltage noise, suggesting possible limits on reliable neural integration.

title: Channel Noise in Excitable Neural Membranes

abstract: I consider a topographic projection between two neuronal layers with dif(cid:173) ferent densities of neurons. Given the number of output neurons con(cid:173) nected to each input neuron (divergence or fan-out) and the number of input neurons synapsing on each output neuron (convergence or fan-in) I determine the widths of axonal and dendritic arbors which minimize the total volume ofaxons and dendrites. My analytical results can be sum(cid:173) marized qualitatively in the following rule: neurons of the sparser layer should have arbors wider than those of the denser layer. This agrees with the anatomical data from retinal and cerebellar neurons whose morphol(cid:173) ogy and connectivity are known. The rule may be used to infer connec(cid:173) tivity of neurons from their morphology.

paragraphs: This paper asks how wide axonal and dendritic branching structures should be when two neuronal layers connect topographically and have different neuron densities. It treats the problem as one of minimizing the total volume occupied by axons and dendrites. The numbers of outputs reached by each input neuron and inputs received by each output neuron are taken as given.

Under that setup, the author analytically determines the arbor widths that minimize wiring volume. The qualitative rule is that neurons in the sparser layer should have wider arbors than neurons in the denser layer. This relates the spatial extent of neural branches to the density of the populations they connect.

The rule agrees with anatomical data from retinal and cerebellar neurons whose morphology and connectivity are known. The author also suggests that it may help infer connectivity from morphology. That potential application runs the relationship in reverse: observed branching shapes could offer clues about connections, using the volume-minimization framework and its specified connectivity constraints.
summary.tldr: Minimizing wiring volume predicts wider neuronal arbors in the sparser of two connected layers, consistent with cited anatomical observations.

title: Optimal Sizes of Dendritic and Axonal Arbors

abstract: We propose a novel probabilistic framework for semantic video in(cid:173) dexing. We define probabilistic multimedia objects (multijects) to map low-level media features to high-level semantic labels. A graphical network of such multijects (multinet) captures scene con(cid:173) text by discovering intra-frame as well as inter-frame dependency relations between the concepts. The main contribution is a novel application of a factor graph framework to model this network. We model relations between semantic concepts in terms of their co-occurrence as well as the temporal dependencies between these concepts within video shots. Using the sum-product algorithm [1] for approximate or exact inference in these factor graph multinets, we attempt to correct errors made during isolated concept detec(cid:173) tion by forcing high-level constraints. This results in a significant improvement in the overall detection performance.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic framework for assigning semantic labels to video content. Its basic units, called multijects, connect low-level media features with higher-level concepts. A network of these units, called a multinet, represents contextual relationships among concepts both within a frame and across frames.

The main technical contribution is modeling this network as a factor graph. The relationships include which concepts occur together and how concepts depend on one another over time within a video shot. This makes scene context part of the inference process, allowing evidence about one concept to affect the interpretation of another.

The authors use the sum-product algorithm for exact or approximate inference in these networks. High-level constraints are used to try to correct mistakes made when concepts are detected separately. They report a significant improvement in overall detection performance. The result supports the value of combining individual concept detections with learned spatial and temporal context when producing semantic descriptions for video indexing.
summary.tldr: Factor graphs combine concept detections with within-frame and temporal context, significantly improving overall semantic video detection performance.

title: Probabilistic Semantic Video Indexing

abstract: Spike-triggered averaging techniques are effective for linear characterization of neural responses. But neurons exhibit important nonlinear behaviors, such as gain control, that are not captured by such analyses. We describe a spike-triggered covariance method for retrieving suppressive components of the gain control signal in a neuron. We demonstrate the method in simulation and on retinal ganglion cell data. Analysis of physiological data reveals significant suppressive axes and explains neural nonlinearities. This method should be applicable to other sensory areas and modalities.
originalAbstract: Spike-triggered averaging techniques are effective for linear characterization of neural responses. But neurons exhibit important nonlinear behaviors, such as gain control, that are not captured by such analyses. We describe a spike-triggered covariance method for retrieving suppressive components of the gain control signal in a neuron. We demonstrate the method in simulation and on retinal ganglion cell data. Analysis of physiological data reveals significant suppressive axes and explains neural nonlinearities. This method should be applicable to other sensory areas and modalities.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify stimulus components that suppress a neuron's response through gain control. Spike-triggered averaging is useful for describing linear response properties, but important neural behavior is nonlinear. An analysis based only on the average stimulus associated with spikes can therefore leave aspects of response regulation unexplained.

The authors introduce a spike-triggered covariance method to retrieve suppressive components of the gain control signal. Its focus is on variation in the stimuli associated with spikes, giving the analysis a way to identify relevant components beyond those captured by averaging. This broadens the characterization of what influences a neuron from linear response features to suppressive nonlinear effects.

The method is demonstrated both in simulations and with recordings from retinal ganglion cells. In the physiological data, the analysis identifies significant suppressive directions and explains neural nonlinearities. The authors also suggest that the approach should apply to other sensory areas and modalities. That broader applicability is a proposed extension, while the reported demonstrations concern simulations and retinal data.
summary.tldr: Spike-triggered covariance reveals suppressive components of neural gain control that linear averaging methods miss.

title: Characterizing Neural Gain Control using Spike-triggered Covariance

abstract: We describe the RA scanner, a novel system for the examination of pa- tients suffering from rheumatoid arthritis. The RA scanner is based on a novel laser-based imaging technique which is sensitive to the optical characteristics of ﬁnger joint tissue. Based on the laser images, ﬁnger joints are classiﬁed according to whether the inﬂammatory status has improved or worsened. To perform the classiﬁcation task, various lin- ear and kernel-based systems were implemented and their performances were compared. Special emphasis was put on measures to reliably per- form parameter tuning and evaluation, since only a very small data set was available. Based on the results presented in this paper, it was con- cluded that the RA scanner permits a reliable classiﬁcation of patholog- ical ﬁnger joints, thus paving the way for a further development from prototype to product stage.

paragraphs: The paper describes the RA scanner, a prototype system for examining finger joints in people with rheumatoid arthritis. Its laser-based imaging technique responds to the optical characteristics of joint tissue. The task is to classify whether a joint's inflammatory status has improved or worsened using the resulting images.

The authors implement and compare several linear and kernel-based classification systems. Because the available dataset is very small, they place particular emphasis on reliable parameter tuning and evaluation. This makes the assessment procedure an important part of the work: the classification models must be evaluated carefully with the limited observations available.

Based on the reported results, the authors conclude that the scanner permits reliable classification of pathological finger joints. They interpret this as support for further development from a prototype toward a product. The evidence concerns the examined system and dataset, and the stated development goal remains a next stage rather than a claim that a finished clinical product was already established.
summary.tldr: A laser-imaging prototype classifies changes in finger-joint inflammation, with small-dataset results supporting further product development.

title: The RA Scanner: Prediction of Rheumatoid Joint Inflammation Based on Laser Imaging

abstract: Gaussian data is pervasive and many learning algorithms (e.g., k -means) model their inputs as a single sample drawn from a multivariate Gaussian. However, in many real-life settings, each input object is best described by multiple samples drawn from a multivariate Gaussian. Such data can arise, for example, in a movie review database where each movie is rated by several users, or in time-series domains such as sensor networks. Here, each input can be naturally described by both a mean vector and covariance matrix which parameterize the Gaussian distribution. In this paper, we consider the problem of clustering such input objects, each represented as a multivariate Gaussian. We formulate the problem using an information theoretic approach and draw several interesting theoretical connections to Bregman divergences and also Bregman matrix divergences. We evaluate our method across several domains, including synthetic data, sensor network data, and a statistical debugging application.

paragraphs: Some objects are naturally described by a collection of measurements rather than a single observation. A movie may have many user ratings, and a sensor may produce a time series. This paper studies clustering when each object is represented by a multivariate Gaussian distribution fitted to such repeated measurements.

Each representation contains a mean vector and a covariance matrix. The mean describes the center of the measurements, while the covariance describes their variability and relationships. Treating this whole distribution as the input lets the clustering problem retain both aspects of an object, instead of reducing its description to a single representative point.

The authors formulate clustering through an information-theoretic approach and establish connections to Bregman divergences, including their matrix versions. These connections provide a mathematical account of comparing and organizing Gaussian representations. They evaluate the method on synthetic data, sensor-network data, and a statistical debugging application. These evaluations explore the framework across several settings where distributions are meaningful descriptions of individual inputs.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic clustering method groups objects represented by Gaussian means and covariances rather than individual observations.

title: Differential Entropic Clustering of Multivariate Gaussians

abstract: We consider the ensemble clustering problem where the task is to ‘aggregate’ multiple clustering solutions into a single consolidated clustering that maximizes the shared information among given clustering solutions. We obtain several new results for this problem. First, we note that the notion of agreement under such circumstances can be better captured using an agreement measure based on a 2D string encoding rather than voting strategy based methods proposed in literature. Using this generalization, we ﬁrst derive a nonlinear optimization model to max- imize the new agreement measure. We then show that our optimization problem can be transformed into a strict 0-1 Semideﬁnite Program (SDP) via novel con- vexiﬁcation techniques which can subsequently be relaxed to a polynomial time solvable SDP. Our experiments indicate improvements not only in terms of the proposed agreement measure but also the existing agreement measures based on voting strategies. We discuss evaluations on clustering and image segmentation databases.

We obtain several new results for this problem. First, we note that the notion of agreement under such circumstances can be better captured using an agreement measure based on a 2D string encoding rather than voting strategy based methods proposed in literature. Using this generalization, we ﬁrst derive a nonlinear optimization model to max- imize the new agreement measure. We then show that our optimization problem can be transformed into a strict 0-1 Semideﬁnite Program (SDP) via novel con- vexiﬁcation techniques which can subsequently be relaxed to a polynomial time solvable SDP. The authors argue that an agreement measure based on a two-dimensional string encoding captures this relationship better than the voting-based strategies previously used for aggregation.

They first express maximization of the new agreement measure as a nonlinear optimization problem. Through convexification techniques, they transform it into an exact binary semidefinite program. They then relax the binary formulation to obtain a semidefinite program that can be solved in polynomial time. The efficient solvability claim applies to the relaxed problem, preserving the distinction between the original discrete formulation and its tractable replacement.

This is significant because the reported gains are not confined to the criterion introduced by the authors. The paper contributes both an alternative definition of agreement and an optimization route for using it.
summary.tldr: A new clustering-agreement measure and semidefinite relaxation improve ensemble aggregation under both new and existing evaluation criteria in experiments.

title: Ensemble Clustering using Semidefinite Programming

abstract: In order to represent state in controlled, partially observable, stochastic dynamical systems, some sort of sufﬁcient statistic for history is necessary. Predictive repre- sentations of state (PSRs) capture state as statistics of the future. We introduce a new model of such systems called the “Exponential family PSR,” which deﬁnes as state the time-varying parameters of an exponential family distribution which models n sequential observations in the future. This choice of state representation explicitly connects PSRs to state-of-the-art probabilistic modeling, which allows us to take advantage of current efforts in high-dimensional density estimation, and in particular, graphical models and maximum entropy models. We present a pa- rameter learning algorithm based on maximum likelihood, and we show how a variety of current approximate inference methods apply. We evaluate the qual- ity of our model with reinforcement learning by directly evaluating the control performance of the model.

paragraphs: In a controlled stochastic system with only partial observations, the current observation alone may not summarize everything useful from the past. A state representation must retain sufficient information from that history. Predictive representations of state approach this problem by describing state through statistics of future observations.

This paper introduces an exponential family predictive representation. Its state consists of changing parameters of an exponential family distribution over a sequence of n future observations. That design connects predictive state representations with probabilistic modeling tools for high-dimensional distributions, including graphical models and maximum entropy models. The representation therefore provides a route for applying those modeling techniques to dynamical systems.

The authors present maximum-likelihood parameter learning and explain how several existing approximate inference methods apply. They evaluate the model through reinforcement learning, directly examining its control performance. This evaluation ties the representation to its intended operational use: supporting decisions in a partially observed system. The contribution combines a definition of predictive state with learning and inference machinery drawn from probabilistic modeling.
summary.tldr: Exponential family predictive states connect partially observed dynamical systems to probabilistic density models, learning, and approximate inference.

title: Exponential Family Predictive Representations of State

abstract: Decision making lies at the very heart of many psychiatric diseases. It is also a central theoretical concern in a wide variety of ﬁelds and has undergone detailed, in-depth, analyses. We take as an example Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), applying insights from a Bayesian reinforcement learning framework. We focus on anhedonia and helplessness. Helplessness—a core element in the conceptual- izations of MDD that has lead to major advances in its treatment, pharmacolog- ical and neurobiological understanding—is formalized as a simple prior over the outcome entropy of actions in uncertain environments. Anhedonia, which is an equally fundamental aspect of the disease, is related to the effective reward size. These formulations allow for the design of speciﬁc tasks to measure anhedonia and helplessness behaviorally. We show that these behavioral measures capture explicit, questionnaire-based cognitions. We also provide evidence that these tasks may allow classiﬁcation of subjects into healthy and MDD groups based purely on a behavioural measure and avoiding any verbal reports. There are strong ties between decision making and psychiatry, with maladaptive decisions and be- haviors being very prominent in people with psychiatric disorders. Depression is classically seen as following life events such as divorces and job losses. Longitudinal studies, however, have revealed that a signiﬁcant fraction of the stressors associated with depression do in fact follow MDD onset, and that they are likely due to maladaptive behaviors prominent in MDD (Kendler et al., 1999). Clinically effective ’talking’ therapies for MDD such as cognitive and dialectical behavior therapies (DeRubeis et al., 1999; Bortolotti et al., 2008; Gotlib and Hammen, 2002; Power, 2005) explicitly concentrate on altering patients’ maladaptive behaviors and decision making processes. Decision making is a promising avenue into psychiatry for at least two more reasons. First, it offers powerful analytical tools. Control problems related to decision making are prevalent in a huge diversity of ﬁelds, ranging from ecology to economics, computer science and engineering. These ﬁelds have produced well-founded and thoroughly characterized frameworks within which many issues in decision making can be framed. Here, we will focus on framing issues identiﬁed in psychiatric settings within a normative decision making framework. Its second major strength comes from its relationship to neurobiology, and particularly those neuro- modulatory systems which are powerfully affected by all major clinically effective pharmacothera- pies in psychiatry. The understanding of these systems has beneﬁted signiﬁcantly from theoretical accounts of optimal control such as reinforcement learning (Montague et al., 1996; Kapur and Rem- ington, 1996; Smith et al., 1999; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Dayan and Yu, 2006). Such accounts may be useful to identify in more speciﬁc terms the roles of the neuromodulators in psychiatry (Smith et al., 2004; Williams and Dayan, 2005; Moutoussis et al., 2008; Dayan and Huys, 2008). ∗qhuys@cantab.net, joshuav@jhu.edu, dayan@gatsby.ucl.ac.uk; www.gatsby.ucl.ac.uk/∼qhuys/pub.html

title: Psychiatry: Insights into depression through normative decision-making models

abstract: Mixture of Gaussian processes models extended a single Gaussian process with ability of modeling multi-modal data and reduction of training complexity. Previous inference algorithms for these models are mostly based on Gibbs sampling, which can be very slow, particularly for large-scale data sets. We present a new generative mixture of experts model. Each expert is still a Gaussian process but is reformulated by a linear model. This breaks the dependency among training outputs and enables us to use a much faster variational Bayesian algorithm for training. Our gating network is more flexible than previous generative approaches as inputs for each expert are modeled by a Gaussian mixture model. The number of experts and number of Gaussian components for an expert are inferred automatically. A variety of tests show the advantages of our method.

paragraphs: Mixtures of Gaussian processes extend a single Gaussian process to represent multimodal data and reduce training complexity. However, inference for these mixtures has often relied on Gibbs sampling, which can be slow on large datasets. This paper proposes a generative mixture-of-experts model designed to support faster Bayesian training.

Each expert remains a Gaussian process but is expressed through a linear-model reformulation. This breaks dependence among training outputs in a way that enables a much faster variational Bayesian algorithm. The model also uses a more flexible gating mechanism: the inputs associated with each expert are modeled by a Gaussian mixture.

Both the number of experts and the number of Gaussian components assigned to an expert are inferred automatically. Thus, the proposal addresses training speed, how inputs are allocated among experts, and model size within one framework. A variety of tests demonstrate advantages of the method. The main stated benefit is a more computationally practical and flexible way to train Gaussian-process mixtures.
summary.tldr: A reformulated Gaussian-process mixture enables faster variational training with flexible gating and automatically inferred model sizes.

title: Variational Mixture of Gaussian Process Experts

abstract: Importance sampling is an essential component of off-policy model-free reinforcement learning algorithms. However, its most effective variant, \emph{weighted} importance sampling, does not carry over easily to function approximation and, because of this, it is not utilized in existing off-policy learning algorithms. In this paper, we take two steps toward bridging this gap. First, we show that weighted importance sampling can be viewed as a special case of weighting the error of individual training samples, and that this weighting has theoretical and empirical benefits similar to those of weighted importance sampling. Second, we show that these benefits extend to a new weighted-importance-sampling version of off-policy LSTD(lambda). We show empirically that our new WIS-LSTD(lambda) algorithm can result in much more rapid and reliable convergence than conventional off-policy LSTD(lambda) (Yu 2010, Bertsekas & Yu 2009).

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses experience collected under one policy to learn about another. Importance sampling helps account for this difference, but its weighted variant has been difficult to incorporate into function approximation. This paper develops a way to bring its benefits into learning with linear approximations.

The first step is to interpret weighted importance sampling as a special case of assigning weights to individual training-sample errors. This reframing connects the sampling correction to the objective used for learning from data. The authors show theoretical and empirical benefits from this error-weighting perspective that resemble those of weighted importance sampling itself.

The second step applies the idea to off-policy LSTD(lambda), producing WIS-LSTD(lambda). Empirical results show that the new algorithm can converge much faster and more reliably than conventional off-policy LSTD(lambda). The claim is a demonstrated possibility rather than a universal ordering across all problems. Together, the reformulation and algorithm provide a concrete route for using weighted importance sampling ideas when value estimates are represented by a linear function approximator.
summary.tldr: Recasting weighted importance sampling as sample-error weighting yields an off-policy LSTD variant with potentially faster, more reliable convergence.

title: Weighted importance sampling for off-policy learning with linear function approximation

abstract: In multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL), the objective is to simultaneously learn multiple tasks and exploit their similarity to improve the performance w.r.t.\ single-task learning. In this paper we investigate the case when all the tasks can be accurately represented in a linear approximation space using the same small subset of the original (large) set of features. This is equivalent to assuming that the weight vectors of the task value functions are \textit{jointly sparse}, i.e., the set of their non-zero components is small and it is shared across tasks. Building on existing results in multi-task regression, we develop two multi-task extensions of the fitted $Q$-iteration algorithm. While the first algorithm assumes that the tasks are jointly sparse in the given representation, the second one learns a transformation of the features in the attempt of finding a more sparse representation. For both algorithms we provide a sample complexity analysis and numerical simulations.

paragraphs: Multi-task reinforcement learning aims to learn several tasks together and benefit from their similarities. This paper studies a particular form of shared structure: every task's value function can be accurately represented using the same small subset of a much larger feature collection. The tasks may have different weights, but the locations of their nonzero weights are shared.

This assumption is called joint sparsity. Building on multi-task regression results, the authors develop two extensions of fitted Q-iteration. The first uses joint sparsity in the features already provided. The second learns a transformation of those features in an attempt to find a representation in which the tasks have greater shared sparsity.

The distinction matters because useful common structure may be visible in the original representation or may require changing that representation. For both algorithms, the paper supplies sample-complexity analysis and numerical simulations. The contribution is a pair of ways to exploit a specific relationship among tasks, together with analysis of their data requirements. The representation-learning method seeks a sparser description; the abstract does not claim that this search always succeeds.
summary.tldr: Two multi-task fitted Q-iteration methods exploit shared sparse features, with one also seeking a sparser learned representation.

title: Sparse Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The weighted k-nearest neighbors algorithm is one of the most fundamental non-parametric methods in pattern recognition and machine learning. The question of setting the optimal number of neighbors as well as the optimal weights has received much attention throughout the years, nevertheless this problem seems to have remained unsettled. In this paper we offer a simple approach to locally weighted regression/classification, where we make the bias-variance tradeoff explicit. Our formulation enables us to phrase a notion of optimal weights, and to efficiently find these weights as well as the optimal number of neighbors efficiently and adaptively, for each data point whose value we wish to estimate. The applicability of our approach is demonstrated on several datasets, showing superior performance over standard locally weighted methods.

paragraphs: Weighted nearest-neighbor methods estimate a value or class using nearby examples, but two choices strongly shape the prediction: how many neighbors to include and how much influence each receives. This paper addresses those choices together through a local regression and classification approach that explicitly represents the bias–variance trade-off.

The formulation defines what optimal weights mean within that trade-off and provides an efficient way to find them. It also selects the number of neighbors adaptively for each point being estimated. Thus, the neighborhood size and weighting can change across the data instead of being settled through one shared choice for every prediction.

This local adaptation matters because choosing neighbors and assigning their weights are connected decisions: changing which examples participate changes the available weighting problem. The paper offers a simple formulation that handles both within the same optimization. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate applicability and report better performance than standard locally weighted methods, providing empirical support for the proposed way of balancing local estimation errors.
summary.tldr: An explicit bias–variance formulation adaptively selects neighbor counts and weights for each regression or classification prediction.

title: k*-Nearest Neighbors: From Global to Local

abstract: We consider a learner's problem of acquiring data dynamically for training a regression model, where the training data are collected from strategic data sources. A fundamental challenge is to incentivize data holders to exert effort to improve the quality of their reported data, despite that the quality is not directly verifiable by the learner. In this work, we study a dynamic data acquisition process where data holders can contribute multiple times. Using a bandit framework, we leverage on the long-term incentive of future job opportunities to incentivize high-quality contributions. We propose a Strategic Regression-Upper Confidence Bound (SR-UCB) framework, an UCB-style index combined with a simple payment rule, where the index of a worker approximates the quality of his past contributions and is used by the learner to determine whether the worker receives future work. For linear regression and certain family of non-linear regression problems, we show that SR-UCB enables a $O(\sqrt{\log T/T})$-Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (BNE) where each worker exerting a target effort level that the learner has chosen, with $T$ being the number of data acquisition stages. The SR-UCB framework also has some other desirable properties: (1) The indexes can be updated in an online fashion (hence computationally light). (2) A slight variant, namely Private SR-UCB (PSR-UCB), is able to preserve $(O(\log^{-1} T), O(\log^{-1} T))$-differential privacy for workers' data, with only a small compromise on incentives (achieving $O(\log^{6} T/\sqrt{T})$-BNE).

paragraphs: Training a regression model can involve buying data from people who choose how much effort to invest. The learner wants accurate contributions but cannot directly verify their quality. This paper studies repeated data acquisition, where the prospect of receiving future work can encourage workers to provide better data today.

The proposed SR-UCB framework combines a bandit-style selection index with a simple payment rule. Each worker’s index approximates the quality of previous contributions and helps determine future assignments. The mechanism therefore connects present effort to future opportunities. Its indexes can be updated online, keeping the ongoing computation light.

The approximation improves as the number of acquisition stages grows. A private variant also provides differential privacy for workers’ data, with a weaker incentive guarantee. These results make repeated participation central to both the acquisition strategy and its incentive analysis.
summary.tldr: SR-UCB uses future work opportunities to encourage high-quality regression data, with approximate equilibrium guarantees and a private variant.

title: A Bandit Framework for Strategic Regression

abstract: Attempts to train a comprehensive artificial intelligence capable of solving multiple tasks have been impeded by a chronic problem called catastrophic forgetting. Although simply replaying all previous data alleviates the problem, it requires large memory and even worse, often infeasible in real world applications where the access to past data is limited. Inspired by the generative nature of the hippocampus as a short-term memory system in primate brain, we propose the Deep Generative Replay, a novel framework with a cooperative dual model architecture consisting of a deep generative model (“generator”) and a task solving model (“solver”). With only these two models, training data for previous tasks can easily be sampled and interleaved with those for a new task. We test our methods in several sequential learning settings involving image classification tasks.

paragraphs: When a model learns tasks one after another, training on the latest task can damage what it learned earlier. Replaying all past training data can alleviate this catastrophic forgetting, but storing and accessing those examples may be impractical. This paper proposes Deep Generative Replay as a way to revisit earlier tasks through generated data.

The framework pairs two cooperating models: a generator and a solver. The generator supplies samples representing previous tasks, while the solver learns to perform tasks. During training on a new task, generated samples from earlier tasks are interleaved with new examples, allowing the training process to include both past and present experience.

The approach is inspired by the generative role attributed to the hippocampus as a short-term memory system. Its practical contribution is an architecture that makes replay possible through the two learned models when access to original past data is limited. The authors test it in several sequential image-classification settings, examining this mechanism in the kind of task sequence where forgetting arises.
summary.tldr: Deep Generative Replay mixes generated examples of earlier tasks with new data to address forgetting during sequential learning.

title: Continual Learning with Deep Generative Replay

abstract: We study combinatorial multi-armed bandit with probabilistically triggered arms (CMAB-T) and semi-bandit feedback. We resolve a serious issue in the prior CMAB-T studies where the regret bounds contain a possibly exponentially large factor of 1/p*, where p* is the minimum positive probability that an arm is triggered by any action. We address this issue by introducing a triggering probability modulated (TPM) bounded smoothness condition into the influence maximization bandit and combinatorial cascading bandit satisfy this TPM condition. As a result, we completely remove the factor of 1/p* from the regret bounds, achieving significantly better regret bounds for influence maximization and cascading bandits than before. Finally, we provide lower bound results showing that the factor 1/p* is unavoidable for general CMAB-T problems, suggesting that the TPM condition is crucial in removing this factor.

We address this issue by introducing a triggering probability modulated (TPM) bounded smoothness condition into the influence maximization bandit and combinatorial cascading bandit satisfy this TPM condition. paragraphs: The paper examines combinatorial bandit problems in which an action can trigger individual arms probabilistically and the learner receives semi-bandit feedback. Earlier regret bounds included a factor of 1/p*, where p* is the smallest positive probability of triggering an arm. When that probability is tiny, the factor can become exponentially large.

The authors introduce a triggering-probability-modulated bounded smoothness condition, abbreviated TPM. This condition brings triggering probabilities into the regularity requirement used in the analysis. They show that influence maximization bandits and combinatorial cascading bandits satisfy it. Under this condition, the new regret bounds eliminate the 1/p* factor entirely, substantially improving the guarantees for those applications.

The paper also proves lower bounds showing that the same factor cannot be avoided for general problems in this class. This gives the improvement a precise scope: additional structure permits a better guarantee, while the unrestricted setting can retain the difficulty associated with rare triggering. The TPM condition therefore supplies a substantive reason why the stronger application-specific bounds are possible.
summary.tldr: A triggering-aware smoothness condition removes a potentially exponential factor from regret bounds for influence maximization and cascading bandits.

title: Improving Regret Bounds for Combinatorial Semi-Bandits with Probabilistically Triggered Arms and Its Applications

abstract: We study the resilience to Byzantine failures of distributed implementations of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). So far, distributed machine learning frameworks have largely ignored the possibility of failures, especially arbitrary (i.e., Byzantine) ones. Causes of failures include software bugs, network asynchrony, biases in local datasets, as well as attackers trying to compromise the entire system. Assuming a set of $n$ workers, up to $f$ being Byzantine, we ask how resilient can SGD be, without limiting the dimension, nor the size of the parameter space. We first show that no gradient aggregation rule based on a linear combination of the vectors proposed by the workers (i.e, current approaches) tolerates a single Byzantine failure. We then formulate a resilience property of the aggregation rule capturing the basic requirements to guarantee convergence despite $f$ Byzantine workers. We propose \emph{Krum}, an aggregation rule that satisfies our resilience property, which we argue is the first provably Byzantine-resilient algorithm for distributed SGD. We also report on experimental evaluations of Krum.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent combines updates proposed by multiple workers. This paper asks what happens when some workers behave arbitrarily, a failure model called Byzantine behavior. Such behavior can arise from bugs, asynchronous communication, biased local data, or deliberate attempts to disrupt learning.

The authors consider a population of workers with up to a specified number behaving this way, without restricting parameter-space size or dimension. They first show that aggregation based on a linear combination of submitted vectors cannot tolerate even one Byzantine worker in their setting. This identifies a fundamental weakness in the aggregation step used by the approaches under discussion.

The paper then formulates a resilience property capturing requirements for convergence despite faulty workers and introduces Krum, an aggregation rule satisfying that property. The authors argue that it provides the first provably Byzantine-resilient algorithm for distributed SGD and also report experimental evaluations. The contribution links a failure result for linear aggregation to a constructive rule with a formal resilience guarantee.
summary.tldr: Krum provides a formally resilient gradient aggregation rule for distributed SGD with Byzantine workers.

title: Machine Learning with Adversaries: Byzantine Tolerant Gradient Descent

abstract: The large communication overhead has imposed a bottleneck on the performance of distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for training deep neural networks. Previous works have demonstrated the potential of using gradient sparsification and quantization to reduce the communication cost. However, there is still a lack of understanding about how sparse and quantized communication affects the convergence rate of the training algorithm. In this paper, we study the convergence rate of distributed SGD for non-convex optimization with two communication reducing strategies: sparse parameter averaging and gradient quantization. We show that $O(1/\sqrt{MK})$ convergence rate can be achieved if the sparsification and quantization hyperparameters are configured properly. We also propose a strategy called periodic quantized averaging (PQASGD) that further reduces the communication cost while preserving the $O(1/\sqrt{MK})$ convergence rate. Our evaluation validates our theoretical results and shows that our PQASGD can converge as fast as full-communication SGD with only $3\%-5\%$ communication data size.

This paper analyzes that tradeoff for distributed stochastic gradient descent on nonconvex optimization problems.

The authors study sparse parameter averaging and gradient quantization. They show that a convergence rate of O(1/√(MK)) remains achievable when the sparsification and quantization settings are chosen appropriately. This connects the convergence analysis to a practical reduction in communication volume. The contribution is both a justification for reducing communication and a particular strategy that demonstrates the benefit empirically.
summary.tldr: Properly configured sparse and quantized communication preserves a favorable distributed SGD convergence rate, with PQASGD demonstrating substantial communication savings.

title: A Linear Speedup Analysis of Distributed Deep Learning with Sparse and Quantized Communication

abstract: Representations of data that are invariant to changes in specified factors are useful for a wide range of problems: removing potential biases in prediction problems, controlling the effects of covariates, and disentangling meaningful factors of variation. Unfortunately, learning representations that exhibit invariance to arbitrary nuisance factors yet remain useful for other tasks is challenging. Existing approaches cast the trade-off between task performance and invariance in an adversarial way, using an iterative minimax optimization. We show that adversarial training is unnecessary and sometimes counter-productive; we instead cast invariant representation learning as a single information-theoretic objective that can be directly optimized. We demonstrate that this approach matches or exceeds performance of state-of-the-art adversarial approaches for learning fair representations and for generative modeling with controllable transformations.

The paper argues that this adversarial arrangement is unnecessary and can sometimes be counterproductive. It instead expresses invariant representation learning as a single information-theoretic objective that can be optimized directly, giving an alternative formulation of the same underlying goal.

The authors demonstrate the approach on fair representation learning and generative modeling with controllable transformations. In these settings, it matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art adversarial approaches. The results support direct information-theoretic optimization as a viable way to learn useful invariant representations, without turning the qualified observation about adversarial training into a claim that it is always harmful.
summary.tldr: A directly optimized information-theoretic objective learns invariant representations with performance matching or exceeding adversarial methods in the reported tasks.

title: Invariant Representations without Adversarial Training

abstract: We consider the problem of computing the best-fitting ReLU with respect to square-loss on a training set when the examples have been drawn according to a spherical Gaussian distribution (the labels can be arbitrary). Let $\opt < 1$ be the population loss of the best-fitting ReLU. We prove: \begin{itemize} \item Finding a ReLU with square-loss $\opt + \epsilon$ is as hard as the problem of learning sparse parities with noise, widely thought to be computationally intractable. This is the first hardness result for learning a ReLU with respect to Gaussian marginals, and our results imply --{\em unconditionally}-- that gradient descent cannot converge to the global minimum in polynomial time. \item There exists an efficient approximation algorithm for finding the best-fitting ReLU that achieves error $O(\opt^{2/3})$. The algorithm uses a novel reduction to noisy halfspace learning with respect to $0/1$ loss. \end{itemize} Prior work due to Soltanolkotabi \cite{soltanolkotabi2017learning} showed that gradient descent {\em can} find the best-fitting ReLU with respect to Gaussian marginals, if the training set is {\em exactly} labeled by a ReLU.

paragraphs: This paper studies fitting a single ReLU using squared loss when inputs follow a spherical Gaussian distribution but labels may be arbitrary. That label freedom is crucial: it differs from the setting where a ReLU generates every label exactly. The authors examine how closely an efficient algorithm can approach the best achievable population loss.

Writing that optimal loss as opt, with opt below one, they show that achieving loss opt plus epsilon is as hard as learning sparse parities with noise, a problem widely believed computationally intractable. They also derive an unconditional implication that gradient descent cannot generally reach the global minimum in polynomial time in this setting.

The paper balances this hardness result with an efficient approximation algorithm achieving error of order opt to the two-thirds power. Its method reduces the problem to noisy halfspace learning under zero-one loss. Together, the results distinguish highly accurate fitting from efficiently attainable approximation, and clarify why guarantees for exactly ReLU-labeled Gaussian data do not extend automatically to arbitrary labels.
summary.tldr: With Gaussian inputs and arbitrary labels, near-optimal ReLU fitting faces computational hardness, while a weaker approximation is efficiently achievable.

title: Time/Accuracy Tradeoffs for Learning a ReLU with respect to Gaussian Marginals

abstract: Current state-of-the-art models for video action recognition are mostly based on expensive 3D ConvNets. This results in a need for large GPU clusters to train and evaluate such architectures. To address this problem, we present an lightweight and memory-friendly architecture for action recognition that performs on par with or better than current architectures by using only a fraction of resources. The proposed architecture is based on a combination of a deep subnet operating on low-resolution frames with a compact subnet operating on high-resolution frames, allowing for high efficiency and accuracy at the same time. We demonstrate that our approach achieves a reduction by 3~4 times in FLOPs and ~2 times in memory usage compared to the baseline. This enables training deeper models with more input frames under the same computational budget. To further obviate the need for large-scale 3D convolutions, a temporal aggregation module is proposed to model temporal dependencies in a video at very small additional computational costs. Our models achieve strong performance on several action recognition benchmarks including Kinetics, Something-Something and Moments-in-time. The code and models are available at \url{https://github.com/IBM/bLVNet-TAM}.

paragraphs: Video action recognition often uses expensive three-dimensional convolutional networks, making computation and memory major constraints. This paper proposes a lighter architecture that distributes work between two subnetworks: a deep network processes low-resolution frames, while a compact network processes high-resolution frames. The combination aims to retain recognition accuracy while reducing the cost of processing detailed video input.

Compared with the baseline, the authors report roughly three- to four-fold fewer floating-point operations and about half the memory use. These savings allow deeper models and more input frames within the same computational budget. The design therefore changes how available resources can be spent, providing room for additional depth and video input instead of using the full budget on expensive frame processing.

The models report strong results on Kinetics, Something-Something, and Moments-in-time, with performance matching or exceeding current architectures. Together, the findings support combining unequal subnetworks and lightweight temporal modeling for efficient action recognition.
summary.tldr: A dual-resolution video network with lightweight temporal aggregation maintains strong action recognition while substantially reducing computation and memory.

title: More Is Less: Learning Efficient Video Representations by Big-Little Network and Depthwise Temporal Aggregation

abstract: A disentangled representation encodes information about the salient factors of variation in the data independently. Although it is often argued that this representational format is useful in learning to solve many real-world down-stream tasks, there is little empirical evidence that supports this claim. In this paper, we conduct a large-scale study that investigates whether disentangled representations are more suitable for abstract reasoning tasks. Using two new tasks similar to Raven's Progressive Matrices, we evaluate the usefulness of the representations learned by 360 state-of-the-art unsupervised disentanglement models. Based on these representations, we train 3600 abstract reasoning models and observe that disentangled representations do in fact lead to better down-stream performance. In particular, they enable quicker learning using fewer samples.

This paper examines that benefit empirically for abstract visual reasoning, addressing the gap between a frequently stated motivation for disentanglement and evidence that it helps a downstream task.

The authors introduce two reasoning tasks resembling Raven's Progressive Matrices. They evaluate representations produced by 360 unsupervised disentanglement models, then train 3,600 reasoning models using those representations. This separates the learning of a representation from the subsequent task of learning to reason with it, making downstream usefulness the central outcome of the study.

Across this study, disentangled representations lead to better reasoning performance. In particular, the reasoning models learn more quickly and require fewer examples. These findings support the usefulness of independently represented factors in the tested reasoning settings. The contribution is empirical evidence about learning efficiency and task performance, with the scale of the study extending the comparison beyond a single representation model.
summary.tldr: A large empirical study finds that disentangled representations improve abstract visual reasoning performance and help models learn from fewer examples.

title: Are Disentangled Representations Helpful for Abstract Visual Reasoning?

abstract: We introduce an approach to training a given compact network. To this end, we leverage over-parameterization, which typically improves both neural network optimization and generalization. Specifically, we propose to expand each linear layer of the compact network into multiple consecutive linear layers, without adding any nonlinearity. As such, the resulting expanded network, or ExpandNet, can be contracted back to the compact one algebraically at inference. In particular, we introduce two convolutional expansion strategies and demonstrate their benefits on several tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. As evidenced by our experiments, our approach outperforms both training the compact network from scratch and performing knowledge distillation from a teacher. Furthermore, our linear over-parameterization empirically reduces gradient confusion during training and improves the network generalization.

paragraphs: Overparameterization can make neural networks easier to optimize, but a deployed model may need to remain compact. This paper proposes training a larger parameterization of the desired compact network while preserving the ability to recover the original network form at inference.

Each linear layer is expanded into multiple consecutive linear layers without inserting nonlinearities. Because the composition remains linear, it can be contracted algebraically after training. The authors introduce two convolutional expansion strategies and evaluate them in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

Experiments outperform both direct training of the compact network and knowledge distillation from a teacher. Additional observations show reduced gradient confusion during training and improved generalization. The abstract gives no numerical gains or training-cost comparison. The distinctive result is that training can benefit from extra parameters while inference uses the contracted compact architecture.
summary.tldr: ExpandNets train compact networks through temporary linear expansion that can be algebraically removed.

title: ExpandNets: Linear Over-parameterization to Train Compact Convolutional Networks

abstract: Understanding the behavior of no-regret dynamics in general N-player games is a fundamental question in online learning and game theory. A folk result in the field states that, in finite games, the empirical frequency of play under no-regret learning converges to the game’s set of coarse correlated equilibria. By contrast, our understanding of how the day-to-day behavior of the dynamics correlates to the game’s Nash equilibria is much more limited, and only partial results are known for certain classes of games (such as zero-sum or congestion games). In this paper, we study the dynamics of follow the regularized leader (FTRL), arguably the most well-studied class of no-regret dynamics, and we establish a sweeping negative result showing that the notion of mixed Nash equilibrium is antithetical to no-regret learning. Specifically, we show that any Nash equilibrium which is not strict (in that every player has a unique best response) cannot be stable and attracting under the dynamics of FTRL. This result has significant implications for predicting the outcome of a learning process as it shows unequivocally that only strict (and hence, pure) Nash equilibria can emerge as stable limit points thereof.

paragraphs: No-regret learning has a known connection to the long-run frequency of actions in finite games: those frequencies approach the set of coarse correlated equilibria. That statement leaves a different question open. It does not establish whether players’ actual, day-to-day strategies settle near a Nash equilibrium.

This paper studies that question for follow the regularized leader, or FTRL, a widely studied family of no-regret learning dynamics. The authors prove that a Nash equilibrium cannot be both stable and attracting under FTRL unless it is strict. Strictness means that each player has a unique best response at the equilibrium.

Because strict Nash equilibria are pure, the result rules out mixed Nash equilibria as stable attracting outcomes of these dynamics. The conclusion concerns which equilibria can serve as stable limiting behavior; it does not assert that learning always converges to a strict equilibrium. This distinction matters when using equilibrium concepts to predict the outcome of repeated learning: guarantees about aggregate frequencies do not supply the same prediction as guarantees about the evolving strategies themselves.
summary.tldr: Under FTRL dynamics, only strict, and therefore pure, Nash equilibria can be stable attracting limits.

title: No-Regret Learning and Mixed Nash Equilibria: They Do Not Mix

abstract: In this paper, we propose the first continuous optimization algorithms that achieve a constant factor approximation guarantee for the problem of monotone continuous submodular maximization subject to a linear constraint. We first prove that a simple variant of the vanilla coordinate ascent, called \COORDINATE-ASCENT+, achieves a $(\frac{e-1}{2e-1}-\eps)$-approximation guarantee while performing $O(n/\epsilon)$ iterations, where the computational complexity of each iteration is roughly $O(n/\sqrt{\epsilon}+n\log n)$ (here, $n$ denotes the dimension of the optimization problem). We then propose \COORDINATE-ASCENT++, that achieves the tight $(1-1/e-\eps)$-approximation guarantee while performing the same number of iterations, but at a higher computational complexity of roughly $O(n^3/\eps^{2.5} + n^3 \log n / \eps^2)$ per iteration. However, the computation of each round of \COORDINATE-ASCENT++ can be easily parallelized so that the computational cost per machine scales as $O(n/\sqrt{\epsilon}+n\log n)$.

The goal is to obtain a guaranteed fraction of the best achievable objective value. The authors present the first continuous optimization algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for this setting, extending the scope indicated by the paper’s focus beyond DR-submodularity.

The first method, COORDINATE-ASCENT+, modifies ordinary coordinate ascent. It guarantees an approximation factor of (e−1)/(2e−1) minus epsilon and uses O(n/epsilon) iterations, where n is the problem dimension. The results make explicit a trade-off between approximation quality and computation, including how parallel execution can distribute the more demanding method’s work.
summary.tldr: Two coordinate-ascent algorithms provide constant-factor guarantees for constrained continuous submodular maximization, trading more computation for a tight approximation.

title: Continuous Submodular Maximization: Beyond DR-Submodularity

abstract: Boosting is one of the most successful ideas in machine learning, achieving great practical performance with little fine-tuning. The success of boosted classifiers is most often attributed to improvements in margins. The focus on margin explanations was pioneered in the seminal work by Schaphire et al. (1998) and has culminated in the $k$'th margin generalization bound by Gao and Zhou (2013), which was recently proved to be near-tight for some data distributions (Gr\o nlund et al. 2019). In this work, we first demonstrate that the $k$'th margin bound is inadequate in explaining the performance of state-of-the-art gradient boosters. We then explain the short comings of the $k$'th margin bound and prove a stronger and more refined margin-based generalization bound that indeed succeeds in explaining the performance of modern gradient boosters. Finally, we improve upon the recent generalization lower bound by Gr\o nlund et al. (2019).

paragraphs: Boosted classifiers often work well with relatively little fine-tuning, and their success is commonly explained through margins. A generalization bound connects properties of a trained classifier to expectations about performance beyond its training data. This paper examines whether an influential margin-based bound actually explains the behavior of modern gradient boosting methods.

The authors show that the existing kth-margin bound is inadequate for explaining the performance of state-of-the-art gradient boosters. This is significant because that bound had been shown to be nearly tight for some data distributions. Being difficult to improve in certain cases does not by itself make a bound an adequate account of the methods performing well in practice.

The paper analyzes the shortcomings and proves a stronger, more refined margin-based generalization bound that does explain the performance under study. It also improves an existing generalization lower bound. The contribution therefore refines the mathematical explanation of boosting: the inadequacy of the earlier margin account leads to a more informative margin-based analysis, rather than abandoning that analytical framework.
summary.tldr: The paper shows why an existing margin bound fails to explain modern gradient boosting and proves a stronger, more informative bound.

title: Margins are Insufficient for Explaining Gradient Boosting

abstract: The existence of simple, uncoupled no-regret dynamics that converge to correlated equilibria in normal-form games is a celebrated result in the theory of multi-agent systems. Specifically, it has been known for more than 20 years that when all players seek to minimize their internal regret in a repeated normal-form game, the empirical frequency of play converges to a normal-form correlated equilibrium. Extensive-form (that is, tree-form) games generalize normal-form games by modeling both sequential and simultaneous moves, as well as private information. Because of the sequential nature and presence of partial information in the game, extensive-form correlation has significantly different properties than the normal-form counterpart, many of which are still open research directions. Extensive-form correlated equilibrium (EFCE) has been proposed as the natural extensive-form counterpart to normal-form correlated equilibrium. However, it was currently unknown whether EFCE emerges as the result of uncoupled agent dynamics. In this paper, we give the first uncoupled no-regret dynamics that converge to the set of EFCEs in n-player general-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall. First, we introduce a notion of trigger regret in extensive-form games, which extends that of internal regret in normal-form games. When each player has low trigger regret, the empirical frequency of play is a close to an EFCE. Then, we give an efficient no-trigger-regret algorithm. Our algorithm decomposes trigger regret into local subproblems at each decision point for the player, and constructs a global strategy of the player from the local solutions at each decision point.

This paper asks whether a corresponding result holds in extensive-form games, which represent sequential decisions, simultaneous moves, and private information. These features make correlation more complicated than in the normal-form setting.
