They show that when every player has low trigger regret, the empirical frequency of play is close to an extensive-form correlated equilibrium. They then construct an efficient algorithm that reduces trigger regret by decomposing it into local problems at each of a player’s decision points.

The local solutions are assembled into a global strategy, yielding uncoupled no-regret dynamics that converge to the set of extensive-form correlated equilibria. The result applies to n-player general-sum games with perfect recall. It establishes a learning-based route to this equilibrium concept under that assumption, connecting individually controlled local updates to a collective property of repeated play.
summary.tldr: Trigger-regret minimization yields efficient uncoupled learning dynamics converging to extensive-form correlated equilibria in games with perfect recall.

title: No-Regret Learning Dynamics for Extensive-Form Correlated Equilibrium

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular framework for optimizing black-box functions. In many applications, the objective function can be evaluated at multiple fidelities to enable a trade-off between the cost and accuracy. To reduce the optimization cost, many multi-fidelity BO methods have been proposed. Despite their success, these methods either ignore or over-simplify the strong, complex correlations across the fidelities. While the acquisition function is therefore easy and convenient to calculate, these methods can be inefficient in estimating the objective function. To address this issue, we propose Deep Neural Network Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization (DNN-MFBO) that can flexibly capture all kinds of complicated relationships between the fidelities to improve the objective function estimation and hence the optimization performance. We use sequential, fidelity-wise Gauss-Hermite quadrature and moment-matching to compute a mutual information-based acquisition function in a tractable and highly efficient way. We show the advantages of our method in both synthetic benchmark datasets and real-world applications in engineering design.

We show the advantages of our method in both synthetic benchmark datasets and real-world applications in engineering design.

paragraphs: Some expensive optimization problems allow several versions of an evaluation, trading accuracy against cost. Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization tries to use those alternatives to reduce the expense of finding a good solution. Its effectiveness depends partly on understanding how results at different fidelities relate to one another.

The authors argue that existing methods often ignore or simplify these relationships too aggressively. DNN-MFBO uses deep neural networks to model complex connections across fidelities more flexibly. Better modeling is intended to improve estimates of the objective function, so information obtained from one evaluation level can more effectively guide the overall search.

A flexible model also makes deciding what to evaluate next more demanding. The paper addresses this with sequential, fidelity-wise Gauss-Hermite quadrature and moment matching to compute a mutual-information-based acquisition function efficiently. This combines richer modeling with a tractable selection procedure. Results on synthetic benchmarks and engineering design applications demonstrate advantages for the proposed method, supporting the value of representing cross-fidelity relationships without making the optimization decision prohibitively expensive.
summary.tldr: DNN-MFBO models complex relationships between evaluation fidelities and efficiently computes an information-based rule for choosing evaluations.

title: Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization via Deep Neural Networks

abstract: In this work, we propose TGLS, a novel framework for unsupervised Text Generation by Learning from Search. We start by applying a strong search algorithm (in particular, simulated annealing) towards a heuristically defined objective that (roughly) estimates the quality of sentences. Then, a conditional generative model learns from the search results, and meanwhile smooth out the noise of search. The alternation between search and learning can be repeated for performance bootstrapping. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TGLS on two real-world natural language generation tasks, unsupervised paraphrasing and text formalization. Our model significantly outperforms unsupervised baseline methods in both tasks. Especially, it achieves comparable performance to strong supervised methods for paraphrase generation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to train a text generator by first searching for useful outputs. The learning stage also smooths noise in the search results. Search and learning can then alternate, allowing the process to bootstrap performance through repeated rounds. The two stages have complementary roles: search seeks sentences favored by the quality objective, while the generative model learns from those sentences and reduces the influence of their noise.

It significantly outperforms the unsupervised baselines in both tasks and reaches performance comparable to strong supervised methods for paraphrase generation. These results support search-generated training material as a useful basis for unsupervised generation. The supervised comparison applies specifically to paraphrasing, while the reported advantage over unsupervised alternatives covers both evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Alternating heuristic search with generative-model learning improves unsupervised paraphrasing and formalization, with paraphrasing performance comparable to strong supervised methods.

title: Unsupervised Text Generation by Learning from Search

abstract: In clustering problems, a central decision-maker is given a complete metric graph over vertices and must provide a clustering of vertices that minimizes some objective function. In fair clustering problems, vertices are endowed with a color (e.g., membership in a group), and the requirements of a valid clustering might also include the representation of colors in the solution. Prior work in fair clustering assumes complete knowledge of group membership. In this paper, we generalize this by assuming imperfect knowledge of group membership through probabilistic assignments, and present algorithms in this more general setting with approximation ratio guarantees. We also address the problem of "metric membership", where group membership has a notion of order and distance. Experiments are conducted using our proposed algorithms as well as baselines to validate our approach, and also surface nuanced concerns when group membership is not known deterministically.

paragraphs: Clustering groups points while minimizing an objective based on distances between them. Fair clustering adds requirements about the representation of groups within the solution. Earlier work described in the abstract assumes each point's group membership is fully known, an assumption this paper replaces with probabilistic assignments.

The authors develop algorithms for this more general setting and provide approximation-ratio guarantees. These guarantees address the quality of the clustering solution relative to its optimization objective while working within the probabilistic formulation. The paper also considers metric membership, where group membership carries an ordering and distances rather than being only a categorical label.

The contribution is to make uncertainty about group membership an explicit part of fair clustering. This matters because representation requirements must then be interpreted alongside probabilistic information, rather than relying on the complete membership knowledge assumed in the earlier setting.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic fair clustering handles uncertain group membership with approximation guarantees and also considers memberships with order and distance.

title: Probabilistic Fair Clustering

abstract: Recent semantic segmentation methods model the relationship between pixels to construct the contextual representations. In this paper, we introduce the \emph{Region Attention Network} (RANet), a novel attention network for modeling the relationship between object regions. RANet divides the image into object regions, where we select the representative information. In contrast to the previous methods, RANet configures the information pathways between the pixels in different regions, enabling the region interaction to exchange the regional context for enhancing all of the pixels in the image. We train the construction of object regions, the selection of the representative regional contents, the configuration of information pathways and the context exchange between pixels, jointly, to improve the segmentation accuracy. We extensively evaluate our method on the challenging segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating that RANet effectively helps to achieve the state-of-the-art results. Code will be available at: \url{https://github.com/dingguo1996/RANet}.

RANet organizes this context around relationships between object regions. The approach divides an image into regions and selects representative information from each, giving the network regional content to exchange across the image.

The network configures pathways between pixels in different regions so that regional interactions can enrich pixel representations. Region construction, representative-content selection, pathway configuration, and context exchange are trained jointly. These components therefore form one learned segmentation system, with the regional organization and the use of its information optimized together.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging segmentation benchmarks and report that RANet helps achieve state-of-the-art results. The stated findings support region-level interaction as an effective way to build context for pixel-level prediction. The central contribution is the coordinated design: regions provide representative content, learned connections determine where that content travels, and exchanges between regions enhance information available to pixels. This connects object-region organization directly to the final task of assigning labels throughout an image.
summary.tldr: RANet jointly learns object regions and information exchange between them to improve pixel-level semantic segmentation.

title: RANet: Region Attention Network for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Photo-realistic free-viewpoint rendering of real-world scenes using classical computer graphics techniques is challenging, because it requires the difficult step of capturing detailed appearance and geometry models. Recent studies have demonstrated promising results by learning scene representations that implicitly encodes both geometry and appearance without 3D supervision. However, existing approaches in practice often show blurry renderings caused by the limited network capacity or the difficulty in finding accurate intersections of camera rays with the scene geometry. Synthesizing high-resolution imagery from these representations often requires time-consuming optical ray marching. In this work, we introduce Neural Sparse Voxel Fields (NSVF), a new neural scene representation for fast and high-quality free-viewpoint rendering. The NSVF defines a series of voxel-bounded implicit fields organized in a sparse voxel octree to model local properties in each cell. We progressively learn the underlying voxel structures with a differentiable ray-marching operation from only a set of posed RGB images. With the sparse voxel octree structure, rendering novel views at inference time can be accelerated by skipping the voxels without relevant scene content. Our method is over 10 times faster than the state-of-the-art while achieving higher quality results. Furthermore, by utilizing an explicit sparse voxel representation, our method can be easily applied to scene editing and scene composition. we also demonstrate various kinds of challenging tasks, including multi-object learning, free-viewpoint rendering of a moving human, and large-scale scene rendering.

paragraphs: Neural Sparse Voxel Fields address the cost and quality of rendering a scene from new viewpoints. Earlier implicit scene representations can produce blurry images and require expensive ray marching. NSVF divides the representation into local implicit fields bounded by voxels, organized in a sparse octree.

The system progressively learns the voxel structure using differentiable ray marching from RGB images with known camera poses. It therefore learns the scene without requiring direct 3D supervision. Demonstrations include learning multiple objects, rendering a moving human from different viewpoints, and handling large scenes. These results connect local neural representations with spatial structure that is useful both for rendering efficiency and for manipulating scenes.
summary.tldr: NSVF learns local neural fields in a sparse voxel structure, accelerating novel-view rendering by skipping space without relevant content.

title: Neural Sparse Voxel Fields

abstract: We develop two methods for the following fundamental statistical task: given an $\eps$-corrupted set of $n$ samples from a $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distribution, return an approximate top eigenvector of the covariance matrix. Our first robust PCA algorithm runs in polynomial time, returns a $1 - O(\eps\log\eps^{-1})$-approximate top eigenvector, and is based on a simple iterative filtering approach. Our second, which attains a slightly worse approximation factor, runs in nearly-linear time and sample complexity under a mild spectral gap assumption. These are the first polynomial-time algorithms yielding non-trivial information about the covariance of a corrupted sub-Gaussian distribution without requiring additional algebraic structure of moments. As a key technical tool, we develop the first width-independent solvers for Schatten-$p$ norm packing semidefinite programs, giving a $(1 + \eps)$-approximate solution in $O(p\log(\tfrac{nd}{\eps})\eps^{-1})$ input-sparsity time iterations (where $n$, $d$ are problem dimensions).

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a leading covariance direction when a fraction of the samples has been corrupted. The uncorrupted data comes from a sub-Gaussian distribution. The goal is an approximate top eigenvector, giving useful information about the covariance despite the contaminated observations.

The authors provide two algorithms with different tradeoffs. An iterative filtering method runs in polynomial time and obtains an approximation factor of 1 minus a term of order epsilon times log(1/epsilon). A second method achieves a slightly weaker approximation but uses nearly linear time and sample complexity under a mild spectral-gap assumption.

The authors identify these as the first polynomial-time methods obtaining nontrivial covariance information in this setting without additional algebraic structure in the moments. A key technical contribution is a family of width-independent solvers for Schatten-p packing semidefinite programs. Those solvers provide approximate solutions using input-sparsity-time iterations, linking the robust statistical guarantees to advances in the efficiency of the underlying matrix optimization.
summary.tldr: Two robust PCA algorithms estimate leading covariance directions from corrupted sub-Gaussian samples, with a faster method requiring a mild spectral gap.

title: Robust Sub-Gaussian Principal Component Analysis and Width-Independent Schatten Packing

abstract: We consider the task of decentralized minimization of the sum of smooth strongly convex functions stored across the nodes of a network. For this problem, lower bounds on the number of gradient computations and the number of communication rounds required to achieve $\varepsilon$ accuracy have recently been proven. We propose two new algorithms for this decentralized optimization problem and equip them with complexity guarantees. We show that our first method is optimal both in terms of the number of communication rounds and in terms of the number of gradient computations. Unlike existing optimal algorithms, our algorithm does not rely on the expensive evaluation of dual gradients. Our second algorithm is optimal in terms of the number of communication rounds, without a logarithmic factor. Our approach relies on viewing the two proposed algorithms as accelerated variants of the Forward Backward algorithm to solve monotone inclusions associated with the decentralized optimization problem. We also verify the efficacy of our methods against state-of-the-art algorithms through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The paper considers minimizing a sum of functions stored across a network, with each function assumed smooth and strongly convex. Efficiency has two dimensions: the number of gradient computations and the number of communication rounds needed to reach a desired accuracy. Existing lower bounds describe the best achievable requirements for these resources.

The authors propose two algorithms with complexity guarantees. The first is optimal in both gradient computations and communication rounds. It also avoids expensive dual-gradient evaluations required by existing optimal algorithms, addressing a practical cost alongside the theoretical counts. The second achieves optimal communication complexity without a logarithmic factor.

Both methods are developed by viewing decentralized optimization through associated monotone inclusions and accelerating a Forward Backward algorithm for solving them. This supplies a shared mathematical basis for the two designs. Numerical experiments compare the methods with leading alternatives and verify their efficacy. The results combine optimal resource guarantees under the stated smoothness and strong-convexity assumptions with attention to the operations those guarantees require.
summary.tldr: Two decentralized optimization algorithms achieve optimal complexity guarantees, including one optimal in both communication and gradient computations without dual-gradient evaluations.

title: Optimal and Practical Algorithms for Smooth and Strongly Convex Decentralized Optimization

abstract: In forming learning objectives, one oftentimes needs to aggregate a set of individual values to a single output. Such cases occur in the aggregate loss, which combines individual losses of a learning model over each training sample, and in the individual loss for multi-label learning, which combines prediction scores over all class labels. In this work, we introduce the sum of ranked range (SoRR) as a general approach to form learning objectives. A ranked range is a consecutive sequence of sorted values of a set of real numbers. The minimization of SoRR is solved with the difference of convex algorithm (DCA). We explore two applications in machine learning of the minimization of the SoRR framework, namely the AoRR aggregate loss for binary classification and the TKML individual loss for multi-label/multi-class classification. Our empirical results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed optimization framework and demonstrate the applicability of proposed losses using synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Learning objectives often reduce many numbers to one value. A model may combine losses across training examples or combine prediction scores across labels. This paper introduces the sum of ranked range as a general way to perform that aggregation, making the ordering of values part of how the objective is constructed.

The procedure sorts a set of real numbers and sums a consecutive portion of the resulting sequence. A ranked range therefore specifies which positions in the ordering contribute to the objective. The authors solve the resulting minimization problem using the difference of convex algorithm, providing an optimization approach alongside the proposed form of aggregation.

The paper develops two applications: an AoRR aggregate loss for binary classification and a TKML individual loss for multi-label or multi-class classification. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the applicability of these losses and the effectiveness of the optimization framework. The shared contribution is a way to formulate objectives at two different levels, across examples and across labels, using the same ranked-range principle.
summary.tldr: The sum of ranked range builds learning objectives by aggregating consecutive portions of sorted losses or scores.

title: Learning by Minimizing the Sum of Ranked Range

abstract: Continuous-time event data are common in applications such as individual behavior data, financial transactions, and medical health records. Modeling such data can be very challenging, in particular for applications with many different types of events,since it requires a model to predict the event types as well as the time of occurrence. Recurrent neural networks that parameterize time-varying intensity functions are the current state-of-the-art for predictive modeling with such data. These models typically assume that all event sequences come from the same data distribution. However, in many applications event sequences are generated by different sources,or users, and their characteristics can be very different. In this paper, we extend the broad class of neural marked point process models to mixtures of latent embeddings,where each mixture component models the characteristic traits of a given user. Our approach relies on augmenting these models with a latent variable that encodes user characteristics, represented by a mixture model over user behavior that is trained via amortized variational inference. We evaluate our methods on four large real-world datasets and demonstrate systematic improvements from our approach over existing work for a variety of predictive metrics such as log-likelihood, next event ranking, and source-of-sequence identification.

paragraphs: Continuous-time event prediction must determine both what happens next and when it happens. Such sequences appear in behavioral records, transactions, and medical data. Existing neural models commonly treat all sequences as coming from the same distribution, although different users or sources can exhibit substantially different behavior.

This paper extends neural marked point process models with a latent variable encoding user characteristics. A mixture of latent embeddings represents variation in user behavior, with mixture components modeling characteristic traits. The model is trained through amortized variational inference, providing a learned inference mechanism for the latent representation within the event-sequence framework.

Evaluation on four large real-world datasets shows systematic improvements over existing work across several predictive measures. These include log-likelihood, ranking the next event, and identifying a sequence’s source. The range of improvements suggests that representing user differences benefits both event prediction and recognition of who generated a sequence. The contribution makes source-dependent variation part of the model rather than relying on a single shared distribution to explain all observed event histories.
summary.tldr: Latent user embeddings improve neural continuous-time event models by explicitly representing differences between the sources of event sequences.

title: User-Dependent Neural Sequence Models for Continuous-Time Event Data

abstract: We provide a detailed asymptotic study of gradient flow trajectories and their implicit optimization bias when minimizing the exponential loss over "diagonal linear networks". This is the simplest model displaying a transition between "kernel" and non-kernel ("rich" or "active") regimes. We show how the transition is controlled by the relationship between the initialization scale and how accurately we minimize the training loss. Our results indicate that some limit behavior of gradient descent only kick in at ridiculous training accuracies (well beyond 10^-100). Moreover, the implicit bias at reasonable initialization scales and training accuracies is more complex and not captured by these limits.
originalAbstract: We provide a detailed asymptotic study of gradient flow trajectories and their implicit optimization bias when minimizing the exponential loss over "diagonal linear networks". This is the simplest model displaying a transition between "kernel" and non-kernel ("rich" or "active") regimes. We show how the transition is controlled by the relationship between the initialization scale and how accurately we minimize the training loss. Our results indicate that some limit behavior of gradient descent only kick in at ridiculous training accuracies (well beyond 10^-100). Moreover, the implicit bias at reasonable initialization scales and training accuracies is more complex and not captured by these limits.

paragraphs: Training can favor particular solutions even without an explicit penalty specifying those preferences. This paper studies that implicit optimization bias in diagonal linear networks trained with exponential loss. The model provides a simple setting that still exhibits a transition between kernel behavior and a richer, active learning regime.

The analysis follows gradient-flow trajectories asymptotically and identifies a relationship between initialization scale and how far training reduces the loss. These two factors jointly control the transition between regimes. Consequently, a characterization based only on initialization or only on extremely accurate training can miss how their interaction shapes the selected solution.

The authors find that some limiting behavior associated with gradient descent emerges only at extraordinarily small training-loss levels, well beyond 10^-100. At more reasonable initialization scales and training accuracies, the implicit bias is more complex than those limits describe. The result highlights a concrete issue in interpreting asymptotic theories: a mathematically valid limiting description may become relevant only after training reaches an extreme level of accuracy.
summary.tldr: In diagonal linear networks, initialization scale and training accuracy jointly determine implicit bias, with some asymptotic regimes appearing only at extreme accuracies.

title: Implicit Bias in Deep Linear Classification: Initialization Scale vs Training Accuracy

abstract: We provide improved gap-dependent regret bounds for reinforcement learning in finite episodic Markov decision processes. Compared to prior work, our bounds depend on alternative definitions of gaps. These definitions are based on the insight that, in order to achieve a favorable regret, an algorithm does not need to learn how to behave optimally in states that are not reached by an optimal policy. We prove tighter upper regret bounds for optimistic algorithms and accompany them with new information-theoretic lower bounds for a large class of MDPs. Our results show that optimistic algorithms can not achieve the information-theoretic lower bounds even in deterministic MDPs unless there is a unique optimal policy.

These definitions are based on the insight that, in order to achieve a favorable regret, an algorithm does not need to learn how to behave optimally in states that are not reached by an optimal policy. We prove tighter upper regret bounds for optimistic algorithms and accompany them with new information-theoretic lower bounds for a large class of MDPs. paragraphs: Regret bounds describe how much reward a learning agent loses relative to optimal behavior as it gains experience. This paper improves bounds that depend on the difficulty of a particular finite episodic Markov decision process. It does so by changing how the relevant gaps between decisions are defined, rather than relying only on earlier value-function gap definitions.

The key observation is that favorable regret does not require learning optimal behavior in states that an optimal policy never reaches. The alternative gaps account for this distinction. Using them, the authors prove tighter upper bounds for optimistic algorithms and derive new information-theoretic lower bounds for a large class of Markov decision processes.

The comparison also exposes a limitation of optimistic algorithms: they cannot achieve the information-theoretic lower bounds even in deterministic environments unless the optimal policy is unique. Uniqueness is stated as a necessary condition here, not a sufficient guarantee of attaining the bound. The work therefore refines both the description of instance difficulty and the understanding of when optimism falls short of the best theoretically possible regret.
summary.tldr: Reachability-aware gap definitions tighten reinforcement-learning regret bounds and reveal limits of optimism when optimal policies are not unique.

title: Beyond Value-Function Gaps: Improved Instance-Dependent Regret Bounds for Episodic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Thompson Sampling (TS) from Gaussian Process (GP) models is a powerful tool for the optimization of black-box functions. Although TS enjoys strong theoretical guarantees and convincing empirical performance, it incurs a large computational overhead that scales polynomially with the optimization budget. Recently, scalable TS methods based on sparse GP models have been proposed to increase the scope of TS, enabling its application to problems that are sufficiently multi-modal, noisy or combinatorial to require more than a few hundred evaluations to be solved. However, the approximation error introduced by sparse GPs invalidates all existing regret bounds. In this work, we perform a theoretical and empirical analysis of scalable TS. We provide theoretical guarantees and show that the drastic reduction in computational complexity of scalable TS can be enjoyed without loss in the regret performance over the standard TS. These conceptual claims are validated for practical implementations of scalable TS on synthetic benchmarks and as part of a real-world high-throughput molecular design task.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling with Gaussian-process models is a useful approach to optimizing functions whose internal form is unknown. Its computational overhead grows polynomially with the evaluation budget, making long optimization runs costly. Sparse Gaussian-process approximations offer a more scalable alternative for problems requiring many evaluations, including noisy, multimodal, or combinatorial tasks.

The difficulty is that introducing an approximation changes the basis for existing theoretical guarantees. Earlier regret bounds no longer apply directly to sparse models. This paper supplies a theoretical and empirical analysis of scalable Thompson sampling, establishing guarantees that account for the approximation rather than assuming the standard analysis remains valid.

The authors show that the substantial reduction in computation can be obtained without losing the regret performance of standard Thompson sampling. They support these claims with practical implementations on synthetic benchmarks and a high-throughput molecular-design task. The contribution gives theoretical backing to scalable variants and checks that the anticipated computational and optimization benefits appear in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: The paper provides theoretical and empirical support for sparse-GP Thompson sampling that reduces computation without losing standard Thompson sampling's regret performance.

title: Scalable Thompson Sampling using Sparse Gaussian Process Models

abstract: Discovering a solution in a combinatorial space is prevalent in many real-world problems but it is also challenging due to diverse complex constraints and the vast number of possible combinations. To address such a problem, we introduce a novel formulation, combinatorial construction, which requires a building agent to assemble unit primitives (i.e., LEGO bricks) sequentially -- every connection between two bricks must follow a fixed rule, while no bricks mutually overlap. To construct a target object, we provide incomplete knowledge about the desired target (i.e., 2D images) instead of exact and explicit volumetric information to the agent. This problem requires a comprehensive understanding of partial information and long-term planning to append a brick sequentially, which leads us to employ reinforcement learning. The approach has to consider a variable-sized action space where a large number of invalid actions, which would cause overlap between bricks, exist. To resolve these issues, our model, dubbed Brick-by-Brick, adopts an action validity prediction network that efficiently filters invalid actions for an actor-critic network. We demonstrate that the proposed method successfully learns to construct an unseen object conditioned on a single image or multiple views of a target object.

This problem requires a comprehensive understanding of partial information and long-term planning to append a brick sequentially, which leads us to employ reinforcement learning. To resolve these issues, our model, dubbed Brick-by-Brick, adopts an action validity prediction network that efficiently filters invalid actions for an actor-critic network. We demonstrate that the proposed method successfully learns to construct an unseen object conditioned on a single image or multiple views of a target object.

paragraphs: This paper studies construction as a sequence of decisions: an agent must assemble an object from LEGO bricks while obeying connection rules and preventing overlap. The target is supplied through one or more images, rather than a complete description of its volume. The agent therefore has to interpret incomplete visual information while choosing actions that support later construction.

The authors use reinforcement learning because each placement affects the possibilities available afterward. A central challenge is that the action space changes size as construction progresses and contains many invalid placements. Their Brick-by-Brick model includes an action validity prediction network that filters out invalid actions before an actor-critic network chooses how to continue building.

The reported demonstrations show that the method learns to construct an unseen object from a single image or multiple views. The contribution combines reasoning about a visually specified target with sequential planning under geometric constraints. Filtering invalid actions addresses a practical obstacle within that planning process: many available placements would otherwise create overlapping bricks.
summary.tldr: Brick-by-Brick learns to assemble objects from images using reinforcement learning and a network that filters invalid brick placements.

title: Brick-by-Brick: Combinatorial Construction with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study a class of classification problems best exemplified by the \emph{bank loan} problem, where a lender decides whether or not to issue a loan. The lender only observes whether a customer will repay a loan if the loan is issued to begin with, and thus modeled decisions affect what data is available to the lender for future decisions. As a result, it is possible for the lender's algorithm to ``get stuck'' with a self-fulfilling model. This model never corrects its false negatives, since it never sees the true label for rejected data, thus accumulating infinite regret. In the case of linear models, this issue can be addressed by adding optimism directly into the model predictions. However, there are few methods that extend to the function approximation case using Deep Neural Networks. We present Pseudo-Label Optimism (PLOT), a conceptually and computationally simple method for this setting applicable to DNNs. \PLOT{} adds an optimistic label to the subset of decision points the current model is deciding on, trains the model on all data so far (including these points along with their optimistic labels), and finally uses the resulting \emph{optimistic} model for decision making. \PLOT{} achieves competitive performance on a set of three challenging benchmark problems, requiring minimal hyperparameter tuning. We also show that \PLOT{} satisfies a logarithmic regret guarantee, under a Lipschitz and logistic mean label model, and under a separability condition on the data.

This feedback loop can trap a classifier in self-confirming decisions and cause regret to accumulate indefinitely. The paper addresses this selective-feedback problem with a method usable by deep neural networks.

Pseudo-Label Optimism, or PLOT, temporarily assigns favorable labels to a subset of the points currently awaiting decisions. It trains on the observations collected so far together with those optimistically labeled points, then uses the resulting model to decide. The intervention makes optimism part of training rather than requiring a direct adjustment to neural-network predictions.

PLOT performs competitively on three challenging benchmarks with minimal hyperparameter tuning. The authors also establish logarithmic regret under a Lipschitz and logistic mean-label model and a separability condition on the data. The empirical results support its practicality, while the conditional guarantee explains when its optimistic exploration can control accumulated decision errors.
summary.tldr: PLOT trains neural classifiers with optimistic temporary labels to counter feedback loops caused by observing outcomes only for accepted decisions.

title: Neural Pseudo-Label Optimism for the Bank Loan Problem

abstract: Modelers use automatic differentiation (AD) of computation graphs to implement complex Deep Learning models without defining gradient computations. Stochastic AD extends AD to stochastic computation graphs with sampling steps, which arise when modelers handle the intractable expectations common in Reinforcement Learning and Variational Inference. However, current methods for stochastic AD are limited: They are either only applicable to continuous random variables and differentiable functions, or can only use simple but high variance score-function estimators. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Storchastic, a new framework for AD of stochastic computation graphs. Storchastic allows the modeler to choose from a wide variety of gradient estimation methods at each sampling step, to optimally reduce the variance of the gradient estimates. Furthermore, Storchastic is provably unbiased for estimation of any-order gradients, and generalizes variance reduction techniques to higher-order gradient estimates. Finally, we implement Storchastic as a PyTorch library at github.com/HEmile/storchastic.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation makes it possible to train complex models without manually deriving every gradient. Sampling operations complicate this process because the quantities being optimized often involve expectations that cannot be computed directly. Storchastic extends the automatic differentiation workflow to these stochastic computation graphs, including those used in reinforcement learning and variational inference.

Existing approaches described in the paper either require continuous random variables and differentiable functions or rely on simple score-function estimators with high variance. Storchastic lets users choose among a broad range of gradient estimators separately at each sampling step. This flexibility allows variance-reduction methods to be matched to different parts of the same computation.

The framework comes with a proof of unbiased gradient estimation at arbitrary order and extends variance-reduction techniques to higher-order derivatives. Unbiasedness means the estimate agrees with the desired gradient on average; reducing variance addresses how much individual estimates fluctuate. These are complementary properties. The authors also implement Storchastic as a PyTorch library, turning the framework into a tool for constructing and differentiating models with sampling.
summary.tldr: Storchastic supports flexible gradient estimators at individual sampling steps with provably unbiased derivatives of any order.

title: Storchastic: A Framework for General Stochastic Automatic Differentiation

abstract: We consider the phenomenon of adversarial examples in ReLU networks with independent Gaussian parameters. For networks of constant depth and with a large range of widths (for instance, it suffices if the width of each layer is polynomial in that of any other layer), small perturbations of input vectors lead to large changes of outputs. This generalizes results of Daniely and Schacham (2020) for networks of rapidly decreasing width and of Bubeck et al (2021) for two-layer networks. Our proof shows that adversarial examples arise in these networks because the functions they compute are \emph{locally} very similar to random linear functions. Bottleneck layers play a key role: the minimal width up to some point in the network determines scales and sensitivities of mappings computed up to that point. The main result is for networks with constant depth, but we also show that some constraint on depth is necessary for a result of this kind, because there are suitably deep networks that, with constant probability, compute a function that is close to constant.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why small input changes can produce large output changes in ReLU networks whose parameters are independent Gaussian random variables. Its main result covers networks of constant depth across a broad range of layer widths. For example, it is sufficient for every layer's width to be polynomial in the width of any other layer.

The explanation comes from the networks' local behavior: near an input, their computed functions closely resemble random linear functions. This makes local sensitivity central to the existence of adversarial examples in the studied setting. The proof also identifies bottlenecks as important: the smallest layer encountered so far controls scales and sensitivities of the mapping through that portion of the network.

These findings extend earlier results for two-layer networks and networks whose widths decrease rapidly. The depth condition also has substantive meaning. The authors show that suitably deep networks can compute a nearly constant function with constant probability, so some restriction on depth is necessary for this kind of sensitivity result.
summary.tldr: Constant-depth random Gaussian ReLU networks admit small input perturbations with large output effects because their local behavior resembles random linear functions.

title: Adversarial Examples in Multi-Layer Random ReLU Networks

abstract: Poisoning attacks have emerged as a significant security threat to machine learning algorithms. It has been demonstrated that adversaries who make small changes to the training set, such as adding specially crafted data points, can hurt the performance of the output model. Most of these attacks require the full knowledge of training data. This leaves open the possibility of achieving the same attack results using poisoning attacks that do not have the full knowledge of the clean training set.In this work, we initiate a theoretical study of the problem above. Specifically, for the case of feature selection with LASSO, we show that \emph{full information} adversaries (that craft poisoning examples based on the rest of the training data) are provably much more devastating compared to the optimal attacker that is \emph{oblivious} to the training set yet has access to the distribution of the data. Our separation result shows that the two settings of data-aware and data-oblivious are fundamentally different and we cannot hope to achieve the same attack or defense results in these scenarios.

paragraphs: Poisoning attacks damage a learned model by changing its training data, for example by inserting carefully chosen examples. Many such attacks assume the attacker knows the clean training set. This paper asks whether an attacker without that access could achieve equally damaging results, even if they know the distribution from which the training data comes.

The authors study this question theoretically for feature selection with LASSO. They compare an attacker who tailors poisoned examples to the actual training set with the strongest possible attacker who knows the data distribution but cannot inspect that set. They prove a separation: access to the particular training examples can make the attacker substantially more damaging.

The result makes the attacker's information a central part of the security question. In the studied setting, knowing the population distribution does not substitute for knowing the realized training set. Consequently, attack capabilities and defense results cannot simply be transferred between these two information settings. The demonstrated separation concerns LASSO feature selection, rather than establishing the same conclusion for every learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: For LASSO feature selection, attackers who see the training set can provably cause much more damage than optimal attackers who know only its distribution.

title: A Separation Result Between Data-oblivious and Data-aware Poisoning Attacks

abstract: In design, fabrication, and control problems, we are often faced with the task of synthesis, in which we must generate an object or configuration that satisfies a set of constraints while maximizing one or more objective functions. The synthesis problem is typically characterized by a physical process in which many different realizations may achieve the goal. This many-to-one map presents challenges to the supervised learning of feed-forward synthesis, as the set of viable designs may have a complex structure. In addition, the non-differentiable nature of many physical simulations prevents efficient direct optimization. We address both of these problems with a two-stage neural network architecture that we may consider to be an autoencoder. We first learn the decoder: a differentiable surrogate that approximates the many-to-one physical realization process. We then learn the encoder, which maps from goal to design, while using the fixed decoder to evaluate the quality of the realization. We evaluate the approach on two case studies: extruder path planning in additive manufacturing and constrained soft robot inverse kinematics. We compare our approach to direct optimization of the design using the learned surrogate, and to supervised learning of the synthesis problem. We find that our approach produces higher quality solutions than supervised learning, while being competitive in quality with direct optimization, at a greatly reduced computational cost.

paragraphs: Design synthesis asks for a configuration that meets constraints while achieving a desired objective. Several different designs can produce the same outcome, making the inverse mapping from goals to designs difficult to learn through supervision. Physical simulators introduce another obstacle when they cannot provide derivatives for direct optimization.

The paper addresses both issues with a two-stage neural architecture. First, it trains a differentiable surrogate to predict the physical outcome of a design. It then fixes this surrogate and trains a second network to map goals to designs, evaluating those designs through the surrogate. This resembles an autoencoder whose decoder is learned first and then used to train its encoder.

The authors evaluate the approach on extruder path planning for additive manufacturing and constrained soft robot inverse kinematics. In these cases, it produces higher-quality solutions than supervised synthesis. Its solution quality is also competitive with directly optimizing designs through the learned surrogate, while requiring much less computation. The result supports amortizing synthesis into a trained goal-to-design mapping for these tasks.
summary.tldr: A learned physical surrogate trains a goal-to-design network that produces competitive constrained designs at much lower computational cost in two case studies.

title: Amortized Synthesis of Constrained Configurations Using a Differentiable Surrogate

abstract: We study discrete-time mirror descent applied to the unregularized empirical risk in matrix sensing. In both the general case of rectangular matrices and the particular case of positive semidefinite matrices, a simple potential-based analysis in terms of the Bregman divergence allows us to establish convergence of mirror descent---with different choices of the mirror maps---to a matrix that, among all global minimizers of the empirical risk, minimizes a quantity explicitly related to the nuclear norm, the Frobenius norm, and the von Neumann entropy. In both cases, this characterization implies that mirror descent, a first-order algorithm minimizing the unregularized empirical risk, recovers low-rank matrices under the same set of assumptions that are sufficient to guarantee recovery for nuclear-norm minimization. When the sensing matrices are symmetric and commute, we show that gradient descent with full-rank factorized parametrization is a first-order approximation to mirror descent, in which case we obtain an explicit characterization of the implicit bias of gradient flow as a by-product.

paragraphs: This paper studies which matrix an optimization algorithm selects when several matrices minimize the same empirical loss. It examines discrete-time mirror descent for matrix sensing without adding an explicit regularization penalty. The central issue is implicit regularization: the algorithm's own structure can favor particular solutions even when the objective does not specify that preference.

Using an analysis based on Bregman divergence, the authors characterize convergence for rectangular matrices and positive semidefinite matrices under different mirror maps. Among global loss minimizers, the selected matrix minimizes a quantity explicitly connected to nuclear norm, Frobenius norm, and von Neumann entropy. This characterization yields low-rank recovery under the same assumptions sufficient for nuclear-norm minimization.

The paper also connects mirror descent to gradient descent on a full-rank factorization when the sensing matrices are symmetric and commute. Under those conditions, factorized gradient descent is a first-order approximation to mirror descent. The connection additionally provides an explicit description of gradient flow's implicit bias, linking algorithm choice to the structure of recovered solutions.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes mirror descent's implicit preference among matrix-sensing solutions and proves low-rank recovery under assumptions sufficient for nuclear-norm minimization.

title: Implicit Regularization in Matrix Sensing via Mirror Descent

abstract: Active learning effectively collects data instances for training deep learning models when the labeled dataset is limited and the annotation cost is high. Data augmentation is another effective technique to enlarge the limited amount of labeled instances. The scarcity of labeled dataset leads us to consider the integration of data augmentation and active learning. One possible approach is a pipelined combination, which selects informative instances via the acquisition function and generates virtual instances from the selected instances via augmentation. However, this pipelined approach would not guarantee the informativeness of the virtual instances. This paper proposes Look-Ahead Data Acquisition via augmentation, or LADA framework, that looks ahead the effect of data augmentation in the process of acquisition. LADA jointly considers both 1) unlabeled data instance to be selected and 2) virtual data instance to be generated by data augmentation, to construct the acquisition function. Moreover, to generate maximally informative virtual instances, LADA optimizes the data augmentation policy to maximize the predictive acquisition score, resulting in the proposal of InfoSTN and InfoMixup. The experimental results of LADA show a significant improvement over the recent augmentation and acquisition baselines that were independently applied.

paragraphs: Active learning selects examples to label, while data augmentation produces additional training examples from existing ones. Applying them in sequence leaves an important disconnect: selecting an informative original example does not guarantee that its augmented versions will also be informative. LADA brings the effects of augmentation into the selection decision itself.

Its acquisition function considers both the unlabeled example being selected and the virtual example that augmentation would generate. This look-ahead design evaluates acquisition in light of the training data it will help create. LADA also optimizes the augmentation policy to maximize a predictive acquisition score, leading to the proposed InfoSTN and InfoMixup methods.

The experiments report significant improvements over recent augmentation and acquisition baselines applied independently. These results support coordinating the two operations when labels are scarce and annotation is expensive. The optimization targets the chosen acquisition score, while the empirical evaluation provides evidence that this coordination improves learning; the abstract does not present informativeness as an unconditional guarantee.
summary.tldr: LADA selects examples with their future augmentations in mind and optimizes augmentation to improve the acquisition score.

title: LADA: Look-Ahead Data Acquisition via Augmentation for Deep Active Learning

abstract: Goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) has shown promising results for solving complex and long-horizon RL tasks. However, the action space of high-level policy in the goal-conditioned HRL is often large, so it results in poor exploration, leading to inefficiency in training. In this paper, we present HIerarchical reinforcement learning Guided by Landmarks (HIGL), a novel framework for training a high-level policy with a reduced action space guided by landmarks, i.e., promising states to explore. The key component of HIGL is twofold: (a) sampling landmarks that are informative for exploration and (b) encouraging the high level policy to generate a subgoal towards a selected landmark. For (a), we consider two criteria: coverage of the entire visited state space (i.e., dispersion of states) and novelty of states (i.e., prediction error of a state). For (b), we select a landmark as the very first landmark in the shortest path in a graph whose nodes are landmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that our framework outperforms prior-arts across a variety of control tasks, thanks to efficient exploration guided by landmarks.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning uses a high-level policy to propose subgoals. For complex, long-horizon tasks, the possible subgoals can form a large action space, making exploration inefficient. HIGL addresses this by guiding the high-level policy with landmarks: states selected as promising places to explore.

Landmark selection uses two complementary criteria. One favors coverage of the states already visited, while the other favors novelty measured through state prediction error. The method then organizes landmarks into a graph and selects the first landmark along a shortest path. Training encourages the high-level policy to generate a subgoal toward that selected landmark.

This structure reduces the high-level action space and gives exploration an intermediate direction. Coverage and novelty influence which states become landmarks, while graph paths influence which landmark guides the next subgoal. Experiments across a variety of control tasks report improvements over prior methods, attributed to more efficient landmark-guided exploration. The findings support this combination of state selection and subgoal guidance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: HIGL improves hierarchical exploration by guiding subgoals toward landmarks selected for coverage and novelty.

title: Landmark-Guided Subgoal Generation in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We explore task-free continual learning (CL), in which a model is trained to avoid catastrophic forgetting in the absence of explicit task boundaries or identities. Among many efforts on task-free CL, a notable family of approaches are memory-based that store and replay a subset of training examples. However, the utility of stored seen examples may diminish over time since CL models are continually updated. Here, we propose Gradient based Memory EDiting (GMED), a framework for editing stored examples in continuous input space via gradient updates, in order to create more "challenging" examples for replay. GMED-edited examples remain similar to their unedited forms, but can yield increased loss in the upcoming model updates, thereby making the future replays more effective in overcoming catastrophic forgetting. By construction, GMED can be seamlessly applied in conjunction with other memory-based CL algorithms to bring further improvement. Experiments validate the effectiveness of GMED, and our best method significantly outperforms baselines and previous state-of-the-art on five out of six datasets.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to keep learning without losing what it learned earlier. This paper considers the harder setting where task identities and boundaries are not supplied. A common approach stores a subset of past examples and replays them during training, but those unchanged examples may become less useful as the model evolves.

Gradient based Memory EDiting, or GMED, updates stored examples themselves using gradients in continuous input space. The edited examples remain similar to their originals while becoming more challenging for upcoming model updates. By anticipating examples that can incur higher loss, the method aims to make future replay more effective at countering forgetting.

GMED is designed to combine with other memory-based continual learning algorithms, making it a way to improve replay rather than a requirement to replace the surrounding learning method. Experiments support its effectiveness, with the strongest combined method significantly outperforming baselines and previous leading approaches on five of six datasets. The results suggest that maintaining a useful memory can involve adapting its contents over time.
summary.tldr: GMED edits stored training examples to make replay more challenging and reduce forgetting during continual learning without task boundaries.

title: Gradient-based Editing of Memory Examples for Online Task-free Continual Learning

abstract: Grounded language acquisition is a major area of research combining aspects of natural language processing, computer vision, and signal processing, compounded by domain issues requiring sample efficiency and other deployment constraints. In this work, we present a multimodal dataset of RGB+depth objects with spoken as well as textual descriptions. We analyze the differences between the two types of descriptive language and our experiments demonstrate that the different modalities affect learning. This will enable researchers studying the intersection of robotics, NLP, and HCI to better investigate how the multiple modalities of image, depth, text, speech, and transcription interact, as well as how differences in the vernacular of these modalities impact results.

paragraphs: Learning language grounded in objects means connecting descriptions to what can be seen or sensed. This paper introduces a dataset that brings these signals together: objects represented through color images and depth information, accompanied by both spoken and written descriptions. It supports studying language alongside the physical information that gives it meaning.

The researchers examine differences between spoken and textual descriptions, rather than assuming they provide interchangeable language supervision. Their experiments show that the choice of modality affects learning. This matters because a system learning from written descriptions may encounter different descriptive language when people interact with it through speech.

The dataset makes it possible to investigate interactions among images, depth, text, speech, and transcriptions within a shared resource. Its contribution is particularly relevant to research connecting robotics, language processing, and human-computer interaction. The stated findings motivate paying attention both to how information is recorded and to the language people use in each modality.
summary.tldr: A dataset pairs object imagery and depth with spoken and written descriptions, showing that language modality affects learning.

title: A Spoken Language Dataset of Descriptions for Speech-Based Grounded Language Learning

abstract: An important step towards explaining deep image classifiers lies in the identification of image regions that contribute to individual class scores in the model's output. However, doing this accurately is a difficult task due to the black-box nature of such networks. Most existing approaches find such attributions either using activations and gradients or by repeatedly perturbing the input. We instead address this challenge by training a second deep network, the Explainer, to predict attributions for a pre-trained black-box classifier, the Explanandum. These attributions are provided in the form of masks that only show the classifier-relevant parts of an image, masking out the rest. Our approach produces sharper and more boundary-precise masks when compared to the saliency maps generated by other methods. Moreover, unlike most existing approaches, ours is capable of directly generating very distinct class-specific masks in a single forward pass. This makes the proposed method very efficient during inference. We show that our attributions are superior to established methods both visually and quantitatively with respect to the PASCAL VOC-2007 and Microsoft COCO-2014 datasets.

Most existing approaches find such attributions either using activations and gradients or by repeatedly perturbing the input. We instead address this challenge by training a second deep network, the Explainer, to predict attributions for a pre-trained black-box classifier, the Explanandum. These attributions are provided in the form of masks that only show the classifier-relevant parts of an image, masking out the rest. Our approach produces sharper and more boundary-precise masks when compared to the saliency maps generated by other methods. Moreover, unlike most existing approaches, ours is capable of directly generating very distinct class-specific masks in a single forward pass. This makes the proposed method very efficient during inference. We show that our attributions are superior to established methods both visually and quantitatively with respect to the PASCAL VOC-2007 and Microsoft COCO-2014 datasets.

paragraphs: Explaining an image classifier often means identifying which image regions contribute to a particular class score. Many methods use internal activations and gradients or repeatedly modify the input. This paper instead trains a separate network to predict explanations for an already pretrained black-box classifier.

The second network, called the Explainer, produces masks that retain classifier-relevant image regions and hide the rest. Its target classifier is called the Explanandum. The approach can directly generate distinct masks for different classes in one forward pass, making explanation generation efficient after the Explainer has been trained.

The authors report masks with sharper, more precise boundaries than saliency maps from other methods. Evaluations on PASCAL VOC-2007 and Microsoft COCO-2014 show both visual and quantitative improvements over established approaches. The contribution combines a learned explanation mechanism with class-specific outputs: the same image can receive different masks depending on the class being explained. The evidence supports the quality and inference efficiency of these attributions in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: A separately trained Explainer generates sharp, class-specific image masks in one forward pass for a pretrained black-box classifier.

title: What You See is What You Classify: Black Box Attributions

abstract: Branched optimal transport (BOT) is a generalization of optimal transport in which transportation costs along an edge are subadditive. This subadditivity models an increase in transport efficiency when shipping mass along the same route, favoring branched transportation networks. We here study the NP-hard optimization of BOT networks connecting a finite number of sources and sinks in $\mathbb{R}^2$. First, we show how to efficiently find the best geometry of a BOT network for many sources and sinks, given a topology. Second, we argue that a topology with more than three edges meeting at a branching point is never optimal. Third, we show that the results obtained for the Euclidean plane generalize directly to optimal transportation networks on two-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. Finally, we present a simple but effective approximate BOT solver combining geometric optimization with a combinatorial optimization of the network topology.

The abstract describes it as simple and effective but supplies no numerical evaluation or global approximation factor. The work distinguishes an efficiently solvable geometric subproblem from the harder choice of connectivity, using theoretical structure to guide a practical approach to the combined optimization.
summary.tldr: Branched transport combines efficient geometry optimization with approximate search over network topology.

title: Theory and Approximate Solvers for Branched Optimal Transport with Multiple Sources

abstract: A flexible conformal inference method is developed to construct confidence intervals for the frequencies of queried objects in very large data sets, based on a much smaller sketch of those data. The approach is data-adaptive and requires no knowledge of the data distribution or of the details of the sketching algorithm; instead, it constructs provably valid frequentist confidence intervals under the sole assumption of data exchangeability. Although our solution is broadly applicable, this paper focuses on applications involving the count-min sketch algorithm and a non-linear variation thereof. The performance is compared to that of frequentist and Bayesian alternatives through simulations and experiments with data sets of SARS-CoV-2 DNA sequences and classic English literature.

This paper asks how to attach trustworthy uncertainty intervals to frequency estimates obtained from such summaries. The target is the number of occurrences of a queried object.

The proposed conformal inference method adapts to the data without requiring the underlying distribution or the internal details of the sketching algorithm. Its confidence intervals have a provable frequentist validity guarantee under exchangeability, meaning that the data's joint distribution does not depend on their ordering. That assumption is central to the guarantee, while detailed distributional modeling is unnecessary.

Although the approach is broadly applicable, the paper concentrates on count-min sketches and a nonlinear variant. It compares the method with frequentist and Bayesian alternatives using simulations, SARS-CoV-2 DNA sequences, and English literature. The contribution is a way to quantify uncertainty around compressed-data frequency queries with a guarantee that is largely independent of the chosen sketch's implementation.
summary.tldr: A conformal method provides valid frequency-estimation intervals from data sketches under exchangeability, without knowing the distribution or sketch details.

title: Conformal Frequency Estimation with Sketched Data

abstract: Learning stable dynamics from observed time-series data is an essential problem in robotics, physical modeling, and systems biology. Many of these dynamics are represented as an inputs-output system to communicate with the external environment. In this study, we focus on input-output stable systems, exhibiting robustness against unexpected stimuli and noise. We propose a method to learn nonlinear systems guaranteeing the input-output stability. Our proposed method utilizes the differentiable projection onto the space satisfying the Hamilton-Jacobi inequality to realize the input-output stability. The problem of finding this projection can be formulated as a quadratic constraint quadratic programming problem, and we derive the particular solution analytically. Also, we apply our method to a toy bistable model and the task of training a benchmark generated from a glucose-insulin simulator. The results show that the nonlinear system with neural networks by our method achieves the input-output stability, unlike naive neural networks. Our code is available at https://github.com/clinfo/DeepIOStability .

When the system receives external inputs, its response to unexpected stimulation and noise also matters. This paper focuses on learning nonlinear input-output systems with a stability guarantee, motivated by applications such as robotics, physical modeling, and systems biology.

The method enforces stability through a differentiable projection onto a space satisfying the Hamilton-Jacobi inequality. In effect, the learned system is constrained through a mathematical condition that realizes input-output stability. Finding the projection can be expressed as a quadratically constrained quadratic programming problem, and the authors derive an analytical particular solution.

In those evaluations, their neural nonlinear systems achieve input-output stability, unlike the naive neural networks used for comparison. The contribution connects a trainable neural representation with an explicit stability mechanism, so the desired response property is built into learning rather than judged only from ordinary prediction behavior.
summary.tldr: A differentiable projection enforces a mathematical stability condition while learning nonlinear input-output dynamics.

title: Learning Deep Input-Output Stable Dynamics

abstract: Methods for sequential decision-making are often built upon a foundational assumption that the underlying decision process is stationary. This limits the application of such methods because real-world problems are often subject to changes due to external factors (\textit{passive} non-stationarity), changes induced by interactions with the system itself (\textit{active} non-stationarity), or both (\textit{hybrid} non-stationarity). In this work, we take the first steps towards the fundamental challenge of on-policy and off-policy evaluation amidst structured changes due to active, passive, or hybrid non-stationarity. Towards this goal, we make a \textit{higher-order stationarity} assumption such that non-stationarity results in changes over time, but the way changes happen is fixed. We propose, OPEN, an algorithm that uses a double application of counterfactual reasoning and a novel importance-weighted instrument-variable regression to obtain both a lower bias and a lower variance estimate of the structure in the changes of a policy's past performances. Finally, we show promising results on how OPEN can be used to predict future performances for several domains inspired by real-world applications that exhibit non-stationarity.

paragraphs: Evaluating a decision policy becomes difficult when the environment changes over time. Those changes may arise from external forces, from the agent's own actions, or from both. This paper studies on-policy and off-policy evaluation under these forms of non-stationarity, with the goal of predicting a policy's future performance from past information.

The key assumption is higher-order stationarity: the environment can change, but the mechanism describing how it changes stays fixed. This supplies structure that an evaluation algorithm can learn. The proposed method, OPEN, applies counterfactual reasoning twice and combines it with importance-weighted instrumental-variable regression to estimate patterns in the policy's past performance.

The authors describe this construction as yielding lower bias and lower variance when estimating the structure of performance changes. Experiments in several domains inspired by real applications give promising results for forecasting future policy performance. The contribution depends on stable structure in the change process, making that assumption central to how OPEN addresses environments whose ordinary decision dynamics are not stationary.
summary.tldr: OPEN estimates future policy performance in changing environments by assuming that the mechanism governing change remains stable.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation for Action-Dependent Non-stationary Environments

abstract: Extraction of latent sources of complex stimuli is critical for making sense of the world. While the brain solves this blind source separation (BSS) problem continuously, its algorithms remain unknown. Previous work on biologically-plausible BSS algorithms assumed that observed signals are linear mixtures of statistically independent or uncorrelated sources, limiting the domain of applicability of these algorithms. To overcome this limitation, we propose novel biologically-plausible neural networks for the blind separation of potentially dependent/correlated sources. Differing from previous work, we assume some general geometric, not statistical, conditions on the source vectors allowing separation of potentially dependent/correlated sources. Concretely, we assume that the source vectors are sufficiently scattered in their domains which can be described by certain polytopes. Then, we consider recovery of these sources by the Det-Max criterion, which maximizes the determinant of the output correlation matrix to enforce a similar spread for the source estimates. Starting from this normative principle, and using a weighted similarity matching approach that enables arbitrary linear transformations adaptable by local learning rules, we derive two-layer biologically-plausible neural network algorithms that can separate mixtures into sources coming from a variety of source domains. We demonstrate that our algorithms outperform other biologically-plausible BSS algorithms on correlated source separation problems.

paragraphs: Blind source separation tries to recover underlying signals from their observed mixtures. Previous biologically plausible algorithms often assumed that the sources were statistically independent or uncorrelated. This paper develops neural algorithms that can instead handle sources that may be dependent or correlated.

Thus, the separation principle relies on the arrangement of source values within an allowed domain.

That approach permits adaptable linear transformations through local learning rules, supporting the intended biological plausibility. The networks accommodate a variety of source domains and outperform other biologically plausible separation algorithms on correlated-source problems. Their contribution is a route beyond independence assumptions, while still relying on explicit geometric conditions for the sources.
summary.tldr: The paper derives biologically plausible networks for separating correlated sources under geometric spread assumptions.

title: Biologically-Plausible Determinant Maximization Neural Networks for Blind Separation of Correlated Sources

abstract: There is currently a large gap in performance between the statistically rigorous methods like linear regression or additive splines and the powerful deep methods using neural networks. Previous works attempting to close this gap have failed to fully consider the exponentially growing number of feature combinations which deep networks consider automatically during training. In this work, we develop a tractable selection algorithm to efficiently identify the necessary feature combinations by leveraging techniques in feature interaction detection.Our proposed Sparse Interaction Additive Networks (SIAN) construct a bridge from these simple and interpretable models to a fully connected neural network. SIAN achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods across multiple large-scale tabular datasets and consistently finds an optimal tradeoff between the modeling capacity of neural networks and the generalizability of simpler methods.

paragraphs: Simple regression and additive models offer statistical structure and interpretability, but can fall behind neural networks in predictive performance. Deep networks can consider combinations of inputs during training, whereas explicitly handling all possible combinations becomes difficult because their number grows exponentially.

The selection draws on feature interaction detection techniques. This gives the model a way to include selected interactions while maintaining a connection to simpler additive modeling, rather than requiring an explicit enumeration of every possible feature combination.

Across multiple large-scale tabular datasets, SIAN achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods. The authors report that it consistently finds an optimal tradeoff between neural-network modeling capacity and the generalization associated with simpler methods in those evaluations. The central contribution is a practical mechanism for controlling interaction complexity, linking the flexibility of fully connected networks with the structure of additive models.
summary.tldr: SIAN efficiently selects feature interactions to combine additive model structure with competitive neural-network predictive performance.

title: Sparse Interaction Additive Networks via Feature Interaction Detection and Sparse Selection

abstract: Novel architectures have recently improved generative image synthesis leading to excellent visual quality in various tasks. Much of this success is due to the scalability of these architectures and hence caused by a dramatic increase in model complexity and in the computational resources invested in training these models. Our work questions the underlying paradigm of compressing large training data into ever growing parametric representations. We rather present an orthogonal, semi-parametric approach. We complement comparably small diffusion or autoregressive models with a separate image database and a retrieval strategy. During training we retrieve a set of nearest neighbors from this external database for each training instance and condition the generative model on these informative samples. While the retrieval approach is providing the (local) content, the model is focusing on learning the composition of scenes based on this content. As demonstrated by our experiments, simply swapping the database for one with different contents transfers a trained model post-hoc to a novel domain. The evaluation shows competitive performance on tasks which the generative model has not been trained on, such as class-conditional synthesis, zero-shot stylization or text-to-image synthesis without requiring paired text-image data. With negligible memory and computational overhead for the external database and retrieval we can significantly reduce the parameter count of the generative model and still outperform the state-of-the-art.
