paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode the expectation that transforming an input should produce a corresponding transformation in the output. This can improve learning when the data respect those symmetries. Real data may only approximately satisfy them because of noise, structural variation, or measurement bias. The paper also notes that strict symmetry constraints can make optimization harder even when the data are fully symmetric.

Adaptive Constrained Equivariance, or ACE, starts with a flexible model that is not forced to be equivariant. During training, it gradually tightens a constraint on departures from equivariance. This follows a homotopy-inspired strategy: begin with an easier optimization problem and progressively transform it toward the desired constrained problem.

The gradual process allows the model to settle at a data-driven balance between symmetry and flexibility. Across several architectures and tasks, ACE improves performance, sample efficiency, and robustness to input perturbations relative to strictly equivariant models and heuristic relaxations. These findings support treating the strength of symmetry enforcement as part of the learning process.
summary.tldr: ACE gradually tightens equivariance constraints during training to balance useful symmetries with the flexibility required by data.

title: Learning (Approximately) Equivariant Networks via Constrained Optimization

abstract: We present *Plenodium* (*plenoptic medium*), an effective and efficient 3D representation framework capable of jointly modeling both objects and the participating medium. In contrast to existing medium representations that rely solely on view-dependent modeling, our novel plenoptic medium representation incorporates both directional and positional information through spherical harmonics encoding, enabling highly accurate underwater scene reconstruction. To address the initialization challenge in degraded underwater environments, we propose the pseudo-depth Gaussian complementation to augment COLMAP-derived point clouds with robust depth priors. In addition, a depth ranking regularized loss is developed to optimize the geometry of the scene and improve the ordinal consistency of the depth maps. Extensive experiments on real-world underwater datasets demonstrate that our method achieves significant improvements in 3D reconstruction. Furthermore, we construct a simulated dataset with GT and the controllable scattering medium to demonstrate the restoration capability of our method in underwater scenarios.

To address the initialization challenge in degraded underwater environments, we propose the pseudo-depth Gaussian complementation to augment COLMAP-derived point clouds with robust depth priors. In addition, a depth ranking regularized loss is developed to optimize the geometry of the scene and improve the ordinal consistency of the depth maps. paragraphs: Underwater reconstruction must account for both scene objects and the medium through which they are observed. Plenodium jointly represents these two components. Its medium representation includes position as well as viewing direction, using spherical harmonics encoding to capture information that representations based only on view dependence leave out.

The method also addresses initialization in degraded underwater imagery. It augments point clouds produced by COLMAP with depth priors through a procedure called pseudo-depth Gaussian complementation. A depth-ranking regularization term further guides geometry optimization by improving agreement about which scene points are nearer or farther. These components address the starting reconstruction and its subsequent geometric refinement.

Experiments on real underwater datasets show significant improvements in three-dimensional reconstruction. The authors additionally create a simulated dataset with ground truth and a controllable scattering medium to demonstrate restoration capability. Together, these evaluations support jointly modeling objects and medium effects, while the initialization and depth-ordering components help recover more consistent scene geometry under underwater imaging conditions.
summary.tldr: Plenodium improves underwater 3D reconstruction by jointly modeling objects and the medium, with depth-guided initialization and geometry refinement.

title: Plenodium: Underwater 3D Scene Reconstruction with Plenoptic Medium Representation

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the structure of undirected graphical models with bounded treewidth, within the maximum likelihood framework. This is an NP-hard problem and most approaches consider local search techniques. In this paper, we pose it as a combinatorial optimization problem, which is then relaxed to a convex optimization problem that involves searching over the forest and hyperforest polytopes with special structures. A supergradient method is used to solve the dual problem, with a run-time complexity of O(k^3 n^k+2 \log n) for each iteration, where n is the number of variables and k is a bound on the treewidth. We compare our approach to state-of-the-art methods on synthetic datasets and classical benchmarks, showing the gains of the novel convex approach.

A supergradient method is used to solve the dual problem, with a run-time complexity of O(k^3 n^k+2 \log n) for each iteration, where n is the number of variables and k is a bound on the treewidth. We compare our approach to state-of-the-art methods on synthetic datasets and classical benchmarks, showing the gains of the novel convex approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn the structure of an undirected graphical model by maximum likelihood while placing a bound on its treewidth. The bound restricts the graph structures under consideration. Finding the best structure is NP-hard, and many existing approaches rely on local searches through candidate graphs.

The authors formulate the task as a combinatorial optimization problem and then relax it into a convex problem. The relaxed search uses specially structured forest and hyperforest polytopes, geometric sets that encode aspects of the original discrete choices. This provides a different route for tackling the structural search rather than relying solely on local changes to a graph.

A supergradient method solves the dual formulation. The stated cost per iteration is O(k³ n^(k+2) log n), where n counts variables and k bounds treewidth, making the dependence on the structural bound explicit. Comparisons on synthetic data and established benchmarks show gains from the proposed convex approach. These results concern the relaxation-based method, without turning the underlying NP-hard problem into a general exact convex optimization task.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation provides an alternative to local search for learning bounded-treewidth graphical models, with gains in the reported comparisons.

title: Convex Relaxations for Learning Bounded-Treewidth Decomposable Graphs

abstract: In this paper we introduce a method to learn multiple behaviors in the form of motor primitives from an unlabeled dataset. One of the difficulties of this problem is that in the measurement space, behaviors can be very mixed, despite existing a latent representation where they can be easily separated. We propose a mixture model based on Dirichlet Process (DP) to simultaneously cluster the observed time-series and recover a sparse representation of the behaviors using a Laplacian prior as the base measure of the DP. We show that for linear models, e.g potential functions generated by linear combinations of a large number of features, it is possible to compute analytically the marginal of the observations and derive an efficient sampler. The method is evaluated using robot behaviors and real data from human motion and compared to other techniques.

We show that for linear models, e.g potential functions generated by linear combinations of a large number of features, it is possible to compute analytically the marginal of the observations and derive an efficient sampler. The method is evaluated using robot behaviors and real data from human motion and compared to other techniques.

paragraphs: Demonstrations can contain several behaviors without labels identifying which behavior each recording represents. Their measured trajectories may overlap heavily even when the underlying controllers are easier to distinguish. This paper learns multiple motor primitives by seeking a latent controller representation in which those behaviors can be separated.

The method uses a Dirichlet process mixture model to cluster observed time series while recovering sparse representations of the behaviors. A Laplacian prior serves as the process's base measure and supplies the sparse modeling component. Clustering and representation learning therefore happen together, allowing the inferred controller structure to help organize demonstrations that are mixed in measurement space.

For linear models, including potential functions built as linear combinations of many features, the authors show that the observation marginal can be calculated analytically. This enables an efficient sampler for learning the model. Evaluations use robot behaviors and real human-motion data and compare the method with other techniques, examining its ability to discover multiple behaviors from unlabeled observations.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process mixture jointly clusters unlabeled motion demonstrations and learns sparse latent controller representations.

title: Learning Multiple Behaviors from Unlabeled Demonstrations in a Latent Controller Space

abstract: Many prediction domains, such as ad placement, recommendation, trajectory prediction, and document summarization, require predicting a set or list of options. Such lists are often evaluated using submodular reward functions that measure both quality and diversity. We propose a simple, efficient, and provably near-optimal approach to optimizing such prediction problems based on no-regret learning. Our method leverages a surprising result from online submodular optimization: a single no-regret online learner can compete with an optimal sequence of predictions. Compared to previous work, which either learn a sequence of classifiers or rely on stronger assumptions such as realizability, we ensure both data-efficiency as well as performance guarantees in the fully agnostic setting. Experiments validate the efficiency and applicability of the approach on a wide range of problems including manipulator trajectory optimization, news recommendation and document summarization.

paragraphs: Some prediction tasks need a collection of useful options rather than a single answer. Recommendations, summaries, and possible trajectories must balance the quality of individual choices with the diversity of the collection. This paper studies such problems when that balance is expressed through a submodular reward function.

The proposed method builds on a result from online submodular optimization: one no-regret online learner can compete with an optimal sequence of predictions. This allows the authors to develop a simple, efficient approach with a near-optimality guarantee. Using a single learner also avoids the need to train a separate sequence of classifiers, as some previous approaches do.

The guarantees apply in the fully agnostic setting, without the stronger realizability assumptions used by some earlier methods. The authors also emphasize data efficiency. Experiments in manipulator trajectory optimization, news recommendation, and document summarization support the method's efficiency and applicability. Together, the theory and experiments show how one learning framework can address several kinds of structured, multiple-option prediction.
summary.tldr: A single no-regret learner supports efficient, provably near-optimal prediction of sets and lists under submodular rewards.

title: Learning Policies for Contextual Submodular Prediction

abstract: We prove an extension of McDiarmid’s inequality for metric spaces with unbounded diameter. To this end, we introduce the notion of the \em subgaussian diameter, which is a distribution-dependent refinement of the metric diameter. Our technique provides an alternative approach to that of Kutin and Niyogi’s method of weakly difference-bounded functions, and yields nontrivial, dimension-free results in some interesting cases where the former does not. As an application, we give apparently the first generalization bound in the algorithmic stability setting that holds for unbounded loss functions. This yields a novel risk bound for some regularized metric regression algorithms. We give two extensions of the basic concentration result. The first enables one to replace the independence assumption by appropriate strong mixing. The second generalizes the subgaussian technique to other Orlicz norms.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how tightly random quantities stay near their typical values. This paper extends McDiarmid’s inequality to metric spaces whose diameter is unbounded. The key replacement is a distribution-dependent quantity called the subgaussian diameter, which captures relevant probabilistic behavior even when the largest possible distance cannot provide a finite bound.

This approach yields useful bounds independent of dimension in some cases where an earlier method based on weakly difference-bounded functions does not. The paper then applies the concentration result to algorithmic stability, which studies how changes in training data affect a learning algorithm. The authors describe their result as apparently the first generalization bound in this setting that permits unbounded loss functions, and derive a risk bound for some regularized metric regression algorithms.

Two extensions broaden the framework further. One replaces independence with an appropriate strong-mixing condition, allowing certain forms of dependence. The other extends the technique beyond subgaussian behavior to other Orlicz norms. The contribution is a way to obtain informative probabilistic guarantees through distributional control rather than a finite worst-case diameter.
summary.tldr: A distribution-sensitive extension of McDiarmid’s inequality enables stability-based learning guarantees for certain unbounded losses.

title: Concentration in unbounded metric spaces and algorithmic stability

abstract: We introduce a novel algorithmic approach to content recommendation based on adaptive clustering of exploration-exploitation (“bandit") strategies. We provide a sharp regret analysis of this algorithm in a standard stochastic noise setting, demonstrate its scalability properties, and prove its effectiveness on a number of artificial and real-world datasets. Our experiments show a significant increase in prediction performance over state-of-the-art methods for bandit problems.
originalAbstract: We introduce a novel algorithmic approach to content recommendation based on adaptive clustering of exploration-exploitation (“bandit") strategies. We provide a sharp regret analysis of this algorithm in a standard stochastic noise setting, demonstrate its scalability properties, and prove its effectiveness on a number of artificial and real-world datasets. Our experiments show a significant increase in prediction performance over state-of-the-art methods for bandit problems.

paragraphs: Content recommendation involves a continuing choice between exploring options and exploiting what has already been learned. Bandit strategies formalize this trade-off. This paper introduces an approach that adaptively clusters such strategies, making the grouping itself part of the online recommendation process.

The authors analyze the algorithm's regret in a standard stochastic noise setting. Regret measures the performance lost through the choices made while learning, so this analysis addresses the cost of exploration as well as recommendation quality. The abstract describes the analysis as sharp and also reports evidence of the algorithm's scalability, connecting its theoretical treatment with its ability to handle larger problems.

Experiments on artificial and real-world datasets show a significant improvement in prediction performance over state-of-the-art bandit methods. These findings support adaptive clustering as a useful ingredient in content recommendation. The contribution combines a new way to organize exploration–exploitation strategies, a conditional regret analysis, and empirical evidence that the organization can improve predictions in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Adaptive clustering of bandit strategies improves recommendation predictions in experiments and comes with regret analysis under stochastic noise.

title: Online Clustering of Bandits

abstract: We describe and analyze a simple algorithm for principal component analysis and singular value decomposition, VR-PCA, which uses computationally cheap stochastic iterations, yet converges exponentially fast to the optimal solution. In contrast, existing algorithms suffer either from slow convergence, or computationally intensive iterations whose runtime scales with the data size. The algorithm builds on a recent variance-reduced stochastic gradient technique, which was previously analyzed for strongly convex optimization, whereas here we apply it to an inherently non-convex problem, using a very different analysis.

The algorithm builds on a recent variance-reduced stochastic gradient technique, which was previously analyzed for strongly convex optimization, whereas here we apply it to an inherently non-convex problem, using a very different analysis.

paragraphs: The paper introduces VR-PCA, an algorithm for principal component analysis and singular value decomposition. These problems seek directions or components that capture important structure in a dataset. The computational challenge highlighted here is a tradeoff in existing algorithms: some make inexpensive progress slowly, while others use costly iterations whose runtime grows with the dataset size.

VR-PCA combines computationally cheap stochastic iterations with an exponential convergence rate to the optimal solution. The mechanism builds on a variance-reduced stochastic gradient technique. Reducing the variability of stochastic updates is central to obtaining rapid progress while retaining the computational appeal of iterations that avoid the expense described for existing alternatives.

A theoretical contribution is extending this technique beyond the setting where it had previously been analyzed. Earlier analysis concerned strongly convex optimization, whereas the PCA and SVD problem considered here is inherently non-convex. The authors therefore supply a substantially different analysis. The stated result connects inexpensive stochastic computation with a fast convergence guarantee for this particular non-convex problem.
summary.tldr: VR-PCA brings variance reduction to non-convex PCA and SVD, combining cheap stochastic iterations with exponential convergence.

title: A Stochastic PCA and SVD Algorithm with an Exponential Convergence Rate

abstract: Many neural networks exhibit stability in their activation patterns over time in response to inputs from sensors operating under real-world conditions. By capitalizing on this property of natural signals, we propose a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) architecture called a delta network in which each neuron transmits its value only when the change in its activation exceeds a threshold. The execution of RNNs as delta networks is attractive because their states must be stored and fetched at every timestep, unlike in convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We show that a naive run-time delta network implementation offers modest improvements on the number of memory accesses and computes, but optimized training techniques confer higher accuracy at higher speedup. With these optimizations, we demonstrate a 9X reduction in cost with negligible loss of accuracy for the TIDIGITS audio digit recognition benchmark. Similarly, on the large Wall Street Journal (WSJ) speech recognition benchmark, pretrained networks can also be greatly accelerated as delta networks and trained delta networks show a 5.7x improvement with negligible loss of accuracy. Finally, on an end-to-end CNN-RNN network trained for steering angle prediction in a driving dataset, the RNN cost can be reduced by a substantial 100X.

paragraphs: Sensor-driven neural networks often have activations that change little between nearby moments. Delta networks exploit this temporal stability in recurrent neural networks: a neuron transmits its value only when its activation changes by more than a threshold. The goal is to reduce repeated computation and memory access when little has changed.

This is particularly relevant to recurrent networks because their states must be stored and fetched at every timestep. A straightforward runtime implementation provides only modest savings. The paper therefore develops optimized training techniques that achieve greater acceleration while maintaining higher accuracy, making training part of the efficiency strategy.

With these optimizations, the authors report a ninefold cost reduction on TIDIGITS with negligible accuracy loss. Trained delta networks show a 5.7-fold improvement on Wall Street Journal speech recognition, also with negligible accuracy loss, and pretrained networks can be accelerated as well. In a driving model combining convolutional and recurrent components, the recurrent component's cost falls by 100 times. That final figure concerns the RNN portion of the network.
summary.tldr: Delta networks transmit recurrent activations only after sufficiently large changes, substantially reducing computation in the reported sensor tasks.

title: Delta Networks for Optimized Recurrent Network Computation

abstract: In multi-task learning, a learner is given a collection of prediction tasks and needs to solve all of them. In contrast to previous work, which required that annotated training data must be available for all tasks, we consider a new setting, in which for some tasks, potentially most of them, only unlabeled training data is provided. Consequently, to solve all tasks, information must be transferred between tasks with labels and tasks without labels. Focusing on an instance-based transfer method we analyze two variants of this setting: when the set of labeled tasks is fixed, and when it can be actively selected by the learner. We state and prove a generalization bound that covers both scenarios and derive from it an algorithm for making the choice of labeled tasks (in the active case) and for transferring information between the tasks in a principled way. We also illustrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on synthetic and real data.

Focusing on an instance-based transfer method we analyze two variants of this setting: when the set of labeled tasks is fixed, and when it can be actively selected by the learner. We state and prove a generalization bound that covers both scenarios and derive from it an algorithm for making the choice of labeled tasks (in the active case) and for transferring information between the tasks in a principled way. We also illustrate the effectiveness of the algorithm on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-task learning when some tasks, potentially most of them, have no labeled training examples. The learner still needs to solve every task, so it must transfer information from tasks with annotations to those represented only by unlabeled data. This changes the role of sharing information across tasks.

The authors focus on instance-based transfer and analyze two versions of the problem. In one, the labeled tasks are already fixed. In the other, the learner can actively choose which tasks receive labels. The second version makes annotation choice part of the learning strategy, alongside the decision about how information should be transferred.

A proved generalization bound covers both settings. The authors use that bound to derive an algorithm for transferring information and, when selection is available, choosing the labeled tasks. Experiments on synthetic and real data illustrate its effectiveness. The work thus connects the theoretical treatment of tasks without labels to concrete decisions about both annotation allocation and transfer.
summary.tldr: A generalization bound guides information transfer to unlabeled tasks and, when possible, the selection of tasks to annotate.

title: Multi-task Learning with Labeled and Unlabeled Tasks

abstract: Minwise hashing is a fundamental and one of the most successful hashing algorithm in the literature. Recent advances based on the idea of densification (Shrivastava \& Li, 2014) have shown that it is possible to compute $k$ minwise hashes, of a vector with $d$ nonzeros, in mere $(d + k)$ computations, a significant improvement over the classical $O(dk)$. These advances have led to an algorithmic improvement in the query complexity of traditional indexing algorithms based on minwise hashing. Unfortunately, the variance of the current densification techniques is unnecessarily high, which leads to significantly poor accuracy compared to vanilla minwise hashing, especially when the data is sparse. In this paper, we provide a novel densification scheme which relies on carefully tailored 2-universal hashes. We show that the proposed scheme is variance-optimal, and without losing the runtime efficiency, it is significantly more accurate than existing densification techniques. As a result, we obtain a significantly efficient hashing scheme which has the same variance and collision probability as minwise hashing. Experimental evaluations on real sparse and high-dimensional datasets validate our claims. We believe that given the significant advantages, our method will replace minwise hashing implementations in practice.

paragraphs: Minwise hashing is useful for hashing and indexing, but generating many hashes can be costly. Existing densification methods reduce the work for k hashes of a vector with d nonzero entries from O(dk) to O(d + k). Their drawback is unnecessarily high variance, which can substantially reduce accuracy, especially for sparse data.

This paper introduces a densification scheme built from carefully designed 2-universal hashes. The authors prove that the scheme is variance-optimal while retaining the runtime efficiency of densification. They also establish that it matches the variance and collision probability of conventional minwise hashing, addressing the accuracy cost of earlier fast methods.

Experiments on real sparse, high-dimensional datasets support the theoretical claims. The significance is the combination of speed and statistical quality: the method preserves the computational advantage of densification while recovering key properties of standard minwise hashing. The authors anticipate broad practical adoption, but the demonstrated contribution is the scheme's analysis and empirical validation, rather than evidence that such adoption has already occurred.
summary.tldr: A variance-optimal densification scheme retains fast hashing while matching conventional minwise hashing's variance and collision probability.

title: Optimal Densification for Fast and Accurate Minwise Hashing

abstract: We point out important problems with the common practice of using the best single model performance for comparing deep learning architectures, and we propose a method that corrects these flaws. Each time a model is trained, one gets a different result due to random factors in the training process, which include random parameter initialization and random data shuffling. Reporting the best single model performance does not appropriately address this stochasticity. We propose a normalized expected best-out-of-$n$ performance ($\text{Boo}_n$) as a way to correct these problems.
originalAbstract: We point out important problems with the common practice of using the best single model performance for comparing deep learning architectures, and we propose a method that corrects these flaws. Each time a model is trained, one gets a different result due to random factors in the training process, which include random parameter initialization and random data shuffling. Reporting the best single model performance does not appropriately address this stochasticity. We propose a normalized expected best-out-of-$n$ performance ($\text{Boo}_n$) as a way to correct these problems.

paragraphs: Comparisons between deep learning architectures often highlight the best score obtained from a single trained model. This paper argues that such a score does not properly account for randomness in training. Even with the same architecture, changing the initial parameters or the order of training examples can produce different results.

The proposed alternative is a normalized expected best-out-of-n performance measure, called Boo_n. Its central idea is to evaluate the best performance one would expect from a collection of n training runs. This makes the number of opportunities to obtain a strong result an explicit part of the comparison, while accounting for variation across runs.

The contribution concerns how architecture performance is evaluated. A standout run gives an observed success, whereas an expected best-of-n quantity describes performance under a specified repeated-training setup. The paper proposes this measure to correct flaws in best-single-model reporting and make comparisons more responsive to the stochastic process that actually produces trained models.
summary.tldr: Boo_n compares architectures through normalized expected best-of-n performance, accounting for randomness across training runs.

title: A Boo(n) for Evaluating Architecture Performance

abstract: Accelerated algorithms have broad applications in large-scale optimization, due to their generality and fast convergence. However, their stability in the practical setting of noise-corrupted gradient oracles is not well-understood. This paper provides two main technical contributions: (i) a new accelerated method AGDP that generalizes Nesterov’s AGD and improves on the recent method AXGD (Diakonikolas & Orecchia, 2018), and (ii) a theoretical study of accelerated algorithms under noisy and inexact gradient oracles, which is supported by numerical experiments. This study leverages the simplicity of AGDP and its analysis to clarify the interaction between noise and acceleration and to suggest modifications to the algorithm that reduce the mean and variance of the error incurred due to the gradient noise.

This paper provides two main technical contributions: (i) a new accelerated method AGDP that generalizes Nesterov’s AGD and improves on the recent method AXGD (Diakonikolas & Orecchia, 2018), and (ii) a theoretical study of accelerated algorithms under noisy and inexact gradient oracles, which is supported by numerical experiments. This study leverages the simplicity of AGDP and its analysis to clarify the interaction between noise and acceleration and to suggest modifications to the algorithm that reduce the mean and variance of the error incurred due to the gradient noise.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization methods are attractive because they converge quickly across many large-scale problems. Their behavior becomes harder to understand when the supplied gradients contain noise or other inaccuracies. This paper studies how acceleration interacts with those imperfect gradient signals, treating stability as a central part of evaluating an optimization method.

The authors introduce AGDP, an accelerated algorithm that generalizes Nesterov’s accelerated gradient descent and improves on AXGD. Its comparatively simple form and analysis provide a basis for examining noisy and inexact gradient oracles. The algorithm is therefore both a methodological contribution and a vehicle for understanding acceleration under imperfect information.

The theoretical study is supported by numerical experiments. It also motivates modifications intended to reduce both the mean and variance of the error caused by gradient noise. These two targets address the average magnitude of noise-related error and its variability. The findings clarify how accelerated methods can be adjusted in noisy settings, without claiming that acceleration is universally insensitive to gradient corruption.
summary.tldr: AGDP provides a new accelerated optimization method and an analysis that motivates reducing the average and variability of errors from noisy gradients.

title: On Acceleration with Noise-Corrupted Gradients

abstract: We present two novel enhancements of an online importance-weighted active learning algorithm IWAL, using the properties of disagreements among hypotheses. The first enhancement, IWALD, prunes the hypothesis set with a more aggressive strategy based on the disagreement graph. We show that IWAL-D improves the generalization performance and the label complexity of the original IWAL, and quantify the improvement in terms of the disagreement graph coefficient. The second enhancement, IZOOM, further improves IWAL-D by adaptively zooming into the current version space and thus reducing the best-in-class error. We show that IZOOM admits favorable theoretical guarantees with the changing hypothesis set. We report experimental results on multiple datasets and demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve better test performances than IWAL given the same amount of labeling budget.
originalAbstract: We present two novel enhancements of an online importance-weighted active learning algorithm IWAL, using the properties of disagreements among hypotheses. The first enhancement, IWALD, prunes the hypothesis set with a more aggressive strategy based on the disagreement graph. We show that IWAL-D improves the generalization performance and the label complexity of the original IWAL, and quantify the improvement in terms of the disagreement graph coefficient. The second enhancement, IZOOM, further improves IWAL-D by adaptively zooming into the current version space and thus reducing the best-in-class error. We show that IZOOM admits favorable theoretical guarantees with the changing hypothesis set. We report experimental results on multiple datasets and demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve better test performances than IWAL given the same amount of labeling budget.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks to make effective use of a limited labeling budget. This paper improves IWAL, an online importance-weighted active learning algorithm, by using information about disagreements among candidate hypotheses. The central idea is that the structure of those disagreements can guide how the learner updates the collection of hypotheses it considers.

The first enhancement, IWAL-D, uses a disagreement graph to prune that collection more aggressively. The authors show improvements in both generalization performance and label complexity relative to IWAL, expressing the improvement through a disagreement graph coefficient. This ties the benefit to a property of the hypothesis disagreements rather than presenting it only as an experimental observation.

The second enhancement, IZOOM, adaptively focuses on the current version space and reduces the best error achievable within its changing hypothesis class. The paper provides theoretical guarantees that accommodate this changing set. Experiments on multiple datasets also show better test performance than IWAL at the same labeling budget, supporting the practical value of both enhancements.
summary.tldr: IWAL-D and IZOOM use hypothesis disagreements to improve active learning guarantees and test performance at a fixed labeling budget.

title: Active Learning with Disagreement Graphs

abstract: In this paper, we describe a novel approach to imitation learning that infers latent policies directly from state observations. We introduce a method that characterizes the causal effects of latent actions on observations while simultaneously predicting their likelihood. We then outline an action alignment procedure that leverages a small amount of environment interactions to determine a mapping between the latent and real-world actions. We show that this corrected labeling can be used for imitating the observed behavior, even though no expert actions are given. We evaluate our approach within classic control environments and a platform game and demonstrate that it performs better than standard approaches. Code for this work is available at https://github.com/ashedwards/ILPO.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we describe a novel approach to imitation learning that infers latent policies directly from state observations. We introduce a method that characterizes the causal effects of latent actions on observations while simultaneously predicting their likelihood. We then outline an action alignment procedure that leverages a small amount of environment interactions to determine a mapping between the latent and real-world actions. We show that this corrected labeling can be used for imitating the observed behavior, even though no expert actions are given. We evaluate our approach within classic control environments and a platform game and demonstrate that it performs better than standard approaches. Code for this work is available at https://github.com/ashedwards/ILPO.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes harder when demonstrations show states but omit the expert’s actions. The learner sees how behavior unfolds without being told which controls produced it. This paper addresses that setting by inferring a policy over latent actions directly from observations, creating an intermediate description of the demonstrated behavior.

The method learns the causal effects of these hidden actions on observations while predicting their likelihood. It then uses a small amount of interaction with the environment to align latent actions with real actions. This alignment supplies the connection between the model’s inferred action categories and the controls that the learner can actually execute.

Once aligned, the corrected action labels can support imitation even though expert action labels were never provided. Evaluations in classic control environments and a platform game show better performance than standard approaches. The contribution is a way to combine observation-based inference with limited active interaction: demonstrations reveal behavioral structure, and interaction establishes how to reproduce it through real controls.
summary.tldr: The method learns hidden actions from observed behavior and uses limited environment interaction to map them onto executable controls.

title: Imitating Latent Policies from Observation

abstract: We address the problem of unsupervised disentanglement of discrete and continuous explanatory factors of data. We first show a simple procedure for minimizing the total correlation of the continuous latent variables without having to use a discriminator network or perform importance sampling, via cascading the information flow in the beta-VAE framework. Furthermore, we propose a method which avoids offloading the entire burden of jointly modeling the continuous and discrete factors to the variational encoder by employing a separate discrete inference procedure. This leads to an interesting alternating minimization problem which switches between finding the most likely discrete configuration given the continuous factors and updating the variational encoder based on the computed discrete factors. Experiments show that the proposed method clearly disentangles discrete factors and significantly outperforms current disentanglement methods based on the disentanglement score and inference network classification score. The source code is available at https://github.com/snumllab/DisentanglementICML19.

Furthermore, we propose a method which avoids offloading the entire burden of jointly modeling the continuous and discrete factors to the variational encoder by employing a separate discrete inference procedure. This leads to an interesting alternating minimization problem which switches between finding the most likely discrete configuration given the continuous factors and updating the variational encoder based on the computed discrete factors. Experiments show that the proposed method clearly disentangles discrete factors and significantly outperforms current disentanglement methods based on the disentanglement score and inference network classification score. The source code is available at https://github.com/snumllab/DisentanglementICML19.

paragraphs: Data can reflect both categorical distinctions and smoothly varying properties. This paper studies how to separate these explanatory factors without supervision. The challenge is to learn discrete and continuous representations together while preventing the continuous variables from becoming entangled and avoiding placing the entire joint inference task on one variational encoder.

The first component reduces total correlation, a measure of dependence among continuous latent variables, by cascading information flow within a beta-VAE framework. It does so without a discriminator network or importance sampling. The second component introduces a separate procedure for discrete inference, dividing responsibility between that procedure and the encoder.

Training alternates between finding the most likely discrete configuration given the continuous factors and updating the encoder using the inferred discrete factors. This gives the two parts a repeated opportunity to inform each other. Experiments report clear separation of discrete factors and significant improvements over the compared disentanglement methods on disentanglement and inference-network classification scores. The evidence supports the combined alternating approach on those reported measures.
summary.tldr: Alternating discrete inference with variational encoder updates improves unsupervised separation of discrete and continuous factors in the reported experiments.

title: Learning Discrete and Continuous Factors of Data via Alternating Disentanglement

abstract: Relying on recent advances in statistical estimation of covariance distances based on random matrix theory, this article proposes an improved covariance and precision matrix estimation for a wide family of metrics. The method is shown to largely outperform the sample covariance matrix estimate and to compete with state-of-the-art methods, while at the same time being computationally simpler and faster. Applications to linear and quadratic discriminant analyses also show significant gains, therefore suggesting practical interest to statistical machine learning.

The method is shown to largely outperform the sample covariance matrix estimate and to compete with state-of-the-art methods, while at the same time being computationally simpler and faster. Applications to linear and quadratic discriminant analyses also show significant gains, therefore suggesting practical interest to statistical machine learning.

paragraphs: This paper proposes improved estimation of covariance and precision matrices using developments in random matrix theory. Its starting point is progress in estimating distances between covariance matrices. The authors turn that progress into a method for matrix estimation across a broad family of metrics.

The breadth of the metric family matters because the proposal is not tied to a single way of judging an estimate. The paper reports that the method substantially outperforms the sample covariance estimate and competes with leading alternatives. It also reports simpler and faster computation. The stated result therefore combines estimation quality with computational practicality, rather than presenting accuracy as the only criterion for comparing methods.

Applications to linear and quadratic discriminant analysis show significant gains as well. These downstream results provide evidence that the estimation improvements can benefit statistical machine learning tasks, beyond comparisons of the matrices themselves. The authors describe this as suggesting practical interest, supported by the combination of competitive estimation, lower computational burden, and improvements in the reported classification applications.
summary.tldr: Random matrix theory supports covariance and precision estimates that combine competitive accuracy with simpler computation and gains in discriminant analysis.

title: Random Matrix Improved Covariance Estimation for a Large Class of Metrics

abstract: The Differential privacy overview of Apple states, “Apple retains the collected data for a maximum of three months." Analysis of recent data is formalized by the sliding window model . This begs the question: what is the price of privacy in the sliding window model? In this paper, we study heavy hitters in the sliding window model with window size $w$. Previous works of Chan et al. (2012) estimates heavy hitters with an error of order $\theta w$ for a constant $\theta >0$. In this paper, we give an efficient differentially private algorithm to estimate heavy hitters in the sliding window model with $\widetilde O(w^{3/4})$ additive error and using $\widetilde O(\sqrt{w})$ space.

(2012) estimates heavy hitters with an error of order $\theta w$ for a constant $\theta >0$. In this paper, we give an efficient differentially private algorithm to estimate heavy hitters in the sliding window model with $\widetilde O(w^{3/4})$ additive error and using $\widetilde O(\sqrt{w})$ space.

paragraphs: When analysis concerns only recent data, a sliding window provides a formal way to specify which observations count. This paper studies how to estimate heavy hitters within such a window while preserving differential privacy. Its central question is the cost of privacy when the relevant data continually changes as the window advances.

For a window containing w observations, earlier work had additive error proportional to w with a fixed positive proportionality constant. The proposed efficient algorithm achieves additive error of order w to the three quarters power, up to logarithmic factors. It uses space of order the square root of w, again up to logarithmic factors. Both stated quantities grow sublinearly with the window size.

The result improves the dependence of estimation error on window size while also keeping memory below linear growth. This addresses accuracy and storage together for private analysis of recent observations. The contribution is an algorithmic guarantee for heavy hitters in the sliding window setting, rather than a reported empirical comparison.
summary.tldr: A private sliding window heavy hitter algorithm achieves roughly w^(3/4) additive error using roughly square-root-of-w space, up to logarithmic factors.

title: Sublinear Space Private Algorithms Under the Sliding Window Model

abstract: The goal of standard 1-bit compressive sensing is to accurately recover an unknown sparse vector from binary-valued measurements, each indicating the sign of a linear function of the vector. Motivated by recent advances in compressive sensing with generative models, where a generative modeling assumption replaces the usual sparsity assumption, we study the problem of 1-bit compressive sensing with generative models. We first consider noiseless 1-bit measurements, and provide sample complexity bounds for approximate recovery under i.i.d. Gaussian measurements and a Lipschitz continuous generative prior, as well as a near-matching algorithm-independent lower bound. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Binary $\epsilon$-Stable Embedding property, which characterizes the robustness of the reconstruction to measurement errors and noise, also holds for 1-bit compressive sensing with Lipschitz continuous generative models with sufficiently many Gaussian measurements. In addition, we apply our results to neural network generative models, and provide a proof-of-concept numerical experiment demonstrating significant improvements over sparsity-based approaches.

Motivated by recent advances in compressive sensing with generative models, where a generative modeling assumption replaces the usual sparsity assumption, we study the problem of 1-bit compressive sensing with generative models. We first consider noiseless 1-bit measurements, and provide sample complexity bounds for approximate recovery under i.i.d. Gaussian measurements and a Lipschitz continuous generative prior, as well as a near-matching algorithm-independent lower bound. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Binary $\epsilon$-Stable Embedding property, which characterizes the robustness of the reconstruction to measurement errors and noise, also holds for 1-bit compressive sensing with Lipschitz continuous generative models with sufficiently many Gaussian measurements. In addition, we apply our results to neural network generative models, and provide a proof-of-concept numerical experiment demonstrating significant improvements over sparsity-based approaches.

paragraphs: One-bit compressive sensing reconstructs an unknown vector from measurements that retain only the sign of a linear function. Traditional formulations assume the vector is sparse. This paper studies an alternative structural assumption: the vector is described by a generative model. The question becomes how many binary measurements are needed for accurate approximate recovery under that prior.

For noiseless measurements, the authors establish sample-complexity bounds using independent Gaussian measurements and a Lipschitz-continuous generative prior. They also give a nearly matching lower bound that applies regardless of the reconstruction algorithm. Together, the bounds describe both what can be achieved and how much measurement information is fundamentally required within the studied setting.

The paper additionally establishes a binary stable embedding property when sufficiently many Gaussian measurements are available. This property characterizes robustness to measurement errors and noise. The results are applied to neural network generators, and a proof-of-concept numerical experiment shows substantial improvements over sparsity-based approaches. That experiment illustrates the potential benefit of the generative assumption alongside the formal measurement guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the binary measurements needed for recovery under Lipschitz generative priors and establishes a stability property for sufficiently many Gaussian measurements.

title: Sample Complexity Bounds for 1-bit Compressive Sensing and Binary Stable Embeddings with Generative Priors

abstract: The choice of the control frequency of a system has a relevant impact on the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to learn a highly performing policy. In this paper, we introduce the notion of action persistence that consists in the repetition of an action for a fixed number of decision steps, having the effect of modifying the control frequency. We start analyzing how action persistence affects the performance of the optimal policy, and then we present a novel algorithm, Persistent Fitted Q-Iteration (PFQI), that extends FQI, with the goal of learning the optimal value function at a given persistence. After having provided a theoretical study of PFQI and a heuristic approach to identify the optimal persistence, we present an experimental campaign on benchmark domains to show the advantages of action persistence and proving the effectiveness of our persistence selection method.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system must decide both what action to take and how often it can change that action. The paper studies this second choice through action persistence: repeating an action for a fixed number of decision steps. Changing persistence changes the effective control frequency and can affect the quality of the policy that learning produces.

The authors first analyze how persistence changes the performance of the optimal policy. They then introduce Persistent Fitted Q-Iteration, or PFQI, an extension of Fitted Q-Iteration designed to learn the optimal value function for a specified persistence. This gives the control-frequency choice an explicit place in the learning procedure.

The paper provides a theoretical study of PFQI and a heuristic for selecting persistence. Benchmark experiments demonstrate advantages from action persistence and support the effectiveness of the selection method. These results suggest that control frequency deserves attention as part of policy learning, while the persistence-selection procedure remains a heuristic rather than a stated guarantee of finding the best setting.
summary.tldr: PFQI incorporates repeated actions into batch reinforcement learning, with theory and experiments showing the value of choosing control frequency carefully.

title: Control Frequency Adaptation via Action Persistence in Batch Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We investigate the generalisation performance of Distributed Gradient Descent with implicit regularisation and random features in the homogenous setting where a network of agents are given data sampled independently from the same unknown distribution. Along with reducing the memory footprint, random features are particularly convenient in this setting as they provide a common parameterisation across agents that allows to overcome previous difficulties in implementing decentralised kernel regression. Under standard source and capacity assumptions, we establish high probability bounds on the predictive performance for each agent as a function of the step size, number of iterations, inverse spectral gap of the communication matrix and number of random features. By tuning these parameters, we obtain statistical rates that are minimax optimal with respect to the total number of samples in the network. The algorithm provides a linear improvement over single-machine gradient descent in memory cost and, when agents hold enough data with respect to the network size and inverse spectral gap, a linear speed up in computational run-time for any network topology. We present simulations that show how the number of random features, iterations and samples impact predictive performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning across a communicating network of agents, each receiving independent data from the same unknown distribution. It combines distributed gradient descent with random features and implicit regularization. Random features reduce memory requirements and give every agent a shared parameterization, addressing implementation difficulties in decentralized kernel regression.

Under source and capacity assumptions, the authors bound each agent's predictive performance with high probability. The bounds account for the step size, training iterations, number of random features, and the communication matrix's inverse spectral gap. Tuning these quantities yields statistical rates that are minimax optimal relative to the total amount of data across the network.

The algorithm offers a linear improvement in memory cost over single-machine gradient descent. A linear computational speedup is also available for any network topology when each agent holds enough data relative to network size and inverse spectral gap. Simulations examine how features, iterations, and sample counts affect prediction, connecting the theoretical choices to observed behavior.
summary.tldr: Random features support decentralized learning with optimal statistical rates and conditional linear computational speedups.

title: Decentralised Learning with Random Features and Distributed Gradient Descent

abstract: In label-noise learning, the transition matrix plays a key role in building statistically consistent classifiers. Existing consistent estimators for the transition matrix have been developed by exploiting anchor points. However, the anchor-point assumption is not always satisfied in real scenarios. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end framework for solving label-noise learning without anchor points, in which we simultaneously optimize two objectives: the cross entropy loss between the noisy label and the predicted probability by the neural network, and the volume of the simplex formed by the columns of the transition matrix. Our proposed framework can identify the transition matrix if the clean class-posterior probabilities are sufficiently scattered. This is by far the mildest assumption under which the transition matrix is provably identifiable and the learned classifier is statistically consistent. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Learning with incorrect labels often relies on a transition matrix describing how clean labels become noisy ones. Estimating this matrix can help produce statistically consistent classifiers. Existing consistent estimators use anchor points, but the assumption that such points exist does not always hold in real data.

This paper proposes an end-to-end framework that learns without anchor points. It simultaneously optimizes cross entropy between observed noisy labels and network predictions, and the volume of a simplex formed by the transition matrix's columns. The geometric objective adds structure to matrix estimation alongside the objective that fits the observed labels.

The guarantee depends on clean class-posterior probabilities being sufficiently scattered. Under that condition, the framework can identify the transition matrix and learn a statistically consistent classifier. The authors characterize this as the mildest known assumption supporting those conclusions. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness and robustness. The advance therefore removes the anchor-point requirement while retaining an explicit alternative condition that makes recovery provable; it does not claim that arbitrary label corruption can be resolved without assumptions.
summary.tldr: Joint prediction and geometric optimization recover label-noise transitions without anchor points when clean class probabilities are sufficiently scattered.

title: Provably End-to-end Label-noise Learning without Anchor Points

abstract: Descent methods for deep networks are notoriously capricious: they require careful tuning of step size, momentum and weight decay, and which method will work best on a new benchmark is a priori unclear. To address this problem, this paper conducts a combined study of neural architecture and optimisation, leading to a new optimiser called Nero: the neuronal rotator. Nero trains reliably without momentum or weight decay, works in situations where Adam and SGD fail, and requires little to no learning rate tuning. Also, Nero’s memory footprint is square root that of Adam or LAMB. Nero combines two ideas: (1) projected gradient descent over the space of balanced networks; (2) neuron-specific updates, where the step size sets the angle through which each neuron’s hyperplane turns. The paper concludes by discussing how this geometric connection between architecture and optimisation may impact theories of generalisation in deep learning.

paragraphs: Training deep networks often requires carefully choosing a learning rate, momentum, and weight decay, with limited guidance about which optimizer will work on a new benchmark. This paper studies architecture and optimization together to develop Nero, an optimizer whose updates have a direct geometric interpretation at the level of individual neurons.

Nero combines projected gradient descent over balanced networks with neuron-specific updates. Its step size controls the angle through which a neuron’s hyperplane rotates. This connects the scale of an optimization step to a geometric change in the neuron, making the architecture part of how the update is defined.

The authors report reliable training without momentum or weight decay, little to no learning-rate tuning, and success in situations where Adam and SGD fail. They also state that Nero’s memory footprint is the square root of that of Adam or LAMB. The paper closes by discussing possible implications for theories of generalization; these are prospective implications of the geometric connection, separate from the reported optimization behavior.
summary.tldr: Nero uses neuron-specific rotations and balanced-network constraints to train with little tuning and without momentum or weight decay.

title: Learning by Turning: Neural Architecture Aware Optimisation

abstract: Designing learning algorithms that are resistant to perturbations of the underlying data distribution is a problem of wide practical and theoretical importance. We present a general approach to this problem focusing on unsupervised learning. The key assumption is that the perturbing distribution is characterized by larger losses relative to a given class of admissible models. This is exploited by a general descent algorithm which minimizes an $L$-statistic criterion over the model class, weighting small losses more. Our analysis characterizes the robustness of the method in terms of bounds on the reconstruction error relative to the underlying unperturbed distribution. As a byproduct, we prove uniform convergence bounds with respect to the proposed criterion for several popular models in unsupervised learning, a result which may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments with \textsc{kmeans} clustering and principal subspace analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general approach to unsupervised learning when the observed data distribution has been perturbed. Its key assumption is that the perturbing distribution produces larger losses relative to the allowed class of models. This creates a basis for distinguishing the perturbation’s influence through the losses encountered during learning.

The proposed descent algorithm minimizes an L-statistic criterion that assigns greater weight to smaller losses. Under the stated assumption, this weighting reduces the influence associated with the perturbing distribution. The analysis measures robustness through bounds on reconstruction error relative to the original, unperturbed distribution, connecting the modified objective to the quality of the desired reconstruction.

The authors also prove uniform convergence bounds for the criterion across several popular unsupervised models. These results provide theoretical support for learning with the proposed loss weighting. Numerical experiments on k-means clustering and principal subspace analysis demonstrate effectiveness in the tested settings. The assumption linking perturbations to higher losses is central to the approach’s robustness argument.
summary.tldr: Weighting smaller losses more heavily supports robust unsupervised learning when perturbing data produces larger losses.

title: Robust Unsupervised Learning via L-statistic Minimization

abstract: Many recent studies have highlighted the susceptibility of virtually all machine-learning models to adversarial attacks. Adversarial attacks are imperceptible changes to an input example of a given prediction model. Such changes are carefully designed to alter the otherwise correct prediction of the model. In this paper, we study the generalization properties of adversarial learning. In particular, we derive high-probability generalization bounds on the adversarial risk in terms of the empirical adversarial risk, the complexity of the function class and the adversarial noise set. Our bounds are generally applicable to many models, losses, and adversaries. We showcase its applicability by deriving adversarial generalization bounds for the multi-class classification setting and various prediction models (including linear models and Deep Neural Networks). We also derive optimistic adversarial generalization bounds for the case of smooth losses. These are the first fast-rate bounds valid for adversarial deep learning to the best of our knowledge.

paragraphs: An adversarial attack makes a carefully chosen, imperceptible change to an input to disrupt a model’s prediction. Measuring resistance on training examples leaves a further question: how well does that resistance extend to new examples? This paper studies that generalization question through theoretical bounds on adversarial risk.

The bounds hold with high probability and relate adversarial risk to three ingredients: empirical adversarial risk, the complexity of the prediction class, and the set of perturbations available to the adversary. Including the perturbation set makes the threat model part of the generalization analysis. The framework applies broadly across models, losses, and adversaries.

The authors demonstrate its use for multiclass classification and several prediction families, including linear models and deep neural networks. They also derive optimistic bounds for smooth losses, obtaining fast-rate guarantees for adversarial deep learning that they describe as the first known to them. These results provide tools for analyzing robust generalization, with the stronger rate statements specifically tied to the smooth-loss case.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds adversarial generalization using training risk, model complexity, and allowed perturbations, with fast-rate results for smooth losses.

title: On the Generalization Analysis of Adversarial Learning

abstract: In scalable machine learning systems, model training is often parallelized over multiple nodes that run without tight synchronization. Most analysis results for the related asynchronous algorithms use an upper bound on the information delays in the system to determine learning rates. Not only are such bounds hard to obtain in advance, but they also result in unnecessarily slow convergence. In this paper, we show that it is possible to use learning rates that depend on the actual time-varying delays in the system. We develop general convergence results for delay-adaptive asynchronous iterations and specialize these to proximal incremental gradient descent and block coordinate descent algorithms. For each of these methods, we demonstrate how delays can be measured on-line, present delay-adaptive step-size policies, and illustrate their theoretical and practical advantages over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Distributed training often lets computing nodes work without waiting for one another, so updates can rely on information that is already old. Many analyses choose learning rates using an upper bound on these delays. Such a bound may be difficult to know beforehand, and planning around it can make convergence unnecessarily slow.

This paper develops learning rates that respond to the delays actually encountered as the system runs. The authors establish general convergence results for asynchronous iterations with these adaptive step sizes. The key change is to make the timing information part of the update policy, rather than setting the learning rate solely from a fixed delay bound.

The framework is specialized to proximal incremental gradient descent and block coordinate descent. For both, the authors explain how to measure delays online and provide corresponding step-size policies. They illustrate theoretical and practical advantages over the state of the art, connecting the convergence analysis to update rules that can use changing conditions in a running system.
summary.tldr: Delay-adaptive learning rates use observed information delays to improve asynchronous optimization without relying solely on a preset worst-case delay bound.

title: Delay-Adaptive Step-sizes for Asynchronous Learning

abstract: In this paper, we establish efficient and uncoupled learning dynamics so that, when employed by all players in multiplayer perfect-recall imperfect-information extensive-form games, the trigger regret of each player grows as $O(\log T)$ after $T$ repetitions of play. This improves exponentially over the prior best known trigger-regret bound of $O(T^{1/4})$, and settles a recent open question by Bai et al. (2022). As an immediate consequence, we guarantee convergence to the set of extensive-form correlated equilibria and coarse correlated equilibria at a near-optimal rate of $\frac{\log T}{T}$. Building on prior work, at the heart of our construction lies a more general result regarding fixed points deriving from rational functions with polynomial degree, a property that we establish for the fixed points of (coarse) trigger deviation functions. Moreover, our construction leverages a refined regret circuit for the convex hull, which—unlike prior guarantees—preserves the RVU property introduced by Syrgkanis et al. (NIPS, 2015); this observation has an independent interest in establishing near-optimal regret under learning dynamics based on a CFR-type decomposition of the regret.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated learning in multiplayer games with sequential decisions and imperfect information. It assumes perfect recall, so players retain their own past information and actions. The authors construct efficient, uncoupled learning dynamics and analyze what happens when every player uses them, focusing on regret associated with trigger deviations.

After T repetitions, each player's trigger regret grows only logarithmically in T, improving the previous bound of order T to the one-quarter power. This yields convergence to extensive-form correlated equilibria and coarse correlated equilibria at a rate of log T divided by T. The guarantee is therefore about the collective behavior generated when all players follow the proposed dynamics.

The construction uses a general result about fixed points derived from rational functions of polynomial degree, together with a refined method for combining regret computations over a convex hull. That refinement preserves a technical property called RVU, which supports the improved analysis. Beyond the equilibrium rate, the work supplies tools for establishing near-optimal regret in learning dynamics built from a counterfactual-regret-style decomposition.
summary.tldr: Efficient learning dynamics achieve logarithmic trigger regret and near-optimal correlated-equilibrium convergence when all players use them in the specified games.

title: Near-Optimal $Φ$-Regret Learning in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image generation with diffusion models present transformative capabilities in image quality. However, user controllability of the generated image, and fast adaptation to new tasks still remains an open challenge, currently mostly addressed by costly and long re-training and fine-tuning or ad-hoc adaptations to specific image generation tasks. In this work, we present MultiDiffusion, a unified framework that enables versatile and controllable image generation, using a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model, without any further training or finetuning. At the center of our approach is a new generation process, based on an optimization task that binds together multiple diffusion generation processes with a shared set of parameters or constraints. We show that MultiDiffusion can be readily applied to generate high quality and diverse images that adhere to user-provided controls, such as desired aspect ratio (e.g., panorama), and spatial guiding signals, ranging from tight segmentation masks to bounding boxes.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce compelling images, but adapting them to specific user controls often requires additional training or specialized modifications. MultiDiffusion tackles control at generation time. It uses an already trained text-to-image diffusion model and introduces a generation framework that requires no further training or fine-tuning.

The central idea is to bind multiple diffusion generation processes through an optimization problem. Those processes share parameters or constraints, so their evolution is coordinated rather than independent. This provides a common mechanism for applying different kinds of controls while continuing to use the capabilities of the pretrained model. The optimization becomes the point where the generation processes are brought together.

The authors demonstrate high-quality, diverse images that follow requested aspect ratios, including panoramas, as well as spatial guidance. That guidance can range from detailed segmentation masks to looser bounding boxes. These findings show that the same framework can accommodate controls with different levels of spatial precision, making pretrained image generation adaptable to several user-directed tasks without retraining.
summary.tldr: MultiDiffusion coordinates multiple diffusion processes to generate images with user-specified shapes and spatial layouts without additional training.

title: MultiDiffusion: Fusing Diffusion Paths for Controlled Image Generation

abstract: Statistical whitening transformations play a fundamental role in many computational systems, and may also play an important role in biological sensory systems. Existing neural circuit models of adaptive whitening operate by modifying synaptic interactions; however, such modifications would seem both too slow and insufficiently reversible. Motivated by the extensive neuroscience literature on gain modulation, we propose an alternative model that adaptively whitens its responses by modulating the gains of individual neurons. Starting from a novel whitening objective, we derive an online algorithm that whitens its outputs by adjusting the marginal variances of an overcomplete set of projections. We map the algorithm onto a recurrent neural network with fixed synaptic weights and gain-modulating interneurons. We demonstrate numerically that sign-constraining the gains improves robustness of the network to ill-conditioned inputs, and a generalization of the circuit achieves a form of local whitening in convolutional populations, such as those found throughout the visual or auditory systems.

paragraphs: Statistical whitening adjusts the relationships and variation in a population’s responses. It is useful in computational systems and may also matter in biological sensory processing. Existing circuit models achieve adaptive whitening by changing synaptic interactions, but the authors argue that these changes appear too slow and insufficiently reversible for the intended adaptation.

The proposed alternative changes individual neurons’ gains while keeping synaptic weights fixed. Starting from a new whitening objective, the authors derive an online algorithm that adjusts the individual variances of an overcomplete collection of projections. They then express this algorithm as a recurrent neural circuit containing interneurons that modulate gain.

Numerical results show that constraining the signs of the gains makes the circuit more robust to ill-conditioned inputs. An extension also produces a form of local whitening in convolutional neural populations, relevant to structures found in visual and auditory systems. These results provide a computational account of how gain modulation could support adaptive whitening, without establishing that biological circuits necessarily implement this particular mechanism.
summary.tldr: A neural circuit model performs adaptive whitening by changing neuronal gains while keeping synaptic weights fixed.

title: Adaptive Whitening in Neural Populations with Gain-modulating Interneurons

abstract: Evaluating the performance of perception modules in autonomous driving is one of the most critical tasks in developing the complex intelligent system. While module-level unit test metrics adopted from traditional computer vision tasks are feasible to some extent, it remains far less explored to measure the impact of perceptual noise on the driving quality of autonomous vehicles in a consistent and holistic manner. In this work, we propose a principled framework that provides a coherent and systematic understanding of the impact an error in the perception module imposes on an autonomous agent’s planning that actually controls the vehicle. Specifically, the planning process is formulated as expected utility maximisation, where all input signals from upstream modules jointly provide a world state description, and the planner strives for the optimal action by maximising the expected utility determined by both world states and actions. We show that, under practical conditions, the objective function can be represented as an inner product between the world state description and the utility function in a Hilbert space. This geometric interpretation enables a novel way to analyse the impact of noise in world state estimation on planning and leads to a universal metric for evaluating perception. The whole framework resembles the idea of transcendental idealism in the classical philosophical literature, which gives the name to our approach.

paragraphs: Perception metrics borrowed from computer vision do not fully describe how perception errors affect an autonomous vehicle’s driving decisions. This paper develops a framework for evaluating perception through its consequences for planning. The central question is how errors in the estimated world state change the decision process that actually controls the vehicle.

The authors express planning as expected-utility maximization. Signals from upstream modules jointly describe the world, and the planner chooses an action according to a utility determined by both that world state and the action. This formulation connects the quality of perception inputs to the objective used when selecting vehicle behavior.

Under practical conditions, the objective can be written as an inner product between a world-state description and a utility function in a Hilbert space. That geometric representation enables analysis of how world-estimation noise affects planning and leads to a proposed universal perception metric. The contribution is a principled connection between perception error and planning utility, with the geometric result depending on the conditions established in the paper.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a geometric framework and perception metric that assess autonomous-driving perception errors through their effects on planning utility.

title: Transcendental Idealism of Planner: Evaluating Perception from Planning Perspective for Autonomous Driving

abstract: Generative flow networks (GFlowNets) are a family of algorithms that learn a generative policy to sample discrete objects $x$ with non-negative reward $R(x)$. Learning objectives guarantee the GFlowNet samples $x$ from the target distribution $p^*(x) \propto R(x)$ when loss is globally minimized over all states or trajectories, but it is unclear how well they perform with practical limits on training resources. We introduce an efficient evaluation strategy to compare the learned sampling distribution to the target reward distribution. As flows can be underdetermined given training data, we clarify the importance of learned flows to generalization and matching $p^*(x)$ in practice. We investigate how to learn better flows, and propose (i) prioritized replay training of high-reward $x$, (ii) relative edge flow policy parametrization, and (iii) a novel guided trajectory balance objective, and show how it can solve a substructure credit assignment problem. We substantially improve sample efficiency on biochemical design tasks.
