paragraphs: GFlowNets learn to generate discrete objects with probabilities proportional to their nonnegative rewards. Their objectives guarantee the desired distribution when the loss is globally minimized across all states or trajectories. This paper investigates what happens under practical training limits, where that ideal optimization condition may not be achieved.

The authors introduce an efficient way to compare the learned sampling distribution with the target reward distribution. They also explain why learned flows matter for generalization: the training data can leave those flows underdetermined. Consequently, the way a model resolves that freedom affects how closely its generated objects follow the desired reward-weighted distribution.

To improve training, the paper proposes prioritized replay of high-reward objects, relative edge-flow policy parameterization, and a guided trajectory-balance objective. It shows how the guided objective can address credit assignment to substructures and reports substantial improvements in sample efficiency on biochemical design tasks. The contribution connects a practical evaluation method with training changes intended to improve distribution matching when available learning resources are limited.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes practical GFlowNet distribution matching and introduces training changes that substantially improve sample efficiency on biochemical design tasks.

title: Towards Understanding and Improving GFlowNet Training

abstract: 3D point clouds serve as a crucial data representation in numerous real-world applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and medical imaging. While the advancements in deep learning have spurred the utilization of 3D point clouds, deep models are notoriously vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Various defense solutions have been proposed to build robust models against adversarial attacks. In this work, we pinpoint a major limitation of the leading empirical defense, adversarial training, when applied to 3D point cloud models: gradient obfuscation, which significantly hampers robustness against potent attacks. To bridge the gap, we propose PointDP, a purification strategy that leverages diffusion models to defend against 3D adversarial attacks. Since PointDP does not rely on predefined adversarial examples for training, it can defend against a variety of threats. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of PointDP across six representative 3D point cloud architectures, employing sixteen strong and adaptive attacks to manifest its foundational robustness. Our evaluation shows that PointDP achieves significantly better (i.e., 12.6%-40.3%) adversarial robustness than state-of-the-art methods under strong attacks bounded by different $\ell_p$ norms.

paragraphs: This paper examines how reliably recognition models handle deliberately altered 3D point clouds. Its starting finding concerns adversarial training, a leading defense: in the studied setting, it can obscure gradients rather than provide robustness against powerful attacks. This distinction matters because difficulty finding an attack does not necessarily mean that a model can withstand one.

The authors propose PointDP, which uses diffusion models to purify point clouds as a defense. Its training does not depend on a predefined collection of adversarial examples. This gives the method a way to address varied threats without tying its defense to that particular collection of attacks.

The evaluation covers six representative point cloud architectures and sixteen strong and adaptive attacks. Under strong attacks constrained by different ℓp norms, the authors report adversarial robustness improvements of 12.6%–40.3% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support diffusion-based purification across the evaluated architectures and threats, while the gradient-obfuscation finding explains why demanding attack evaluations are central to assessing the result.
summary.tldr: PointDP uses diffusion-based purification to improve 3D point cloud robustness against strong attacks while exposing weaknesses in adversarial training.

title: A Critical Revisit of Adversarial Robustness in 3D Point Cloud Recognition with Diffusion-Driven Purification

abstract: Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) is an effective tuning method for adapting pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) to downstream tasks. It leverages extra learnable tokens, known as prompts, which steer the frozen pretrained ViTs. Although VPT has demonstrated its applicability with supervised vision transformers, it often underperforms with self-supervised ones. Through empirical observations, we deduce that the effectiveness of VPT hinges largely on the ViT blocks with which the prompt tokens interact. Specifically, VPT shows improved performance on image classification tasks for MAE and MoCo v3 when the prompt tokens are inserted into later blocks rather than the first block. These observations suggest that there exists an optimal location of blocks for the insertion of prompt tokens. Unfortunately, identifying the optimal blocks for prompts within each self-supervised ViT for diverse future scenarios is a costly process. To mitigate this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that learns a gate for each ViT block to adjust its intervention into the prompt tokens. With our method, prompt tokens are selectively influenced by blocks that require steering for task adaptation. Our method outperforms VPT variants in FGVC and VTAB image classification and ADE20K semantic segmentation. The code is available at https://github.com/ryongithub/GatedPromptTuning.

paragraphs: Visual prompt tuning adapts a pretrained vision transformer by learning extra tokens while keeping the pretrained model frozen. Although effective with supervised pretraining, it often performs less well with self-supervised models. This paper investigates whether the problem depends on which transformer blocks interact with the prompts.

For MAE and MoCo v3 image classification, the authors observe better performance when prompts enter later blocks instead of the first block. This suggests that prompt placement matters and that an effective location may vary across models and tasks. Manually identifying the best placement for every future setting would be costly.

The proposed method learns a gate for each block to regulate its interaction with prompt tokens. These gates allow selective influence from blocks relevant to task adaptation, turning a placement decision into something learned during tuning. The method outperforms VPT variants on FGVC and VTAB classification and ADE20K semantic segmentation. The results support controlling where prompts interact with the model as an important part of adapting self-supervised transformers.
summary.tldr: Learned block-level gates improve visual prompt tuning by controlling how prompts interact with self-supervised vision transformers.

title: Improving Visual Prompt Tuning for Self-supervised Vision Transformers

abstract: Combinatorial optimization (CO) is naturally discrete, making machine-learning techniques based on differentiable optimization inapplicable. Karalias & Loukas (2020) adapted the probabilistic method by Erdős & Spencer (1974), to incorporate CO into differentiable optimization. Their work ignited the research on unsupervised learning for CO, composed of two main components: probabilistic objectives and derandomization. However, each component confronts unique challenges. First, deriving objectives under complex conditions and constraints is nontrivial. Second, the derandomization process is underexplored, and the existing derandomization methods are either random sampling or naive rounding. In this work, we aim to tackle complex conditions in unsupervised CO. First, we concretize the targets for probabilistic objective construction and derandomization with theoretical justification. Then, for various complex conditions commonly involved in different CO problems, we derive nontrivial objectives and derandomization to meet the targets. Finally, we apply the derivations to various CO problems. Via extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs, we validate the correctness of our derivations and show our empirical superiority w.r.t. both optimization quality and speed.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization involves discrete choices, which makes direct use of differentiable learning difficult. One approach replaces those choices with probabilistic objectives and then converts the result into a discrete solution. This paper addresses challenges in both stages, especially when problems include complex conditions such as those highlighted in its title.

The authors first specify theoretically justified targets for constructing probabilistic objectives and for derandomization, the process of obtaining a discrete output. They then derive objectives and conversion procedures for conditions that recur across different combinatorial problems. Treating both stages together addresses the gap between optimizing a probabilistic representation and producing a useful discrete solution.

The derivations are applied to several combinatorial optimization problems and evaluated on synthetic and real-world graphs. The authors report evidence validating the derivations and empirical advantages in both solution quality and speed. The contribution is a set of principled tools for handling recurring constraints, supported by experiments showing that improvements to objective construction and derandomization can work together.
summary.tldr: The paper derives probabilistic objectives and derandomization procedures for common combinatorial constraints, reporting gains in solution quality and speed.

title: Tackling Prevalent Conditions in Unsupervised Combinatorial Optimization: Cardinality, Minimum, Covering, and More

abstract: Value functions are an essential component in deep reinforcement learning (RL), that are typically trained via mean squared error regression to match bootstrapped target values. However, scaling value-based RL methods to large networks has proven challenging. This difficulty is in stark contrast to supervised learning: by leveraging a cross-entropy classification loss, supervised methods have scaled reliably to massive networks. Observing this discrepancy, in this paper, we investigate whether the scalability of deep RL can also be improved simply by using classification in place of regression for training value functions. We show that training value functions with categorical cross-entropy significantly enhances performance and scalability across various domains, including single-task RL on Atari 2600 games, multi-task RL on Atari with large-scale ResNets, robotic manipulation with Q-transformers, playing Chess without search, and a language-agent Wordle task with high-capacity Transformers, achieving state-of-the-art results on these domains. Through careful analysis, we show that categorical cross-entropy mitigates issues inherent to value-based RL, such as noisy targets and non-stationarity. We argue that shifting to categorical cross-entropy for training value functions can substantially improve the scalability of deep RL at little-to-no cost.

paragraphs: Value functions are usually trained to match bootstrapped numerical targets using mean squared error. This paper investigates whether that regression objective contributes to the difficulty of scaling value-based reinforcement learning to larger networks. It takes inspiration from supervised learning, where cross-entropy classification objectives have supported training at much larger scales.

The proposed change is to train value functions with categorical cross-entropy. The authors evaluate this choice across single-task Atari, multi-task Atari with large ResNets, robotic manipulation with Q-transformers, chess without search, and a Wordle language-agent task using high-capacity Transformers. They report significant gains in performance and scalability, including state-of-the-art results in these domains.

Their analysis finds that categorical cross-entropy mitigates problems associated with noisy targets and changing learning targets. These are central difficulties in value-based reinforcement learning, so the objective change addresses more than network size alone. The authors argue that switching the training loss offers a way to improve scalability at little or no added cost, supported by the range of evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Training value functions with categorical cross-entropy improves deep reinforcement learning performance and scalability across several evaluated domains.

title: Stop Regressing: Training Value Functions via Classification for Scalable Deep RL

abstract: We address the challenge of actively ranking a set of items/players with varying values/strengths. The comparison outcomes are random, with a greater noise the closer the values. A crucial requirement is that, at each iteration of the algorithm, all items must be compared once, i.e., an iteration is a perfect matching. Furthermore, we presume that comparing two players with closely matched strengths incurs no cost and, in contrast, a unit cost is associated with comparing players whose strength difference is more substantial. Our secondary objective is to determine an optimal matching between players based on this cost function: we propose and analyze an algorithm that draws on concepts from both AKS sorting networks and bandit theory. Our algorithm achieves both objectives with high probability, and the total cost is optimal (up to logarithmic terms).

paragraphs: This paper studies how to rank players or items when comparisons are noisy and every participant must take part in each round. Each round therefore consists of a perfect matching: everyone is paired with exactly one opponent. The comparison noise is greater when the participants have similar underlying strengths, making close distinctions particularly difficult.

The task also includes a matchmaking objective. Under the assumed cost rule, pairing similarly strong players is free, while pairing players with a larger strength difference costs one unit. The algorithm must therefore learn the ranking while controlling the cost of the comparisons it chooses, and also determine an optimal matching under that rule.

The proposed algorithm combines ideas from AKS sorting networks and bandit theory. The authors prove that it achieves both objectives with high probability and that its total cost is optimal up to logarithmic factors. The result connects reliable ranking with economical matchmaking under the specific noise, participation, and cost assumptions of the problem.
summary.tldr: An algorithm ranks noisy competitors and finds an optimal matching while pairing every participant each round, with near-optimal total comparison cost.

title: Active Ranking and Matchmaking, with Perfect Matchings

abstract: The latent space of diffusion model mostly still remains unexplored, despite its great success and potential in the field of generative modeling. In fact, the latent space of existing diffusion models are entangled, with a distorted mapping from its latent space to image space. To tackle this problem, we present Isometric Diffusion, equipping a diffusion model with a geometric regularizer to guide the model to learn a geometrically sound latent space of the training data manifold. This approach allows diffusion models to learn a more disentangled latent space, which enables smoother interpolation, more accurate inversion, and more precise control over attributes directly in the latent space. Our extensive experiments consisting of image interpolations, image inversions, and linear editing show the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: A diffusion model's latent space provides an internal representation from which images can be generated or manipulated. The paper identifies a problem with existing representations: attributes are entangled, and the mapping from latent space to image space is geometrically distorted. As a result, manipulating the representation does not provide the smooth, precise control that a better organized space could offer.

The authors introduce Isometric Diffusion, which adds a geometric regularizer to the model. This extra training constraint guides the learned latent space toward the geometry of the training data manifold. The goal is a more disentangled representation, where changes in latent space support more predictable changes in the resulting images.

The paper evaluates image interpolation, image inversion, and linear editing. These respectively examine transitions between images, recovery of a latent representation for an image, and attribute changes made through latent-space edits. The reported experiments support smoother interpolation, more accurate inversion, and more precise attribute control. The findings connect the geometry of the learned representation to practical image manipulation capabilities.
summary.tldr: Isometric Diffusion adds geometric regularization to improve latent-space disentanglement, image interpolation, inversion, and editing.

title: Isometric Representation Learning for Disentangled Latent Space of Diffusion Models

abstract: Graph out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, aiming to generalize graph neural networks (GNNs) under distribution shifts between training and testing environments, has attracted ever-increasing attention recently. However, existing literature heavily relies on sufficient task-dependent graph labels, which are often scarce or even unavailable, limiting their applications in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we study the self-supervised graph OOD generalization problem, i.e., learning GNNs capable of achieving relatively stable performances under distribution shifts without graph labels. However, the problem remains largely unexplored, with the critical challenge that the invariant and variant information are highly entangled in graphs. To solve this problem, we propose an OOD generalized disentangled graph contrastive learning model (OOD-GCL), which is capable of learning disentangled graph-level representations with self-supervision that can handle distribution shifts between training and testing graph data. Specifically, we first introduce a disentangled graph encoder to map each input graph into the factorized graph representation. Then we propose a tailored disentangled invariant self-supervised learning module to maximize predictive ability of the representations and make sure the representations other than from one specific channel are invariant to the environments partitioned by this latent factor for excluding the information corresponding to this latent factor for disentanglement. Finally, the disentangled graph representations are fed into a linear predictor and finetuned for the downstream tasks. We provide comprehensive theoretical analyses to show that our model can learn disentangled graph representations and achieve OOD generalization. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our model against state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts for graph classification tasks.

paragraphs: Graph models can struggle when the graphs encountered at test time differ from those used for training. Existing approaches to this problem often depend on plentiful task-specific labels. This paper studies how to learn graph representations without those labels while seeking relatively stable performance under distribution shifts. Its central challenge is that stable information and information that changes across environments are mixed together.

OOD-GCL first maps each graph into a representation divided into separate factors. Its self-supervised learning module uses one factor to partition environments, then encourages the other representation channels to remain invariant across those environments. This is intended to exclude information associated with that particular factor from the other channels while preserving predictive ability.

The resulting representations are passed to a linear predictor and fine-tuned for downstream tasks. The paper supplies theoretical analyses supporting disentanglement and out-of-distribution generalization. Experiments on real-world graph-classification datasets report stronger performance than state-of-the-art baselines under distribution shifts. The label-free contribution concerns representation learning; the abstract separately describes downstream prediction and fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: OOD-GCL learns separated graph representations through self-supervision to improve graph classification when training and test distributions differ.

title: Disentangled Graph Self-supervised Learning for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Uncertainty estimation (UE), as an effective means of quantifying predictive uncertainty, is crucial for safe and reliable decision-making, especially in high-risk scenarios. Existing UE schemes usually assume that there are completely-labeled samples to support fully-supervised learning. In practice, however, many UE tasks often have no sufficiently-labeled data to use, such as the Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) with only weak instance annotations. To bridge this gap, this paper, for the first time, addresses the weakly-supervised issue of Multi-Instance UE (MIUE) and proposes a new baseline scheme, Multi-Instance Residual Evidential Learning (MIREL). Particularly, at the fine-grained instance UE with only weak supervision, we derive a multi-instance residual operator through the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Functions. On this operator derivation, we further propose MIREL to jointly model the high-order predictive distribution at bag and instance levels for MIUE. Extensive experiments empirically demonstrate that our MIREL not only could often make existing MIL networks perform better in MIUE, but also could surpass representative UE methods by large margins, especially in instance-level UE tasks. Our source code is available at https://github.com/liupei101/MIREL.

paragraphs: Uncertainty estimation asks how much confidence to place in a prediction. Many approaches assume fully labeled training examples, but multiple-instance learning can provide only weak supervision for individual instances. This paper addresses uncertainty at both the level of a collection, or bag, and the level of its constituent instances under that weaker supervision.

The authors derive a multi-instance residual operator using the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Functions. They build Multi-Instance Residual Evidential Learning, or MIREL, on this operator to jointly model higher-order predictive distributions at bag and instance levels. The mathematical construction supports fine-grained uncertainty estimation even when direct instance annotations are weak.

Experiments show that MIREL can often improve uncertainty estimation when applied to existing multiple-instance learning networks. It can also outperform representative uncertainty methods by large margins, particularly for instance-level uncertainty. These are empirical findings with the stated qualification that improvements occur often. The contribution expands uncertainty modeling to a supervision setting where detailed labels are insufficient, connecting bag-level and instance-level predictive uncertainty within one scheme.
summary.tldr: MIREL jointly estimates bag-level and instance-level uncertainty using weak supervision and a derived residual operator.

title: Weakly-Supervised Residual Evidential Learning for Multi-Instance Uncertainty Estimation

abstract: Despite their exceptional capabilities, large language models (LLMs) are prone to generating unintended text due to false or outdated knowledge. Given the resource-intensive nature of retraining LLMs, there has been a notable increase in the development of knowledge editing. However, current approaches and evaluations rarely explore the perturbation of editing on neighboring knowledge. This paper studies whether updating new knowledge to LLMs perturbs the neighboring knowledge encapsulated within them. Specifically, we seek to figure out whether appending a new answer into an answer list to a factual question leads to catastrophic forgetting of original correct answers in this list, as well as unintentional inclusion of incorrect answers. A metric of additivity is introduced and a benchmark dubbed as Perturbation Evaluation of Appending Knowledge (PEAK) is constructed to evaluate the degree of perturbation to neighboring knowledge when appending new knowledge. Besides, a plug-and-play framework termed Appending via Preservation and Prevention (APP) is proposed to mitigate the neighboring perturbation by maintaining the integrity of the answer list. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of APP coupling with four editing methods on three LLMs.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing offers a way to update a language model without expensive retraining. This paper examines what happens to nearby knowledge when an edit adds new information. Its specific setting is a factual question with several correct answers: adding another answer should preserve the existing correct answers and avoid introducing incorrect ones.

The authors introduce an additivity metric and construct PEAK, a benchmark for measuring these neighboring effects. The evaluation checks both the loss of previously correct answers and the accidental inclusion of wrong answers. This expands the assessment of an edit beyond whether the model can produce the newly supplied fact.

They also propose Appending via Preservation and Prevention, or APP, a plug-and-play framework designed to maintain the integrity of the answer list. Experiments combining APP with four editing methods across three language models demonstrate its effectiveness. The work makes preservation an explicit part of knowledge addition: a successful update must be assessed in relation to the surrounding answers it can disturb.
summary.tldr: PEAK measures how knowledge additions disturb related answers, while APP helps preserve correct answers and prevent incorrect additions.

title: Neighboring Perturbations of Knowledge Editing on Large Language Models

abstract: Conformal prediction is a valuable tool for quantifying predictive uncertainty of machine learning models. However, its applicability relies on the assumption of data exchangeability, a condition which is often not met in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we consider the problem of adaptive conformal inference without any assumptions about the data generating process. Existing approaches for adaptive conformal inference are based on optimizing the pinball loss using variants of online gradient descent. A notable shortcoming of such approaches is in their explicit dependence on and sensitivity to the choice of the learning rates. In this paper, we propose a different approach for adaptive conformal inference that leverages parameter-free online convex optimization techniques. We prove that our method controls long-term miscoverage frequency at a nominal level and demonstrate its convincing empirical performance without any need of performing cumbersome parameter tuning.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction turns model outputs into predictions that express uncertainty, but its usual guarantees depend on exchangeability: roughly, the ordering of observations should not change their statistical role. This paper studies adaptive conformal inference without assuming a particular data-generating process, addressing settings where that requirement may fail.

Existing adaptive methods adjust their predictions by optimizing pinball loss with online gradient descent. Their behavior depends on a learning rate, which determines how strongly each new observation changes the procedure. Choosing this rate can be consequential and sensitive. The authors instead use parameter-free online convex optimization, removing the need to select those learning rates.

The paper proves control of the long-term frequency of missed outcomes at the requested nominal level and reports convincing empirical performance without cumbersome parameter tuning. The guarantee concerns accumulated miscoverage over time, so its significance is reliable long-run error frequency. The contribution combines that theoretical control with a practical reduction in tuning effort.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free adaptive conformal method controls long-term miscoverage without assumptions about the data-generating process.

title: Adaptive Conformal Inference by Betting

abstract: For a large class of feature maps we provide a tight asymptotic characterisation of the test error associated with learning the readout layer, in the high-dimensional limit where the input dimension, hidden layer widths, and number of training samples are proportionally large. This characterization is formulated in terms of the population covariance of the features. Our work is partially motivated by the problem of learning with Gaussian rainbow neural networks, namely deep non-linear fully-connected networks with random but structured weights, whose row-wise covariances are further allowed to depend on the weights of previous layers. For such networks we also derive a closed-form formula for the feature covariance in terms of the weight matrices. We further find that in some cases our results can capture feature maps learned by deep, finite-width neural networks trained under gradient descent.

For such networks we also derive a closed-form formula for the feature covariance in terms of the weight matrices. We further find that in some cases our results can capture feature maps learned by deep, finite-width neural networks trained under gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction error when a model learns its final readout layer on top of an existing feature map. Its main result is a tight asymptotic characterization for a broad class of feature maps. The analysis considers a high-dimensional regime in which input size, hidden-layer widths, and training-sample count grow proportionally.

The characterization expresses test error through the population covariance of the features: the statistical relationships among feature values across the underlying data distribution. This makes feature covariance the central object connecting a representation to the performance of its learned readout. The result concerns this proportional-growth limit, rather than asserting an exact formula for every finite model.

The authors also analyze Gaussian rainbow networks, whose random weights have structure that can depend on earlier layers. For these networks, they derive an explicit feature-covariance formula from the weight matrices. They further find that their results can sometimes capture feature maps learned by finite-width networks trained with gradient descent, suggesting relevance beyond randomly constructed representations.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes readout test error through feature covariance in a proportional high-dimensional limit, including structured random deep networks.

title: Asymptotics of Learning with Deep Structured (Random) Features

abstract: Robustness remains a paramount concern in deep reinforcement learning (DRL), with randomized smoothing emerging as a key technique for enhancing this attribute. However, a notable gap exists in the performance of current smoothed DRL agents, often characterized by significantly low clean rewards and weak robustness. In response to this challenge, our study introduces innovative algorithms aimed at training effective smoothed robust DRL agents. We propose S-DQN and S-PPO, novel approaches that demonstrate remarkable improvements in clean rewards, empirical robustness, and robustness guarantee across standard RL benchmarks. Notably, our S-DQN and S-PPO agents not only significantly outperform existing smoothed agents by an average factor of $2.16\times$ under the strongest attack, but also surpass previous robustly-trained agents by an average factor of $2.13\times$. This represents a significant leap forward in the field. Furthermore, we introduce Smoothed Attack, which is $1.89\times$ more effective in decreasing the rewards of smoothed agents than existing adversarial attacks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/Robust_HighUtil_Smoothed_DRL

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent needs to earn rewards while remaining reliable when its inputs are disturbed. Randomized smoothing is one technique for improving robustness, but existing smoothed agents can perform poorly even without attacks. This paper addresses both sides of that problem: maintaining useful behavior in clean conditions and resisting adversarial interference.

The authors introduce two training approaches, S-DQN and S-PPO, for producing more effective smoothed agents. Across standard reinforcement learning benchmarks, they report improvements in clean rewards, measured resistance to attacks, and robustness guarantees. These are distinct outcomes: performance under tested attacks provides empirical evidence, while a robustness guarantee supplies a theoretical form of assurance.

Under the strongest attack in their evaluation, the agents outperform existing smoothed agents by an average factor of 2.16 and previous robustly trained agents by 2.13. The paper also introduces Smoothed Attack, reported to be 1.89 times more effective at reducing smoothed agents’ rewards than existing attacks. Together, the contributions improve both agent training and the evaluation of smoothed agents’ vulnerabilities.
summary.tldr: S-DQN and S-PPO improve smoothed reinforcement learning agents’ rewards and robustness, while a new attack strengthens their evaluation.

title: Breaking the Barrier: Enhanced Utility and Robustness in Smoothed DRL Agents

abstract: Existing OCR engines or document image analysis systems typically rely on training separate models for text detection in varying scenarios and granularities, leading to significant computational complexity and resource demands. In this paper, we introduce "Detect Any Text" (DAT), an advanced paradigm that seamlessly unifies scene text detection, layout analysis, and document page detection into a cohesive, end-to-end model. This design enables DAT to efficiently manage text instances at different granularities, including word, line, paragraph and page. A pivotal innovation in DAT is the across-granularity interactive attention module, which significantly enhances the representation learning of text instances at varying granularities by correlating structural information across different text queries. As a result, it enables the model to achieve mutually beneficial detection performances across multiple text granularities. Additionally, a prompt-based segmentation module refines detection outcomes for texts of arbitrary curvature and complex layouts, thereby improving DAT’s accuracy and expanding its real-world applicability. Experimental results demonstrate that DAT achieves state-of-the-art performances across a variety of text-related benchmarks, including multi-oriented/arbitrarily-shaped scene text detection, document layout analysis and page detection tasks.

paragraphs: Text detection systems often use separate models for different settings and scales, increasing computational and resource demands. Detect Any Text, or DAT, brings scene text detection, document layout analysis, and page detection into one end-to-end model. It handles text at word, line, paragraph, and page levels within this shared framework.

Its key component is interactive attention across granularities. Different text queries exchange structural information, helping the model learn representations that connect these levels. This allows detection at multiple scales to benefit mutually rather than treating each scale as a separate learning problem. A prompt-based segmentation module further refines the detected regions for curved text and complex layouts.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across benchmarks for oriented and arbitrarily shaped scene text, document layouts, and page detection. These results support the combination of shared structural reasoning and segmentation refinement across distinct text-detection tasks. The practical contribution is a unified detection model whose components explicitly address both relationships between text scales and variation in the shapes of text regions.
summary.tldr: DAT unifies word-to-page text detection through cross-granularity attention and segmentation refinement, reporting state-of-the-art results across multiple detection benchmarks.

title: Towards Unified Multi-granularity Text Detection with Interactive Attention

abstract: Medical vision-language pre-training methods mainly leverage the correspondence between paired medical images and radiological reports. Although multi-view spatial images and temporal sequences of image-report pairs are available in off-the-shelf multi-modal medical datasets, most existing methods have not thoroughly tapped into such extensive supervision signals. In this paper, we introduce the Med-ST framework for fine-grained spatial and temporal modeling to exploit information from multiple spatial views of chest radiographs and temporal historical records. For spatial modeling, Med-ST employs the Mixture of View Expert (MoVE) architecture to integrate different visual features from both frontal and lateral views. To achieve a more comprehensive alignment, Med-ST not only establishes the global alignment between whole images and texts but also introduces modality-weighted local alignment between text tokens and spatial regions of images. For temporal modeling, we propose a novel cross-modal bidirectional cycle consistency objective by forward mapping classification (FMC) and reverse mapping regression (RMR). By perceiving temporal information from simple to complex, Med-ST can learn temporal semantics. Experimental results across four distinct tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of Med-ST, especially in temporal classification tasks. Our code and model are available at https://github.com/SVT-Yang/MedST.

paragraphs: Medical vision-language pretraining commonly learns from paired images and radiology reports. Med-ST uses additional information already present in multimodal datasets: different spatial views and historical image-report sequences. The framework aims to learn from both how an examination is viewed and how its information changes across time.

For spatial modeling, a Mixture of View Expert architecture combines visual features from frontal and lateral chest radiographs. Med-ST aligns whole images with text and also aligns text tokens with image regions using modality-weighted local alignment. These two levels connect broad image-report correspondence with more detailed spatial relationships.

For temporal modeling, the method combines forward mapping classification and reverse mapping regression in a cross-modal bidirectional cycle-consistency objective. This supports learning temporal meaning through information progressing from simple to complex. Experiments across four tasks demonstrate effectiveness, especially for temporal classification. The results support making fuller use of multiple views and historical records during pretraining, with the strongest stated benefit appearing in tasks that directly depend on temporal information.
summary.tldr: Med-ST combines multiple chest-radiograph views, local image-text alignment, and historical records to improve medical multimodal learning, especially temporal classification.

title: Unlocking the Power of Spatial and Temporal Information in Medical Multimodal Pre-training

abstract: We propose VecKM, a local point cloud geometry encoder that is descriptive and efficient to compute. VecKM leverages a unique approach by vectorizing a kernel mixture to represent the local point cloud. Such representation’s descriptiveness is supported by two theorems that validate its ability to reconstruct and preserve the similarity of the local shape. Unlike existing encoders downsampling the local point cloud, VecKM constructs the local geometry encoding using all neighboring points, producing a more descriptive encoding. Moreover, VecKM is efficient to compute and scalable to large point cloud inputs: VecKM reduces the memory cost from $(n^2+nKd)$ to $(nd+np)$; and reduces the major runtime cost from computing $nK$ MLPs to $n$ MLPs, where $n$ is the size of the point cloud, $K$ is the neighborhood size, $d$ is the encoding dimension, and $p$ is a marginal factor. The efficiency is due to VecKM’s unique factorizable property that eliminates the need of explicitly grouping points into neighbors. In the normal estimation task, VecKM demonstrates not only 100x faster inference speed but also highest accuracy and strongest robustness. In classification and segmentation tasks, integrating VecKM as a preprocessing module achieves consistently better performance than the PointNet, PointNet++, and point transformer baselines, and runs consistently faster by up to 10 times.

paragraphs: VecKM turns the geometry around each point in a point cloud into a compact numerical representation. Its central idea is to represent nearby points through a vectorized mixture of kernels. Two theorems support the representation’s ability to reconstruct local shape and preserve similarities between shapes, connecting computational efficiency with the geometric information the encoding retains.

The method uses all neighboring points rather than downsampling the neighborhood. Its factorizable structure also avoids explicitly assembling those neighborhoods. For n points, neighborhood size K, encoding dimension d, and a marginal factor p, the stated memory cost changes from n² + nKd to nd + np. The main neural-network computation falls from nK multilayer perceptron evaluations to n evaluations.

In the reported normal-estimation experiments, VecKM combines 100-fold faster inference with the best accuracy and robustness among the compared methods. Used as preprocessing for classification and segmentation, it improves the evaluated PointNet, PointNet++, and point transformer baselines while running up to ten times faster. These findings show how retaining neighborhood information can coexist with substantial computational savings.
summary.tldr: VecKM encodes local point-cloud geometry using all neighboring points while substantially reducing memory and computation.

title: A Linear Time and Space Local Point Cloud Geometry Encoder via Vectorized Kernel Mixture (VecKM)

abstract: The recent development on large multimodal models (LMMs), especially GPT-4V(ision) and Gemini, has been quickly expanding the capability boundaries of multimodal models beyond traditional tasks like image captioning and visual question answering. In this work, we explore the potential of LMMs like GPT-4V as a generalist web agent that can follow natural language instructions to complete tasks on any given website. We propose SEEACT, a generalist web agent that harnesses the power of LMMs for integrated visual understanding and acting on the web. We evaluate on the recent MIND2WEB benchmark. In addition to standard offline evaluation on cached websites, we enable a new online evaluation setting by developing a tool that allows running web agents on live websites. We show that GPT-4V presents a great potential for web agents—it can successfully complete 51.1% of the tasks on live websites if we manually ground its textual plans into actions on the websites. This substantially outperforms text-only LLMs like GPT-4 or smaller models (FLAN-T5 and BLIP-2) specifically fine-tuned for web agents. However, grounding still remains a major challenge. Existing LMM grounding strategies like set-of-mark prompting turns out to be not effective for web agents, and the best grounding strategy we develop in this paper leverages both the HTML structure and visuals. Yet, there is still a substantial gap with oracle grounding, leaving ample room for further improvement. All code, data, and evaluation tools are available at https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/SeeAct.

paragraphs: SEEACT explores whether a multimodal model can follow natural-language instructions to perform tasks on websites. It combines visual understanding with action selection and evaluates the result on MIND2WEB. The researchers also build tooling for testing agents on live websites, extending evaluation beyond cached pages to an online setting where actions must actually be executed.

A central finding separates planning ability from grounding: translating a textual plan into the correct website action. With manual grounding, GPT-4V completes 51.1% of live-website tasks, substantially outperforming the compared text-only and smaller specialized models. That result depends on human grounding and therefore measures capability under that assistance rather than fully automated task completion.

Automatic grounding remains the major obstacle. The paper finds that set-of-mark prompting is ineffective for these web-agent tasks, while its best developed strategy combines HTML structure with visual information. Even that strategy falls substantially short of oracle grounding. The findings identify a concrete gap between understanding what to do and reliably selecting the corresponding interface action.
summary.tldr: SEEACT shows strong GPT-4V web-task capability with manual action grounding, while identifying automatic grounding as a major remaining bottleneck.

title: GPT-4V(ision) is a Generalist Web Agent, if Grounded

abstract: Predictive tasks on relational databases are critical in real-world applications spanning e-commerce, healthcare, and social media. To address these tasks effectively, Relational Deep Learning (RDL) encodes relational data as graphs, enabling Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit relational structures for improved predictions. However, existing RDL methods often overlook the intrinsic structural properties of the graphs built from relational databases, leading to modeling inefficiencies, particularly in handling many-to-many relationships. Here we introduce RelGNN, a novel GNN framework specifically designed to leverage the unique structural characteristics of the graphs built from relational databases. At the core of our approach is the introduction of atomic routes, which are simple paths that enable direct single-hop interactions between the source and destination nodes. Building upon these atomic routes, RelGNN designs new composite message passing and graph attention mechanisms that reduce redundancy, highlight key signals, and enhance predictive accuracy. RelGNN is evaluated on 30 diverse real-world tasks from Relbench (Fey et al., 2024), and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the vast majority of tasks, with improvements of up to 25%.

paragraphs: Relational deep learning turns database records and their relationships into graphs so graph neural networks can make predictions. However, the resulting graphs have structural properties that general message-passing methods may not exploit well. The paper identifies many-to-many relationships as a particular source of modeling inefficiency.

RelGNN introduces atomic routes: simple paths that support direct, single-hop interactions between source and destination nodes. It builds composite message passing and graph attention mechanisms around these routes. The design aims to reduce redundant information processing and emphasize the signals that matter for prediction while respecting the structure inherited from the database.

The authors evaluate RelGNN on 30 real-world tasks in Relbench. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on the vast majority of those tasks, with reported improvements reaching 25%. That maximum describes the strongest reported improvement, rather than an average across tasks. The results support adapting graph computation to relational database structure, showing that how information travels through the graph can materially affect prediction quality.
summary.tldr: RelGNN uses database-aware routes and composite message passing to reduce redundancy and improve predictions on relational data.

title: RelGNN: Composite Message Passing for Relational Deep Learning

abstract: Diffusion models accomplish remarkable success in data generation tasks across various domains. However, the iterative sampling process is computationally expensive. Consistency models are proposed to learn consistency functions to map from noise to data directly, which allows one-step fast data generation and multistep sampling to improve sample quality. In this paper, we study the convergence of consistency models when the self-consistency property holds approximately under the training distribution. Our analysis requires only mild data assumption and applies to a family of forward processes. When the target data distribution has bounded support or has tails that decay sufficiently fast, we show that the samples generated by the consistency model are close to the target distribution in Wasserstein distance; when the target distribution satisfies some smoothness assumption, we show that with an additional perturbation step for smoothing, the generated samples are close to the target distribution in total variation distance. We provide two case studies with commonly chosen forward processes to demonstrate the benefit of multistep sampling.

paragraphs: Consistency models aim to generate data directly from noise, enabling one-step sampling while allowing additional steps to improve quality. This paper studies when their generated distribution approaches the target distribution. Crucially, the analysis allows self-consistency to hold approximately under the training distribution, rather than requiring exact agreement.

The guarantees depend on properties of the target data. If its support is bounded, or its tails decay sufficiently quickly, the authors establish closeness in Wasserstein distance, a measure that accounts for how far probability mass must move. Under a smoothness assumption, an additional smoothing perturbation enables a guarantee in total variation distance, which compares probabilities assigned to events.

The analysis applies to a family of forward processes and includes two case studies using common choices to demonstrate benefits from multistep sampling. Its contribution is to connect approximate learned consistency with distributional guarantees under stated data conditions. The results also explain why taking multiple sampling steps can be valuable within a framework designed to permit direct generation.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional distributional convergence guarantees for approximately consistent models and demonstrates benefits of multistep sampling.

title: Convergence of Consistency Model with Multistep Sampling under General Data Assumptions

abstract: Unpaired point cloud completion is crucial for real-world applications, where ground-truth data for complete point clouds are often unavailable. By learning a completion map from unpaired incomplete and complete point cloud data, this task avoids the reliance on paired datasets. In this paper, we propose the Unbalanced Optimal Transport Map for Unpaired Point Cloud Completion (UOT-UPC) model, which formulates the unpaired completion task as the (Unbalanced) Optimal Transport (OT) problem. Our method employs a Neural OT model learning the UOT map using neural networks. Our model is the first attempt to leverage UOT for unpaired point cloud completion, achieving competitive or superior performance on both single-category and multi-category benchmarks. In particular, our approach is especially robust under the class imbalance problem, which is frequently encountered in real-world unpaired point cloud completion scenarios.

By learning a completion map from unpaired incomplete and complete point cloud data, this task avoids the reliance on paired datasets. In this paper, we propose the Unbalanced Optimal Transport Map for Unpaired Point Cloud Completion (UOT-UPC) model, which formulates the unpaired completion task as the (Unbalanced) Optimal Transport (OT) problem. Our method employs a Neural OT model learning the UOT map using neural networks. Our model is the first attempt to leverage UOT for unpaired point cloud completion, achieving competitive or superior performance on both single-category and multi-category benchmarks. In particular, our approach is especially robust under the class imbalance problem, which is frequently encountered in real-world unpaired point cloud completion scenarios.

paragraphs: Point-cloud completion reconstructs a complete shape from an incomplete collection of points. In practical settings, an incomplete scan may have no matching complete reference. This paper studies learning from separate collections of incomplete and complete point clouds, allowing training without a paired example for every partial shape.

The proposed UOT-UPC model formulates this learning problem using unbalanced optimal transport. A neural optimal-transport model learns the mapping with neural networks. This provides a framework for connecting the incomplete and complete data collections even though their examples are not individually paired. The authors identify their work as the first use of unbalanced optimal transport for this completion setting.

Results are competitive with or better than alternatives on benchmarks containing a single object category and multiple categories. The method is especially robust when classes are imbalanced, a condition the authors identify as common in real-world unpaired completion. That finding matters because the composition of independently collected datasets can differ. The reported results support this transport-based formulation for learning completion from such unpaired collections.
summary.tldr: UOT-UPC learns point-cloud completion from unpaired data using unbalanced optimal transport, with particular robustness to class imbalance.

title: Unpaired Point Cloud Completion via Unbalanced Optimal Transport

abstract: For federated learning (FL) algorithms such as FedSAM, their generalization capability is crucial for real-word applications. In this paper, we revisit the generalization problem in FL and investigate the impact of data heterogeneity on FL generalization. We find that FedSAM usually performs worse than FedAvg in the case of highly heterogeneous data, and thus propose a novel and effective federated learning algorithm with Stochastic Weight Averaging (called FedSWA), which aims to find flatter minima in the setting of highly heterogeneous data. Moreover, we introduce a new momentum-based stochastic controlled weight averaging FL algorithm (FedMoSWA), which is designed to better align local and global models. Theoretically, we provide both convergence analysis and generalization bounds for FedSWA and FedMoSWA. We also prove that the optimization and generalization errors of FedMoSWA are smaller than those of their counterparts, including FedSAM and its variants. Empirically, experimental results on CIFAR10/100 and Tiny ImageNet demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithms compared to their counterparts.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine local learning when participants hold different kinds of data. This paper investigates how strong data heterogeneity affects generalization. The authors find that FedSAM usually performs worse than FedAvg under highly heterogeneous data, motivating approaches designed specifically for that setting.

Their first method, FedSWA, uses stochastic weight averaging with the aim of finding flatter minima. Their second, FedMoSWA, adds momentum-based stochastic controlled weight averaging to better align local models with the global model. These contributions connect the choice of model weights with the challenge of coordinating learning across participants whose data differ substantially.

The authors provide convergence analyses and generalization bounds for both algorithms. Their theory also establishes smaller optimization and generalization errors for FedMoSWA than for the compared counterparts, including FedSAM and its variants. Experiments on CIFAR10/100 and Tiny ImageNet demonstrate the proposed algorithms’ superiority in the evaluated comparisons. Together, the findings show that methods intended to improve generalization need to account for the degree of disagreement introduced by heterogeneous local data.
summary.tldr: FedSWA and FedMoSWA use weight averaging to improve federated learning when local data are highly heterogeneous.

title: Improving Generalization in Federated Learning with Highly Heterogeneous Data via Momentum-Based Stochastic Controlled Weight Averaging

abstract: Feedback from peer review is essential to improve the quality of scientific articles. However, at present, many manuscripts do not receive sufficient external feedback for refinement before or during submission. Therefore, a system capable of providing detailed and professional feedback is crucial for enhancing research efficiency. In this paper, we have compiled the largest dataset of paper reviews to date by collecting historical open-access papers and their corresponding review comments and standardizing them using LLM. We then developed a multi-agent system that mimics real human review processes, based on LLMs. This system, named Agent Reviewers, includes the innovative introduction of multimodal reviewers to provide feedback on the visual elements of papers. Additionally, a shared memory pool that stores historical papers’ metadata is preserved, which supplies reviewer agents with background knowledge from different fields. Our system is evaluated using ICLR 2024 papers and achieves superior performance compared to existing AI-based review systems. Comprehensive ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of each module and agent in this system.

paragraphs: Agent Reviewers addresses a practical gap in scientific writing: many manuscripts receive too little external feedback to support revision. The paper builds an automated review system around several language-model agents that imitate aspects of human reviewing. Its purpose is to produce detailed, professional feedback that authors can use while refining a paper.

The authors first collect historical open-access papers and their reviews, then use a language model to standardize the material. They describe the resulting review dataset as the largest compiled to date. The system also includes multimodal reviewers that examine visual elements, extending feedback beyond text. A shared memory pool holds metadata about earlier papers and supplies agents with background knowledge from different research fields.

On ICLR 2024 papers, the system performs better than the existing AI review systems included in the evaluation. Ablation studies support the usefulness of its individual modules and agents. Together, these findings support combining specialized reviewers, visual analysis, and shared research context within an automated feedback process.
summary.tldr: Agent Reviewers combines specialized multimodal agents and shared paper metadata to improve automated scientific feedback.

title: Agent Reviewers: Domain-specific Multimodal Agents with Shared Memory for Paper Review

abstract: Recent text-to-image generative models, e.g., Stable Diffusion V3 and Flux, have achieved notable progress. However, these models are strongly restricted to their limited knowledge, a.k.a., their own fixed parameters, that are trained with closed datasets. This leads to significant hallucinations or distortions when facing fine-grained and unseen novel real-world objects, e.g., the appearance of the Tesla Cybertruck. To this end, we present the first real-object-based retrieval-augmented generation framework (RealRAG), which augments fine-grained and unseen novel object generation by learning and retrieving real-world images to overcome the knowledge gaps of generative models. Specifically, to integrate missing memory for unseen novel object generation, we train a reflective retriever by self-reflective contrastive learning, which injects the generator’s knowledge into the sef-reflective negatives, ensuring that the retrieved augmented images compensate for the model’s missing knowledge. Furthermore, the real-object-based framework integrates fine-grained visual knowledge for the generative models, tackling the distortion problem and improving the realism for fine-grained object generation. Our Real-RAG is superior in its modular application to all types of state-of-the-art text-to-image generative models and also delivers remarkable performance boosts with all of them, such as a gain of 16.18% FID score with the auto-regressive model on the Stanford Car benchmark.

summary.tldr: RealRAG trains a retriever to supply real-object images that fill a generator’s visual knowledge gaps and improve realistic image generation.

title: RealRAG: Retrieval-augmented Realistic Image Generation via Self-reflective Contrastive Learning

abstract: Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) has emerged as a prominent method for text-to-3D generation by leveraging the strengths of 2D diffusion models. However, SDS is limited to generation tasks and lacks the capability to edit existing 3D assets. Conversely, variants of SDS that introduce editing capabilities often can not generate new 3D assets effectively. In this work, we observe that the processes of generation and editing within SDS and its variants have unified underlying gradient terms. Building on this insight, we propose Unified Distillation Sampling (UDS), a method that seamlessly integrates both the generation and editing of 3D assets. Essentially, UDS refines the gradient terms used in vanilla SDS methods, unifying them to support both tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UDS not only outperforms baseline methods in generating 3D assets with richer details but also excels in editing tasks, thereby bridging the gap between 3D generation and editing.

The paper identifies a divide in existing methods: standard SDS supports generation but cannot edit existing assets, while variants that enable editing often struggle to generate new assets effectively. This motivates a method that can serve both tasks.

The authors observe that generation and editing in SDS and its variants share underlying gradient terms. These terms determine how optimization changes the asset. Building on that common structure, they introduce Unified Distillation Sampling, or UDS, which refines and unifies the gradients used in standard SDS to support both creation and modification.

Experiments show that UDS generates assets with richer detail than the evaluated baselines and also performs strongly on editing tasks. The contribution is a unified optimization approach to two capabilities that existing variants had difficulty combining. The shared gradient perspective explains how improvements to the distillation procedure can support both starting a new asset and changing an existing one.
summary.tldr: Unified Distillation Sampling refines shared gradient terms to support both detailed 3D generation and editing.

title: Rethinking Score Distilling Sampling for 3D Editing and Generation

abstract: Processing global geometric context while preserving equivariance is crucial when modeling biological, chemical, and physical systems. Yet, this is challenging due to the computational demands of equivariance and global context at scale. Standard methods such as equivariant self-attention suffer from quadratic complexity, while local methods such as distance-based message passing sacrifice global information. Inspired by the recent success of state-space and long-convolutional models, we introduce Geometric Hyena, the first equivariant long-convolutional model for geometric systems. Geometric Hyena captures global geometric context at sub-quadratic complexity while maintaining equivariance to rotations and translations. Evaluated on all-atom property prediction of large RNA molecules and full protein molecular dynamics, Geometric Hyena outperforms existing equivariant models while requiring significantly less memory and compute that equivariant self-attention. Notably, our model processes the geometric context of $30k$ tokens $20 \times$ faster than the equivariant transformer and allows $72 \times$ longer context within the same budget.

paragraphs: Models of molecular and physical systems need to account for geometry across an entire structure while responding consistently to rotations and translations. Equivariant self-attention can provide global context, but its quadratic complexity makes large systems expensive. Local message passing reduces that burden while giving up global information.

Geometric Hyena introduces an equivariant architecture based on long convolutions, inspired by state-space and long-convolution models. It captures global geometric context with sub-quadratic complexity and preserves equivariance to rotations and translations. The design addresses global interaction modeling and geometric consistency within the same scalable architecture.

The authors evaluate it on all-atom property prediction for large RNA molecules and full protein molecular dynamics. They report stronger performance than existing equivariant models and substantially lower memory and compute requirements than equivariant self-attention. In the reported comparison, it processes 30,000 tokens of geometric context 20 times faster than an equivariant transformer and supports 72 times longer context within the same budget. These results demonstrate practical gains for the evaluated large molecular systems.
summary.tldr: Geometric Hyena uses equivariant long convolutions to model global geometry with sub-quadratic complexity and strong reported molecular-task performance.

title: Geometric Hyena Networks for Large-scale Equivariant Learning

abstract: We study model personalization under user-level differential privacy (DP) in the shared representation framework. In this problem, there are $n$ users whose data is statistically heterogeneous, and their optimal parameters share an unknown embedding $U^* \in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$ that maps the user parameters in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to low-dimensional representations in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ll d$. Our goal is to privately recover the shared embedding and the local low-dimensional representations with small excess risk in the federated setting. We propose a private, efficient federated learning algorithm to learn the shared embedding based on the FedRep algorithm in (Collins et al., 2021). Unlike (Collins et al., 2021), our algorithm satisfies differential privacy, and our results hold for the case of noisy labels. In contrast to prior work on private model personalization (Jain et al., 2021), our utility guarantees hold under a larger class of users’ distributions (sub-Gaussian instead of Gaussian distributions). Additionally, in natural parameter regimes, we improve the privacy error term in (Jain et al., 2021) by a factor of $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. Next, we consider the binary classification setting. We present an information-theoretic construction to privately learn the shared embedding and derive a margin-based accuracy guarantee that is independent of $d$. Our method utilizes the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform to reduce the effective dimensions of the shared embedding and the users’ data. This result shows that dimension-independent risk bounds are possible in this setting under a margin loss.

Users have statistically different data, but their optimal model parameters are assumed to share an unknown low-dimensional representation. The goal is to recover that shared structure and each user’s local representation while keeping excess prediction risk small and satisfying privacy requirements.

It uses the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform to reduce the effective dimensions of both the shared embedding and users’ data. This establishes that dimension-independent risk bounds are possible under a margin loss in the studied shared-representation setting.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens private federated personalization guarantees and establishes the possibility of dimension-independent margin-based risk bounds for binary classification.

title: Private Model Personalization Revisited

abstract: Practical reinforcement learning (RL) usually requires agents to be optimized for multiple potentially conflicting criteria, e.g. speed vs. safety. Although Multi-Objective RL (MORL) algorithms have been studied in previous works, their trained agents often cover limited Pareto optimal solutions and they lack precise controllability of the delicate trade-off among multiple objectives. Hence, the resulting agent is not versatile in aligning with customized requests from different users. To bridge the gap, we develop the “Preference controllable (PC) RL” framework, which trains a preference-conditioned meta-policy that takes user preference as input controlling the generated trajectories within the preference region on the Pareto frontier. The PCRL framework is compatible with advanced Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) algorithms that are rarely seen in previous MORL approaches. We also proposed a novel preference-regularized MOO algorithm specifically for PCRL. We provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis to justify its convergence and preference controllability. We evaluate PCRL with different MOO algorithms against state-of-the-art MORL baselines in various challenging environments with up to six objectives. In these experiments, our proposed method exhibits significantly better controllability than existing approaches and can generate Pareto solutions with better diversity and utilities.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often involves competing goals, such as speed and safety. Existing multi-objective methods can cover only a limited range of desirable trade-offs and offer imprecise control over which trade-off a user receives. Preference Controllable RL, or PCRL, trains a meta-policy that accepts user preferences as input.

The intended behavior is to generate trajectories within the requested preference region of the Pareto frontier, the set of trade-offs where improving one objective requires sacrificing another. PCRL supports advanced multi-objective optimization algorithms, and the authors introduce a preference-regularized algorithm specifically for this framework. Their theoretical analysis addresses convergence and preference controllability.

The proposed method shows substantially better controllability and produces Pareto solutions with better diversity and utilities. These findings support learning a policy whose behavior can be adjusted through preferences, while also improving the range and quality of available trade-offs in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: PCRL trains preference-conditioned policies that provide more precise control over competing objectives and better trade-off diversity in the reported experiments.

title: Preference Controllable Reinforcement Learning with Advanced Multi-Objective Optimization

abstract: Graph Foundation Models hold significant potential for advancing multi-domain graph learning, yet their full capabilities remain largely untapped. Existing works show promising task performance with the “pretrain-then-prompt” paradigm, which lacks theoretical foundations to understand why it works and how much knowledge can be transferred from source domains to the target. In this paper, we introduce BRIDGE, a bounded graph foundation model pre-trained on multi-domains with Generalization guarantees. To learn discriminative source knowledge, we align multi-domain graph features with domain-invariant aligners during pre-training. Then, a lightweight Mixture of Experts (MoE) network is proposed to facilitate downstream prompting through self-supervised selective knowledge assembly and transfer. Further, to determine the maximum amount of transferable knowledge, we derive an optimizable generalization error upper bound from a graph spectral perspective given the Lipschitz continuity. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of BRIDGE on both node and graph classification compared with 15 state-of-the-art baselines.

BRIDGE addresses a question behind this workflow: how much source knowledge can usefully transfer? The paper combines a model architecture for selective transfer with a theoretical bound intended to make its generalization behavior more understandable.

During pre-training, domain-invariant aligners bring graph features from different domains into alignment to learn discriminative source knowledge. A lightweight mixture-of-experts network then supports downstream prompting. Through self-supervised selection and assembly, it decides how to combine available knowledge for transfer, giving the model a mechanism for choosing among information learned across domains.

The theoretical analysis uses graph spectral structure and assumes Lipschitz continuity to derive an optimizable upper bound on generalization error. This is a conditional bound, rather than an exact measurement of transfer in every setting. Experiments on node and graph classification report superiority over 15 state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution links selective knowledge transfer with both empirical classification results and a mathematically specified account of generalization.
summary.tldr: BRIDGE aligns multi-domain graph knowledge and selectively transfers it through experts, with an optimizable generalization bound under Lipschitz continuity.

title: How Much Can Transfer? BRIDGE: Bounded Multi-Domain Graph Foundation Model with Generalization Guarantees

abstract: Tensors play a crucial role in numerous scientific and engineering fields. This paper addresses the low-multilinear-rank tensor completion problem, a fundamental task in tensor-related applications. By exploiting the manifold structure inherent to the fixed-multilinear-rank tensor set, we introduce a simple yet highly effective preconditioned Riemannian metric and propose the Preconditioned Riemannian Gradient Descent (PRGD) algorithm. Compared to the standard Riemannian Gradient Descent (RGD), PRGD achieves faster convergence while maintaining the same order of per-iteration computational complexity. Theoretically, we provide the recovery guarantee for PRGD under near-optimal sampling complexity. Numerical results highlight the efficiency of PRGD, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic data and real-world video inpainting tasks.

paragraphs: Tensor completion reconstructs missing entries in multidimensional data using structure in the entries that are available. This paper focuses on tensors with low multilinear rank. It exploits the geometric structure of the set of tensors with a fixed multilinear rank to design a more effective optimization procedure.

The proposed Preconditioned Riemannian Gradient Descent algorithm, or PRGD, introduces a preconditioned metric on that space. The metric changes the geometry used to guide gradient updates. Compared with standard Riemannian Gradient Descent, PRGD converges faster while retaining the same order of computational complexity per iteration, so its stated advantage does not require a higher asymptotic cost for each update.

The authors provide a recovery guarantee under near-optimal sampling complexity, connecting successful reconstruction to the amount of observed data. Numerical experiments on synthetic tensors and real video inpainting report better efficiency than state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theoretical and empirical findings support adapting the optimization geometry as a way to improve low-rank tensor reconstruction.
summary.tldr: PRGD changes the optimization geometry for low-rank tensor completion to improve convergence while retaining the same per-iteration complexity order.

title: Preconditioned Riemannian Gradient Descent Algorithm for Low-Multilinear-Rank Tensor Completion

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful technique for novel view synthesis. However, existing methods struggle to adaptively optimize the distribution of Gaussian primitives based on scene characteristics, making it challenging to balance reconstruction quality and efficiency. Inspired by human perception, we propose scene-adaptive perceptual densification for Gaussian Splatting (Perceptual-GS), a novel framework that integrates perceptual sensitivity into the 3DGS training process to address this challenge. We first introduce a perception-aware representation that models human visual sensitivity while constraining the number of Gaussian primitives. Building on this foundation, we develop a perceptual sensitivity-adaptive distribution to allocate finer Gaussian granularity to visually critical regions, enhancing reconstruction quality and robustness. Extensive evaluations on multiple datasets, including BungeeNeRF for large-scale scenes, demonstrate that Perceptual-GS achieves state-of-the-art performance in reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/eezkni/Perceptual-GS
