paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting represents scenes using Gaussian primitives to synthesize views from new viewpoints. A central challenge is deciding how those primitives should be distributed: reconstruction quality and efficiency depend on matching the representation to the scene. Perceptual-GS addresses this allocation problem by incorporating human visual sensitivity into training.

The method first introduces a perception-aware representation that models visual sensitivity while constraining the number of Gaussian primitives. It then adapts their distribution so visually critical regions receive finer granularity. This connects the amount of representational detail in a region to its perceptual importance, giving the system a scene-dependent way to allocate its available primitives.

Evaluations across multiple datasets, including the large-scale scenes of BungeeNeRF, report state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness. The stated findings support perception-guided densification as a way to improve several aspects of scene reconstruction together. The paper's contribution lies in making perceptual sensitivity part of the training and allocation process, so the distribution of primitives responds to what matters visually in each scene.
summary.tldr: Perceptual-GS allocates finer Gaussian detail to visually important regions, improving reported reconstruction quality, efficiency, and robustness.

title: Perceptual-GS: Scene-adaptive Perceptual Densification for Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Regression is a fundamental task in machine learning that has garnered extensive attention over the past decades. The conventional approach for regression involves employing loss functions that primarily concentrate on aligning model prediction with the ground truth for each individual data sample. Recent research endeavors have introduced novel perspectives by incorporating label similarity into regression through the imposition of additional pairwise regularization or contrastive learning on the latent feature space, demonstrating their effectiveness. However, there are two drawbacks to these approaches: (i) their pairwise operations in the latent feature space are computationally more expensive than conventional regression losses; (ii) they lack theoretical insights behind these methods. In this work, we propose GAR (Gradient Aligned Regression) as a competitive alternative method in label space, which is constituted by a conventional regression loss and two pairwise label difference losses for gradient alignment including magnitude and direction. GAR enjoys: i) the same level efficiency as conventional regression loss because the quadratic complexity for the proposed pairwise losses can be reduced to linear complexity; ii) theoretical insights from learning the pairwise label difference to learning the gradient of the ground truth function. We limit our current scope as regression on the clean data setting without noises, outliers or distributional shifts, etc. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method practically on two synthetic datasets and on eight extensive real-world tasks from six benchmark datasets with other eight competitive baselines. Running time experiments demonstrate the superior efficiency of the proposed GAR compared to existing methods with pairwise regularization or contrastive learning in the latent feature space. Additionally, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component of GAR. The code is open sourced at https://github.com/DixianZhu/GAR.

paragraphs: Standard regression losses compare each prediction with its own target. Gradient Aligned Regression, or GAR, instead introduces pairwise relationships directly in label space, combining an ordinary regression loss with two losses based on label differences.

The pairwise terms target gradient alignment in both magnitude and direction. The paper supplies a theoretical connection between learning differences in labels and learning the gradient of the underlying target function. The study explicitly limits its scope to clean data without noise, outliers, or distribution shifts. Runtime comparisons favor GAR over feature-space pairwise methods, while ablations support the contribution of each component.
summary.tldr: GAR adds efficient pairwise label-difference losses to regression, connecting prediction training with gradient alignment in clean-data settings.

title: Gradient Aligned Regression via Pairwise Losses

abstract: Modern recommender systems are typically trained offline and deployed with parameters held fixed between periodic refreshes, yet user behavior can evolve substantially during deployment. This can cause ranking utility to degrade over time and makes it difficult to provide formal guarantees about recommendation quality. We propose CARE, an adaptive calibration framework that wraps an arbitrary backbone recommender and outputs variable-size recommendation sets with finite-sample performance guarantees over interaction streams. CARE combines (i) a loss-based monitoring module that localizes behavioral changes and triggers threshold recalibration, and (ii) an online aggregation rule that promotes compact recommendation sets by dynamically reweighting candidate set predictors. We provide theoretical results establishing finite-sample guarantees for utility-based risk control and bounds on the expected set size relative to the best constituent predictor. Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone models demonstrate that CARE improves robustness and maintains compact recommendation sets while preserving the desired statistical guarantees. The code and implementation are available in https://github.com/kalpiree/CARE.

paragraphs: Recommendation models are often trained offline and then kept fixed until their next refresh. User behavior can change during that interval, weakening recommendation quality. CARE addresses this deployment problem through an adaptive calibration layer that wraps an arbitrary recommender and produces recommendation sets whose size can vary.

The framework combines monitoring with online aggregation. A loss-based monitor identifies where behavior has changed and triggers recalibration of a threshold. Meanwhile, an aggregation rule adjusts the weights of candidate set predictors to favor compact recommendations. Together, these components adapt the output sets as interactions arrive, rather than relying only on the backbone’s periodic refresh.

The authors establish finite-sample guarantees for controlling utility-based risk over interaction streams. They also bound expected recommendation-set size relative to the best constituent predictor. Experiments across several datasets and backbone models report improved robustness while maintaining compact sets and the desired guarantees. The contribution connects adaptation to changing behavior with explicit statistical control over recommendation quality and set size.
summary.tldr: CARE adapts recommendation-set calibration as behavior changes, combining compact outputs with finite-sample utility-risk guarantees.

title: CARE: Adaptive Calibration for Reliable Recommendations

abstract: We present a batched first-order method for solving multiple linear programs in parallel on GPUs. Our approach extends the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm to efficiently solve batches of related linear programming problems that arise in mixed-integer programming techniques such as strong branching and bound tightening. By leveraging matrix-matrix operations instead of repeated matrix-vector operations, we obtain significant computational advantages on GPU architectures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various case studies and identify the problem sizes where first-order methods outperform traditional simplex-based solvers, depending on the computational environment. This is a significant step toward integer programming algorithms that tightly exploit GPU capabilities. We argue that some specific operations should be allocated to GPUs and performed in full, instead of relying on lightweight heuristic approaches on CPUs.

This paper asks how to solve those related problems together on GPUs. The opportunity lies in organizing the work as a batch, so the hardware can process multiple optimization problems in parallel.

The authors extend the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm, a first-order optimization method, to handle these batches. The central computational change replaces repeated matrix-vector operations with matrix-matrix operations. That change matters because the batched formulation makes better use of GPU architectures, producing significant computational advantages for the workloads examined.

Case studies identify problem sizes where the first-order approach outperforms traditional simplex-based solvers, with the crossover depending on the computing environment. The result therefore supports selective use of GPUs within integer programming. summary.tldr: Batching related linear programs lets a first-order solver exploit GPUs and outperform simplex methods in identified computational settings.

title: Batched First-Order Methods for Parallel LP Solving in MIP

abstract: Understanding when learning is statistically possible yet computationally hard is a central challenge in high-dimensional statistics. In this work, we investigate this question in the context of single- and multi-index models, classes of functions widely studied as benchmarks to probe the ability of machine learning methods to discover features in high-dimensional data. Our main contribution is to show that a Noise Sensitivity Exponent (NSE)—a simple quantity determined by the activation function—governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps within a broad regime of these models. We first establish that, in single-index models with large additive noise, the onset of a computational bottleneck is fully characterized by the NSE. We then demonstrate that the same exponent controls a statistical-computational gap in the specialization transition of large separable multi-index models, where individual components become learnable. Taken together, our results identify the NSE as a unifying property linking noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization in high-dimensional learning.

The result connects the activation’s sensitivity to noise with the difficulty of extracting learnable structure.

The authors then examine large separable multi-index models, focusing on the specialization transition where individual components become learnable. summary.tldr: An activation-dependent noise sensitivity exponent characterizes statistical-computational gaps across specified single- and multi-index learning regimes.

title: A Noise Sensitivity Exponent Controls Large Statistical-to-Computational Gaps in Single- and Multi-Index Models

abstract: Zeroth-order optimization is widely used when gradients are unavailable, but the standard two-point estimator suffers from $\mathcal{O}(r^2)$ truncation bias at smoothing radius $r$. Existing bias-reduction schemes typically increase the leading directional variance under a fixed number of function evaluations per gradient estimate, while variance-reduction schemes generally do not improve the bias order. We propose Romberg-ZOGE, which forms a Romberg-extrapolated linear combination of two-point differences evaluated at radii ${r/2^k}_{k=0}^R$ while reusing the same perturbation direction across all radii. With appropriately chosen weights, Romberg-ZOGE cancels the first $R$ even-order truncation terms and achieves $\mathcal{O}(r^{2R+2})$ bias under $(2R{+}2)$-order smoothness, while preserving the leading directional variance constant of the two-point estimator up to higher-order residual terms. We further characterize the stochastic-oracle setting by deriving an explicit noise-amplification factor and corresponding bias and variance bounds. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks, simulator-based wireless optimization, and black-box prompt tuning of OPT-1.3B demonstrate faster and more stable zeroth-order SGD when the number of function evaluations per gradient estimate is fixed.

paragraphs: When gradients are unavailable, optimization can estimate them from function evaluations at perturbed inputs. A standard two-point estimate has truncation bias proportional to the square of its smoothing radius. Reducing this bias often increases directional variance under a fixed evaluation budget. Romberg-ZOGE targets this trade-off by combining estimates made at several progressively smaller radii.

The estimator reuses the same perturbation direction across all radii and applies carefully selected extrapolation weights. These weights cancel the first R even-order error terms. Under smoothness of order 2R+2, the bias becomes O(r^(2R+2)), while the leading directional variance constant is preserved up to higher-order residual terms. The smoothness requirement is part of the stated guarantee.

The paper separately analyzes noisy function evaluations, deriving an explicit noise-amplification factor and associated bias and variance bounds. Experiments cover synthetic problems, simulator-based wireless optimization, and black-box prompt tuning of OPT-1.3B. With function evaluations per estimate held fixed, the method produces faster and more stable zeroth-order stochastic gradient descent in these tests.
summary.tldr: Romberg-ZOGE combines same-direction estimates at multiple radii to reduce gradient-estimation bias while preserving leading directional variance under stated smoothness conditions.

title: Romberg-Extrapolated Zeroth-Order Gradient Estimator: Higher-Order Bias Reduction with Preserved Leading Directional Variance

abstract: Integrating large language models (LLMs) into text-to-speech (TTS) systems has improved speech expressiveness, yet interpretable emotional control remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily rely on external conditioning or global activation steering, offering limited insight into the internal representations underlying emotional control. In this work, we analyze emotion-related variation in the semantic hidden states of LLM-based TTS models using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify sparse latent features. Our analysis shows that emotional variation is distributed across multiple sparse latent features, while intervening on a small subset enables interpretable emotion control. Building on this observation, we introduce a feature-level intervention framework for bidirectional emotion induction and suppression without modifying backbone parameters. We further show that distinct latent features are associated with specific acoustic attributes (e.g., pitch), suggesting that emotional expression arises from coordinated latent contributions rather than a single global shift. Empirically, steering these sparse latent features achieves comparable or superior emotion induction and suppression performance relative to global steering and existing TTS baselines.

This paper examines the semantic hidden states inside these systems using sparse autoencoders. The goal is to identify a sparse set of latent features through which emotional variation can be understood and deliberately influenced.

The analysis finds that emotional variation is distributed across several features, while modifying a small subset can provide useful control. The work therefore links a more inspectable representation of emotion with an effective means of changing the generated speech.

title: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Emotion Control in Text-to-Speech

abstract: Learning compact state representations in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) has proven crucial for addressing the curse of dimensionality in large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) problems. Existing principled approaches leverage structural priors on the MDP by constructing state representations as linear combinations of the state-graph Laplacian eigenvectors. When the transition graph is unknown or the state space is prohibitively large, the graph spectral features can be estimated directly via sample trajectories. In this work, we prove an upper bound on the approximation error of linear value function approximation under the learned spectral features. We show how this error scales with the algebraic connectivity of the state-graph, grounding the approximation quality in the topological structure of the MDP. We further bound the error introduced by the eigenvector estimation itself, leading to an end-to-end error decomposition across the representation learning pipeline. Additionally, we show how the common expression for the symmetrized MDP Laplacian is easy to misinterpret, and propose a more straightforward reformulation. Our results hold for general (non-uniform) policies without any assumptions on the symmetry of the induced transition kernel. We validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations on gridworld environments.

title: Impact of Connectivity on Laplacian Representations in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Existing research on CodeGen AI security mainly focuses on red teaming, which aims to uncover vulnerabilities and risks in AI-generated code. However, progress on the blue teaming side remains limited, as effective defenses require a deep security analysis of given tasks and edge cases. To fill in this gap, we propose BlueCodeAgent, an end-to-end blue teaming agent powered by automated red teaming. Our red teaming component generates diverse risky instances, providing effective edge cases and guidance for the subsequent blue teaming process. Our blue teaming agent then conducts multi-level defense, leveraging these red teaming examples to detect previously seen and unseen risk scenarios through constitution summarization and dynamic code analysis. Our evaluation across four representative code-related tasks–bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection, and prompt injection detection–shows that BlueCodeAgent achieves significant gains over diverse baselines. In particular, for vulnerability detection tasks, BlueCodeAgent integrates dynamic analysis to effectively reduce false positives, a challenging problem as base models tend to be over-conservative. Overall, with GPT-4o as the base model, BlueCodeAgent achieves an average F1 score improvement of 14.7% across four tasks compared to directly prompting the model, attributed to its ability to summarize actionable constitutions and perform dynamic analysis. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/1mocat/BlueCodeAgent.

summary.tldr: BlueCodeAgent turns automatically generated security edge cases into defensive rules and dynamic analyses that improve code-related risk detection.

title: BlueCodeAgent: A Blue Teaming Agent Powered by Automated Red Teaming for CodeGen AI

abstract: Regional refinement for interactive segmentation is of great necessity to ensure the fidelity of segmented pixels nearby user-prompted locations, which specifies a local window ( focus view) for the latest click after a global prediction, where local pixels are revisited and optimized using numerous refining structures. Previous methods either utilize a two-stage pipeline to estimate the focus view or manually preset a fixed scope for all clicks, while the former is time-consuming, the latter fails to capture the correlation among click position, object geometry, and focus intensity. In this paper, we inherit the core idea of FCFI and dedicate a one-stage framework characterized with Elaborate Focus Prior (EFPNet). Concretely, EFPNet outputs an erroneous mask w.r.t historical feedback and newly-placed click in an end-to-end manner, which deduces precise focus region according to its max-connected component, followed with feedback correction considering image, feature and mask affinity. We further design a clicked-with-focus mechanism for efficient feedback integration. Extensive studies on four benchmarks have revealed outstanding performance of EFPNet for both efficacy and computational overhead.

paragraphs: Interactive segmentation uses user clicks to improve an image’s predicted object mask. After a global prediction, local refinement focuses on a region near the latest click. Choosing that region matters: a fixed window ignores how the click relates to object geometry, while a separate estimation stage adds computational cost.

EFPNet uses a one-stage framework to predict an error mask from previous feedback and the new click. It derives a focused refinement region from the mask’s largest connected component. Correction then considers relationships in the image, its features, and the predicted mask. A clicked-with-focus mechanism further supports efficient integration of user feedback.

The central contribution is to make the refinement region responsive to the current segmentation error and interaction history. This connects where the system looks next with the correction the user is requesting. Studies on four benchmarks report strong performance in both segmentation effectiveness and computational overhead, supporting the value of learning a more precise focus region within an integrated refinement framework.
summary.tldr: EFPNet predicts where segmentation needs correction and uses that learned focus region to integrate user clicks efficiently.

title: Interactive Segmentation with Elaborate Focus Prior

abstract: As AI systems enter institutional workflows, workers must decide whether to delegate task execution to AI and how much effort to invest in verifying AI outputs, while institutions evaluate workers using outcome-based standards that may misalign with workers’ private costs. We model delegation and verification as the solution to a rational worker’s optimization problem, and define worker quality by evaluating an institution-centered utility (distinct from the worker’s objective) at the resulting optimal action. We formally characterize optimal worker workflows and show that AI induces phase transitions, where arbitrarily small differences in verification ability lead to sharply different behaviors. As a result, AI can amplify workers with strong verification reliability while degrading institutional worker quality for others who rationally over-delegate and reduce oversight, even when baseline task success improves and no behavioral biases are present. These results identify a structural mechanism by which AI reshapes institutional worker quality and amplifies quality disparities between workers with different verification reliability.

paragraphs: Introducing AI into a workplace creates two linked decisions: whether to delegate a task and how carefully to check the result. This paper models a rational worker choosing both actions according to their own costs and benefits. It then evaluates the chosen workflow using an institutional objective, which can differ from the worker’s private objective.

The analysis shows that optimal behavior can change sharply with verification ability. In these phase transitions, arbitrarily small differences in a worker’s ability to verify outputs can produce substantially different delegation and oversight choices. This means that similar workers need not respond similarly to the same AI capability when their incentives and verification reliability interact.

Under the model, AI can improve institutional worker quality for strong verifiers while reducing it for others who rationally delegate too much and check too little. That decline can occur even when baseline task success improves and workers have no behavioral biases. The result identifies an incentive-based mechanism for widening quality disparities, rather than attributing the problem solely to irrational trust in AI.
summary.tldr: A formal model shows how rational delegation and verification choices can make AI amplify institutional quality differences between workers.

title: Delegation and Verification under AI

abstract: Mental rotation—the ability to compare objects seen from different viewpoints—is a fundamental example of mental simulation and spatial world modeling in humans. Here we propose a mechanistic model of human mental rotation, leveraging recent advances in deep, equivariant, and neuro-symbolic learning. Our model consists of three stacked components: (1) an equivariant neural encoder, producing 3D spatial representations of objects from images, (2) a neuro-symbolic object encoder, deriving symbolic objects descriptions from these spatial representations, and (3) a neural decision agent, comparing these symbolic descriptions to prescribe rotation simulations in 3D latent space via a recurrent pathway. Our model design is guided by the existing experimental literature on mental rotation, which we complemented with experiments in VR where participants could at times manipulate the objects to compare. Our model captures well the performance, response times and behavior of participants in our and others’ experiments, and through ablation studies we demonstrate the necessity of each component. Our work adds to a recent collection of deep neural models of human spatial reasoning, further demonstrating the potency of integrating deep, equivariant, and symbolic representations to model the human mind.

paragraphs: Mental rotation lets people compare objects even when they see them from different viewpoints. This paper develops a computational account of that ability, asking whether a model that builds spatial representations and actively simulates rotations can reproduce human performance. Its design draws on previous behavioral research and additional virtual-reality experiments in which participants could sometimes manipulate the objects they were comparing.

The model connects three components. An equivariant neural encoder converts images into three-dimensional spatial representations. A second encoder turns those representations into symbolic object descriptions. A neural decision agent compares the descriptions and uses a recurrent connection to prescribe further rotation simulations within the model’s internal three-dimensional space.

The authors report that the model captures participants’ accuracy, response times, and behavior in both their experiments and earlier studies. Removing components in ablation studies demonstrates that each is necessary for the model’s reported performance. These findings support combining neural perception, spatial structure, and symbolic descriptions as a useful approach to modeling human spatial reasoning.
summary.tldr: A model combining spatial encoding, symbolic descriptions, and simulated rotations reproduces several aspects of human mental-rotation behavior.

title: A Deep Learning Model of Mental Rotation Informed by Interactive VR Experiments

abstract: While existing AI-generated image detectors report high performance, we identify that this is largely driven by a critical prediction asymmetry: a bias toward the real class that severely limits sensitivity to generated content, especially under standard post-processing operations such as compression and resizing. We hypothesize that this stems from the model’s reliance on spurious features, distracting signals that obscure true generative artifacts. To address this, we propose DEAR (Dissect and Prune), which leverages inpainted images to identify and prune these interfering components. Specifically, we find that features strongly aligned to either inpainted or non-inpainted regions are less robust to post-processing. By measuring the alignment between channel activations and inpaint masks, DEAR removes features at both extremes, retaining only those that capture genuine generative artifacts. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances robustness against unseen generators and post-processing, effectively mitigating the prediction asymmetry. Our code is available at https://github.com/dahyedahye/dear.

paragraphs: An image detector can report strong performance while still missing generated images disproportionately. This paper identifies a prediction asymmetry favoring the real-image class, especially after compression or resizing. The authors hypothesize that distracting features obscure the artifacts that would reliably reveal generated content.

DEAR uses inpainted images to investigate which internal features are vulnerable. It measures how strongly each channel's activations align with the mask marking the inpainted region. Features strongly associated with either the edited region or its unedited surroundings prove less robust to post-processing. The method prunes channels at both extremes, aiming to retain signals that better capture generative artifacts.

Experiments report substantially better robustness to previously unseen generators and post-processing, along with reduced prediction asymmetry. The approach matters because it changes which evidence the detector relies on, using localized edits to diagnose interfering components. Its reported success supports the usefulness of this pruning strategy; the proposed explanation involving spurious features remains framed as the authors' hypothesis about the original failure.
summary.tldr: DEAR prunes detector features identified through inpainted images, improving robustness to unseen generators and image post-processing.

title: Dissect and Prune: Enhancing Robustness in AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: Geometry-aware generative models and novel view synthesis approaches have shown strong potential in visual fidelity and consistency. In parallel, equivariant representation learning has emerged as a powerful framework for constructing latent spaces where analytically known group transformations could act directly, capturing geometric structure in data and enhancing both interpretability and generalization in novel view synthesis. However, we identify that existing approaches often suffer from latent misalignment, a discrepancy between the intended group action and the actually required transformations in the latent space. Consequently, the learned latents often fail to consistently preserve the equivariant relations imposed by the underlying group symmetry. To address this, we propose Residual Latent Flow, a flow-based framework that corrects the misaligned latents, thereby improving compliance with the underlying equivariance relation. Our comprehensive experiments show that our method significantly reduces latent misalignment and improves novel view synthesis quality, under rotation groups SO(n).

paragraphs: Equivariant representations aim to make transformations of data correspond to known transformations in a model's latent space. For generating a new view, that means geometric changes should be reflected consistently in the internal representation. This paper identifies latent misalignment as a problem that prevents existing approaches from maintaining that correspondence.

The mismatch is between the transformation prescribed by the group symmetry and the transformation the learned latent representation actually needs. As a result, imposing an intended symmetry does not always produce latents that obey it consistently. The proposed Residual Latent Flow uses a flow-based correction to adjust misaligned representations and improve their agreement with the equivariance relation.

Experiments under rotation groups SO(n) report substantial reductions in latent misalignment and better novel-view synthesis quality. These findings connect an internal geometric correction with an improvement in generated views. The contribution is a mechanism for repairing the relationship between known transformations and learned representations, with the reported evidence specifically covering rotational symmetries rather than every possible group action.
summary.tldr: Residual Latent Flow corrects mismatches between intended rotations and learned latent transformations, improving novel-view synthesis in reported experiments.

title: Equivariant Latent Alignment via Flow Matching under Group Symmetries

abstract: We show that contrary to conventional wisdom in the community, graph neural networks (GNNs) are not continuous with respect to all natural modes of graph convergence. As a result, GNNs may generate substantially different latent representations for graphs that are very similar. In particular they assign vastly different latent embeddings to graphs that represent the same underlying object at different resolution scales. We trace this failure of continuity back to a structural obstruction arising from commonly used information-propagation schemes. Building on this insight we then derive a principled modification to standard GNN architectures which equips models with continuity across scales. The proposed modification enables consistent integration of distinct resolutions and reliable generalization between them. We systematically validate our theoretical findings in a wide range of numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Different graphs can describe the same underlying object at different levels of detail. Ideally, a graph neural network would produce compatible representations as that resolution changes. This paper shows that standard GNNs lack continuity under some natural notions of graph convergence, meaning apparently similar graphs can receive substantially different latent representations.

The authors trace this behavior to a structural obstruction in commonly used information-propagation schemes. The issue therefore concerns how information moves through the architecture, rather than merely whether two input graphs look similar. In particular, changing the resolution of an object’s graph representation can lead to very different embeddings even though the underlying object remains the same.

Using that diagnosis, the paper derives a modification to standard GNN architectures that provides continuity across scales. This supports consistent integration of different resolutions and generalization between them. Numerical experiments across a wide range of settings validate the theoretical findings. The contribution links a precise failure of representation stability to an architectural remedy, clarifying why resolution changes need explicit treatment when designing graph models.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies why standard GNNs can produce incompatible embeddings across graph resolutions and derives an architectural modification that restores continuity across scales.

title: Graph Neural Networks Are Not Continuous Across Graph Resolutions

abstract: With the rapid emergence of personal AI agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs), implementing them on-device has become essential for privacy and responsiveness. To handle the inherently personal and context-dependent nature of real-world requests, such agents must ground their generation in device-resident personal context. However, under tight memory budgets, the core bottleneck is what to store so that retrieval remains aligned with the user. We propose EPIC (Efficient Preference-aligned Index Construction), which focuses on user preferences as a compact and stable form of personal context and integrates them throughout the RAG pipeline. EPIC selectively retains preference-relevant information from raw data and aligns retrieval toward preference-aligned contexts. Across four benchmarks covering conversations, debates, explanations, and recommendations, EPIC reduces indexing memory by 2,404$\times$, improves preference-following accuracy by 18.79%p, and achieves 32.17$\times$ lower retrieval latency over the best-performing baseline. In on-device experiments, EPIC maintains under 1 MB memory and achieves 5.21 to 29.35 ms/query latency across three platforms, while supporting streaming updates under preference drift. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/UbiquitousAILab/EPIC.

EPIC centers that selection on preferences, which the authors use as a compact and relatively stable representation of personal context.

These results show substantial benefits from selecting useful personal context before retrieval.
summary.tldr: EPIC builds compact preference-focused memory for on-device retrieval, improving personalization while sharply reducing storage and latency.

title: From Volume to Value: Preference-Aligned Memory Construction for On-Device RAG

abstract: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize well to generic instructions, they struggle with personalized commands such as "bring my cup," where the robot must act on one specific instance among visually similar objects. We study this setting of manipulating personal objects, in which a VLA must identify and control a user-specific object unseen during training using only a few reference images. To address this challenge, we propose Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP), a simple-yet-effective training-free perceptual adapter that equips frozen VLAs with top-down selective attention. VAP treats the reference images as a non-parametric visual memory, grounds the personal object in the scene through open-vocabulary detection and embedding-based matching, and then injects this grounding as a visual prompt by highlighting the object and rewriting the instruction. We construct two simulation benchmarks, Personalized-SIMPLER and Personalized-VLABench, and a real-world tabletop benchmark to evaluate personalized manipulation across multiple robots and tasks. Experiments show that VAP consistently outperforms generic policies and token-learning baselines in both success rate and correct-object manipulation, helping to bridge the gap between semantic understanding and instance-level control.

paragraphs: A robot can understand what a cup is yet still fail to identify which cup belongs to a particular person. This paper studies personalized manipulation: selecting and handling a specific object that was unseen during training, using only a few reference images. The challenge is connecting a general instruction to the correct physical instance among similar objects.

Visual Attentive Prompting, or VAP, adds a perceptual adapter to an existing, frozen vision-language-action model. It stores reference images as visual memory, detects candidate objects in the scene, and compares their visual representations with those references. It then highlights the matched object and rewrites the instruction to direct the model’s attention. This personalization requires no additional model training.

The authors introduce two simulation benchmarks and a real-world tabletop benchmark spanning multiple robots and tasks. VAP consistently improves both task success and manipulation of the correct object compared with generic policies and token-learning baselines. The results support visual prompting as a practical way to translate object recognition into personalized robot actions.
summary.tldr: VAP uses reference images and visual prompts to help frozen robot models manipulate the correct personal object without additional training.

title: Bring My Cup! Personalizing Vision-Language-Action Models with Visual Attentive Prompting

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained and tested extensively on symbolic representations such as code and graphs, yet real-world user tasks are often specified in natural language. To what extent can LLMs generalize across these representations? Here, we approach this question by studying isomorphic tasks involving procedures represented in code, graphs, and natural language (e.g., scheduling steps in planning). We find that training LLMs with popular post-training methods on graphs or code data alone does not reliably generalize to corresponding natural language tasks, while training solely on natural language can lead to inefficient performance gains. To address this gap, we propose a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum that first trains on symbolic, then natural language data. The curriculum substantially improves model performance across model families and tasks. Remarkably, a 1.5B Qwen model trained by our method can closely match zero-shot GPT-4o in naturalistic planning. Finally, our analysis suggests that successful cross-representation generalization can be interpreted as a form of generative analogy, which our curriculum effectively encourages. The dataset and code used in this paper can be found https://github.com/fangru-lin/procedure_generalization_llm.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether learning a procedure in one representation helps a language model perform the same procedure in another. It studies structurally equivalent tasks written as code, graphs, or natural language, including planning tasks that require scheduling steps. This setup separates procedural structure from the form in which a user presents it.

The authors find that popular post-training methods applied only to code or graph examples do not reliably transfer to corresponding natural-language tasks. Training only on natural language can also produce inefficient gains. Their solution is a two-stage reinforcement-learning curriculum: first develop the skill using symbolic data, then train on natural-language versions.

This curriculum substantially improves performance across the tested model families and tasks. A trained 1.5-billion-parameter Qwen model closely matches zero-shot GPT-4o on naturalistic planning. The authors interpret successful transfer as a form of generative analogy: adapting learned procedural structure to a different representation. Their analysis suggests that the curriculum encourages this process, rather than establishing it as the only explanation.
summary.tldr: A curriculum that trains first on symbolic procedures and then on natural language improves procedural transfer across representations.

title: Can Large Language Models Generalize Procedures Across Representations?

abstract: Medical foundation models (MFMs) aim to learn universal representations from multimodal medical images that can generalize effectively to diverse downstream clinical tasks. However, most existing MFMs suffer from information ambiguity that blends multimodal representations in a single embedding space, leading to the degradation of modality specificity and diversity. In this paper, we propose M-IDoL, a self-supervised MFM that introduces Information Decomposition for multimodal representation Learning via two objectives: i) maximizing inter-modality entropy by dispersing multimodal representations into separable Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) subspaces to achieve representation specificity across modalities; and ii) minimizing intra-modality uncertainty by performing fine-grained semantic discrimination within each MoE subspace to enrich representation diversity per modality. By pre-training on 1.15 million medical images, M-IDoL i) delivers superior generalization across 21 downstream clinical tasks, outperforming 20 foundation models on five imaging modalities (e.g., X-ray, fundus, OCT, dermoscopy and pathology), and ii) learns modality-specific and diverse representations, showing clearer separation of feature clusters across modalities and finer-grained feature discrimination within each modality.

paragraphs: M-IDoL addresses a representation problem in medical foundation models trained across imaging modalities. Combining all images in one embedding space can blur the information that distinguishes modalities and the detail within each modality. The paper seeks representations that preserve both kinds of structure while remaining useful across downstream clinical tasks.

Its self-supervised training has two complementary objectives. The first maximizes inter-modality entropy by distributing representations across separable mixture-of-experts subspaces, promoting modality specificity. The second minimizes uncertainty within each modality through fine-grained semantic discrimination inside those subspaces. Together, these objectives aim to distinguish imaging types while also retaining meaningful variation among images of the same type.

After pretraining on 1.15 million medical images, M-IDoL outperforms 20 foundation models across 21 downstream clinical tasks spanning five modalities: X-ray, fundus, OCT, dermoscopy, and pathology. Representation analyses show clearer separation between modalities and finer discrimination within them. These findings connect the method’s explicit decomposition objectives with both the organization of learned features and stronger generalization on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: M-IDoL separates medical imaging modalities into expert subspaces while preserving fine-grained information within each modality.

title: M-IDoL: Information Decomposition for Modality-Specific and Diverse Representation Learning in Medical Foundation Model

abstract: Neural Forecasters (NFs) have become a cornerstone of Long-term Time Series Forecasting (LTSF). However, recent progress has been hampered by an overemphasis on architectural complexity at the expense of fundamental forecasting structures. In this work, we revisit principled designs of LTSF. We begin by formulating a Variance Reduction Hypothesis (VRH), positing that generating and combining multiple forecasts is essential to reducing the inherent uncertainty of NFs. Guided by this, we propose Boosted Direct Output (BDO), a streamlined paradigm that synergistically hybridizes the causal structure of Auto-Regressive (AR) with the stability of Direct Output (DO), while implicitly realizing the principle of forecast combination within a single network. Furthermore, we mitigate a critical validation-test generalization gap by employing parameter smoothing to stabilize optimization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that these trivial yet principled improvements enable a direct temporal MLP to outperform recent, complex state-of-the-art models in nearly all benchmarks, without relying on intricate inductive biases. Finally, we empirically verify our hypothesis, establishing a dynamic performance bound that highlights promising directions for future research. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/Luoauoa/ReNF.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the basic structure of long-term forecasting rather than adding architectural complexity. Its Variance Reduction Hypothesis proposes that generating and combining multiple forecasts is essential for reducing neural forecasters’ inherent uncertainty. The hypothesis motivates a design that embeds forecast combination within one network.

Boosted Direct Output combines the causal organization of autoregressive forecasting with the stability of direct-output forecasting. The resulting model implicitly combines forecasts while retaining a streamlined structure. The authors also use parameter smoothing to stabilize optimization and reduce a gap between validation performance and test generalization, addressing training behavior alongside forecast construction.

With these changes, a direct temporal MLP outperforms recent complex state-of-the-art models on nearly all evaluated benchmarks. The authors also empirically support their variance-reduction hypothesis and establish a dynamic performance bound. The findings indicate that forecast organization and optimization stability can account for substantial performance gains, even in a simple architecture. The hypothesis’s support is empirical, and the reported benchmark advantage is broad but not universal.
summary.tldr: ReNF improves long-term forecasting through implicit forecast combination and parameter smoothing, allowing a simple temporal MLP to beat complex models on nearly all tested benchmarks.

title: ReNF: Rethinking the Design of Neural Long-Term Time Series Forecasters

abstract: Natural-language explanations are widely used to interpret machine learning models, yet many prioritize human plausibility over accurately reflecting or predicting model behavior. Prior approaches often rely on human-written rationales, producing post-hoc explanations that neither align with the model’s decision function nor generalize. We introduce $\textbf{OPeX}$, a natural-language explanation model that directly optimizes for behavioral faithfulness: the ability of an explanation to reflect and predict a model’s observable input–output behavior. $\textbf{OPeX}$ is trained using reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), optimizing two complementary metrics: recoverability, which measures whether explanations recover model predictions on seen examples, and simulatability, which measures prediction of model behavior on unseen inputs. Across structured and text-based tasks, $\textbf{OPeX}$ achieves high simulatability ($\tilde$0.85) and recoverability ($\tilde$0.99), outperforming GPT-4o, LLaMA-3.3-70B, MaNtLE, Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-based models, and human-written explanations, despite using an 8B-parameter backbone. Human user studies show a 15% improvement in classification accuracy over competent baselines.

paragraphs: An explanation can sound convincing without helping someone predict what a model will actually do. This paper makes that predictive usefulness the training target. Its explanation model, OPeX, aims to describe observable input–output behavior faithfully, addressing the gap between plausible rationales and explanations that track the model being explained.

OPeX uses reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization to optimize two complementary measures. Recoverability asks whether an explanation lets a reader or system reconstruct predictions on examples already seen. Simulatability asks whether it supports predicting the model’s responses to new inputs. Together, these measures reward explanations that capture both existing decisions and behavior beyond the examples used to illustrate them.

Across structured and text tasks, the authors report approximately 0.99 recoverability and 0.85 simulatability using an 8-billion-parameter backbone. OPeX outperforms the listed language-model, explanation-method, and human-written alternatives. Human studies also report a 15% improvement in classification accuracy over competent baselines. These findings support directly training explanations for behavioral prediction rather than relying on their apparent plausibility.
summary.tldr: OPeX trains natural-language explanations to recover known model decisions and predict unseen ones, improving behavioral faithfulness and human classification performance.

title: Directly Optimizing Natural Language Explanations for Behavioral Faithfulness: Simulatability and Recoverability

abstract: Two-player games such as board games have long been used as traditional benchmarks for reinforcement learning. This work revisits a policy optimization method with reverse Kullback-Leibler regularization and entropy regularization and analyzes this combination in two-player zero-sum settings from theoretical and empirical perspectives. From a theoretical perspective, we investigate the stability of the policy update rule in two theoretical settings: game-theoretic normal-form games and finite-length games. We provide novel convergence guarantees and verify our theoretical results through numerical experiments on synthetic games. From an empirical perspective, we derive a practical model-free reinforcement learning algorithm based on the regularized policy optimization. We validate the training efficiency of our algorithm through comprehensive experiments on five board games: Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, Go, Hex, and Othello. Experimental results show that our agent learns more efficiently than existing methods across environments.

paragraphs: Learning strategies in two-player zero-sum games requires policy updates that remain stable as players compete. This paper revisits an optimization method that combines reverse Kullback–Leibler regularization with entropy regularization. It studies the combination through both mathematical analysis and practical reinforcement-learning experiments.

The theoretical work examines policy-update stability in normal-form games and finite-length games. The authors establish new convergence guarantees and test the theoretical results numerically on synthetic games. Studying both settings connects the update rule to games expressed through direct strategic choices and games that unfold over a finite sequence of decisions.

The authors then derive a practical model-free reinforcement-learning algorithm from the regularized optimization method. They evaluate training efficiency on Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, Go, Hex, and Othello, reporting more efficient learning than existing methods across the tested environments. The paper's contribution is the connection between a mathematically analyzed regularization scheme and an implementable game-learning algorithm, with evidence addressing both update stability and training efficiency.
summary.tldr: Combining reverse-KL and entropy regularization yields convergence guarantees and a model-free algorithm that learns efficiently across five board games.

title: Revisiting Regularized Policy Optimization for Stable and Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Two-Player Games

abstract: The fields of AI-based disease fingerprinting, drug discovery and repurposing are currently among the emerging frontiers of machine learning applied to medicine. One major challenge is to obtain robust $\textit{in-silico}$ modeling of disease progression while accounting for the vastly different time scales of biochemical interactions, from gene expression to protein abundance and metabolic flux. Discrete sequence models inadequately represent such multi-scale interactions, and standard Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) often fail to train stably under stiffness (different time scales). To address this, a Tri-Scale Stiff NODE, defined by hierarchically coupled latent differential equations that model the causal relationships from genes to proteins and metabolites, is introduced and optimized in this paper in terms of reconstruction error and information-theoretic mutual information. This enables continuous-time modeling of cellular responses to identify not only the disease dynamics, but also drug perturbations that act within narrow time windows, often invisible to discrete-time approaches. Lyapunov analysis provides a theoretical guarantee that the modeled trajectories remain stable and well-behaved even under extreme stiffness. The methodology is validated using the STATegra B-cell and Traxler macrophage datasets, with the former utilized for a proof-of-concept drug repurposing pipeline.

Those differences create stiffness, which can make standard neural differential equations difficult to train stably. Discrete sequence models can also inadequately represent interactions across these time scales and miss brief responses.

The proposed Tri-Scale Stiff NODE uses hierarchically coupled latent differential equations to model relationships from genes to proteins and metabolites. Training combines reconstruction error with an information-theoretic mutual-information objective. summary.tldr: Hierarchically coupled neural ODEs model gene, protein, and metabolic dynamics across time scales with theoretical stability under extreme stiffness.

title: Tri-Scale Neural ODEs for Continuous Multi-Omics Disease Modeling

abstract: Interpretable machine learning is essential in high-stakes domains where decision-making requires accountability, transparency, and trust. While rule-based models offer global and exact interpretability, learning rule sets that simultaneously achieve high predictive performance and low, human-understandable complexity remains challenging. To address this, we introduce TT-Sparse, a flexible neural building block that leverages differentiable truth tables as nodes to learn sparse, effective connections. A key contribution of our approach is a new soft TopK operator with straight-through estimation for learning discrete, cardinality-constrained feature selection in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Crucially, the forward pass remains sparse, enabling each node (and the entire model) to be transformed exactly into compact, globally interpretable DNF/CNF Boolean formulas via Quine–McCluskey minimization. Extensive empirical results across 28 datasets spanning binary, multiclass, and regression tasks show that the learned sparse rules exhibit superior predictive performance with lower complexity compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

To address this, we introduce TT-Sparse, a flexible neural building block that leverages differentiable truth tables as nodes to learn sparse, effective connections. A key contribution of our approach is a new soft TopK operator with straight-through estimation for learning discrete, cardinality-constrained feature selection in an end-to-end differentiable manner. Crucially, the forward pass remains sparse, enabling each node (and the entire model) to be transformed exactly into compact, globally interpretable DNF/CNF Boolean formulas via Quine–McCluskey minimization. paragraphs: Rule-based models can explain their decisions through explicit logic, but learning rules that are both accurate and compact is difficult. TT-Sparse addresses this tradeoff with a neural building block based on differentiable truth tables. Each node learns a sparse set of connections, keeping the resulting computation suitable for conversion into readable rules.

A new soft TopK operator, combined with straight-through estimation, enables end-to-end learning of discrete feature selections with a constrained number of selected inputs. The forward computation remains sparse. That property allows each node and the complete model to be converted exactly into compact Boolean formulas in disjunctive or conjunctive normal form using Quine–McCluskey minimization.

The exact conversion is central to the interpretability claim: the formulas express the learned model's behavior rather than providing an approximate explanation of it. Across 28 datasets covering binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression, the learned rules achieve better predictive performance with lower complexity than compared state-of-the-art methods. The results support sparse differentiable truth tables as a route to effective, globally interpretable models.
summary.tldr: TT-Sparse learns sparse neural rule models that convert exactly into compact Boolean formulas while improving accuracy and complexity in reported tests.

title: TT-Sparse: Learning Sparse Rule Models with Differentiable Truth Tables

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast datasets that may contain sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP), the de facto standard for formal privacy guarantees, provides a principled framework for training LLMs with provable privacy protection. However, state-of-the-art DP training implementations rely on fast gradient clipping techniques with memory overhead $O(B\min(T^2, d^2))$, where $B$ is the batch size, $T$ is the sequence length, and $d$ is the layer width. This becomes prohibitive as both model width and context length grow. We propose DP-SGD-RC, a novel variant of DP-SGD with randomized clipping that reduces memory and compute overhead. DP-SGD-RC leverages stochastic trace estimation methods, specifically Hutchinson’s estimator and its improved variant, Hutch$^{++}$, to reduce the memory footprint of per-sample gradient norm estimation. We provide a tight privacy analysis showing that DP-SGD-RC achieves noise multipliers competitive with deterministic clipping. originalAbstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast datasets that may contain sensitive information. Differential privacy (DP), the de facto standard for formal privacy guarantees, provides a principled framework for training LLMs with provable privacy protection. However, state-of-the-art DP training implementations rely on fast gradient clipping techniques with memory overhead $O(B\min(T^2, d^2))$, where $B$ is the batch size, $T$ is the sequence length, and $d$ is the layer width. This becomes prohibitive as both model width and context length grow. We propose DP-SGD-RC, a novel variant of DP-SGD with randomized clipping that reduces memory and compute overhead. DP-SGD-RC leverages stochastic trace estimation methods, specifically Hutchinson’s estimator and its improved variant, Hutch$^{++}$, to reduce the memory footprint of per-sample gradient norm estimation. We provide a tight privacy analysis showing that DP-SGD-RC achieves noise multipliers competitive with deterministic clipping. Experiments fine-tuning Llama 3.2 1B on long-context benchmarks spanning classification, question answering, and summarization tasks demonstrate that DP-SGD-RC matches baseline utility while significantly reducing memory and compute.

paragraphs: Differentially private language-model training must control the influence of individual training examples. Computing the gradient norms needed for clipping can become expensive as context length and model width increase. The paper identifies a memory bottleneck in existing fast clipping implementations whose overhead grows with batch size and the smaller of squared sequence length and squared layer width.

DP-SGD-RC replaces the relevant norm-estimation computation with randomized clipping based on stochastic trace estimation. It uses Hutchinson’s estimator and Hutch++, which reduce the memory footprint of estimating per-sample gradient norms. Because randomness enters the clipping procedure itself, the authors provide a privacy analysis for the resulting algorithm and show noise multipliers competitive with deterministic clipping.

Experiments fine-tune Llama 3.2 1B on long-context classification, question answering, and summarization benchmarks. In these evaluations, the method matches baseline utility while substantially reducing memory and computation. The contribution connects a cheaper estimation procedure with a formal privacy analysis, showing how the cost of privacy-preserving fine-tuning can be reduced without losing the measured task quality in the reported settings.
summary.tldr: Randomized gradient clipping reduces private LLM fine-tuning costs while preserving competitive privacy noise levels and measured task utility.

title: Efficient DP-SGD for LLMs with Randomized Clipping

abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based Multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown promise in tackling complex collaborative tasks, where agents are typically orchestrated via role-specific prompts. While the quality of these prompts is pivotal, jointly optimizing them across interacting agents remains a non-trivial challenge, primarily due to the misalignment between local agent objectives and holistic system goals. To address this, we introduce MASPO, a novel framework designed to automatically and iteratively refine prompts across the entire system. A core innovation of MASPO is its joint evaluation mechanism, which assesses prompts not merely by their local validity, but by their capacity to facilitate downstream success for successor agents. This effectively bridges the gap between local interactions and global outcomes without relying on ground-truth labels. Furthermore, MASPO employs a data-driven evolutionary beam search to efficiently navigate the high-dimensional prompt space. Extensive empirical evaluations across 6 diverse tasks demonstrate that MASPO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art prompt optimization methods, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 2.9. We release our code at https://github.com/wangzx1219/MASPO.

paragraphs: In a system of collaborating language-model agents, each agent typically receives a prompt describing its role. Improving those prompts independently can miss what makes the whole system succeed: an agent’s locally acceptable output may provide poor input for the agents that follow. MASPO tackles this mismatch by optimizing prompts jointly across the system.

Its evaluation mechanism judges prompts partly by whether they enable downstream agents to succeed, connecting local interactions to overall outcomes without requiring ground-truth labels. The framework repeatedly refines prompts and uses a data-driven evolutionary beam search to explore the many possible combinations. This makes prompt selection sensitive to the way agents depend on one another.

Across six diverse tasks, the authors report that MASPO consistently beats state-of-the-art prompt optimization methods, with an average accuracy improvement of 2.9. The result supports evaluating prompts as parts of an interacting workflow. The central contribution is making downstream usefulness an explicit criterion for automatic prompt improvement.
summary.tldr: MASPO jointly improves multi-agent prompts by evaluating how well each prompt supports downstream success.

title: MASPO: Joint Prompt Optimization for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Standard Bayesian Optimization (BO) assumes uniform smoothness across the search space—an assumption violated in multi-regime problems such as molecular conformation search through distinct energy basins or drug discovery across heterogeneous molecular scaffolds. A single GP either oversmooths sharp transitions or hallucinates noise in smooth regions, yielding miscalibrated uncertainty. We propose RAMBO, a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Gaussian Processes that automatically discovers latent regimes during optimization, each modeled by an independent GP with locally-optimized hyperparameters. We derive collapsed Gibbs sampling that analytically marginalizes latent functions for efficient inference, and introduce adaptive concentration parameter scheduling for coarse-to-fine regime discovery. Our acquisition functions decompose uncertainty into intra-regime and inter-regime components. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world applications—including molecular conformer optimization, virtual screening for drug discovery, and fusion reactor design—demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on multi-regime objectives. Code is available at https://github.com/AnthonyZhangYan/RAMBO.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model and its uncertainty to choose promising evaluations. The paper focuses on objectives with distinct regimes, where smoothness changes across the search space. A single Gaussian process can blur sharp transitions or interpret smooth behavior as noise, producing uncertainty estimates that are poorly matched to the objective.

RAMBO uses a Dirichlet process mixture to discover regimes during optimization and assigns each an independent Gaussian process with locally tuned hyperparameters. Its inference procedure analytically marginalizes latent functions through collapsed Gibbs sampling. An adaptive concentration schedule guides discovery from coarse to finer regimes, allowing the model’s organization of the search space to evolve.

The acquisition functions distinguish uncertainty within a regime from uncertainty between regimes. This makes regime structure relevant both to prediction and to selecting the next evaluation. Experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on multi-regime synthetic objectives and applications involving molecular conformers, drug screening, and fusion reactor design. The findings support adapting the surrogate model’s local behavior when a uniform smoothness assumption is unsuitable.
summary.tldr: RAMBO improves optimization of heterogeneous objectives by discovering local regimes and modeling their behavior and uncertainty separately.

title: Regime-Adaptive Bayesian Optimization via Dirichlet Process Mixtures of Gaussian Processes

abstract: REPresentation Alignment (REPA) improves the training of generative flow models by aligning intermediate hidden states with pretrained teacher features, but its effectiveness in token-conditioned audio Flow Matching critically depends on the choice of supervised layers, which is typically made heuristically based on the depth. In this work, we introduce Attribution-Guided REPresentation Alignment (AG-REPA), a novel causal layer selection strategy for representation alignment in audio Flow Matching. Firstly, we find that layers that best store semantic/acoustic information (high teacher-space similarity) are not necessarily the layers that contribute most to the velocity field that drives generation, and we call it Store-Contribute Dissociation (SCD). To turn this insight into an actionable training guidance, we propose a forward-only gate ablation (FoG-A) that quantifies each layer’s causal contribution via the induced change in the predicted velocity field, enabling sparse layer selection and adaptive weighting for alignment. Across unified speech and general-audio training (LibriSpeech + AudioSet) under different token-conditioning topologies, AG-REPA consistently outperforms REPA baselines. Overall, our results show that alignment is most effective when applied to the causally dominant layers that drive the velocity field, rather than to layers that are representationally rich but functionally passive.

paragraphs: Representation alignment trains a generative model by encouraging its internal features to resemble those of a pretrained teacher. For audio flow matching, choosing which layers receive this supervision matters substantially. AG-REPA investigates that choice instead of relying on a layer’s depth as a heuristic.

The paper identifies a distinction between storing useful information and influencing generation. A layer can closely resemble the teacher’s semantic or acoustic representations without contributing strongly to the velocity field that guides audio generation. The proposed forward-only gate ablation measures each layer’s contribution through the change it induces in the predicted velocity field. These measurements determine a sparse selection of layers and adapt how strongly each receives alignment supervision.

Across joint speech and general-audio training with different arrangements of token conditioning, AG-REPA consistently improves over REPA baselines. The findings support selecting supervision targets according to their measured functional influence: representational similarity alone does not identify the layers where alignment most effectively improves generation.
summary.tldr: AG-REPA improves audio representation alignment by supervising layers according to their measured causal contribution to generation.

title: AG-REPA: Causal Layer Selection for Representation Alignment in Audio Flow Matching

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale by activating only a small subset of experts per token. However, training such models remains challenging because top-$k$ routing is discrete and non-differentiable, requiring gradient estimators for expert selection whose design remains a central open problem. We introduce ProbMoE, a probabilistic routing framework that models expert selection as a distribution over cardinality-constrained expert subsets and formulates routing as probabilistic inference in this discrete subset space. We first propose ProbMoE Exact-$k$ routing, which samples $k$-expert subsets in the forward pass, and the backward pass uses gradients through each expert’s exact marginal probability as a tractable surrogate for the true gradient. ProbMoE naturally generalizes to a dynamic-$k$ routing setting, where both training and inference constrain the routing cardinality to the same predefined range, allowing adaptive expert allocation per token. Across benchmarks and model backbones, ProbMoE Exact-$k$ achieves strong performance compared to competitive baselines, with improved expert utilization and routing diversity; ProbMoE Dynamic-$k$ achieves comparable performance with fewer activated experts. Code is available at: https://github.com/HengHugoZhao/ProbMoE.git

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models save computation by activating only a few experts for each token. Training the selection mechanism is difficult because choosing a discrete subset does not directly support ordinary differentiation. ProbMoE addresses this by representing routing as a probability distribution over expert subsets with constraints on their size.

In Exact-k routing, the forward computation samples a subset containing exactly k experts. During the backward computation, the method differentiates through each expert's exact marginal probability of selection. Those derivatives provide a tractable surrogate for the true routing gradient; the exactness applies to the marginal probabilities, not to the surrogate being the true gradient.

The framework also supports Dynamic-k routing, allowing the number of selected experts to vary within the same predefined range during training and inference. Across evaluated benchmarks and model backbones, Exact-k delivers strong performance alongside better expert utilization and more diverse routing. Dynamic-k achieves comparable performance while activating fewer experts. Together, the results support probabilistic subset modeling as a way to train both fixed and adaptive expert allocation.
summary.tldr: ProbMoE uses distributions over expert subsets to train fixed or adaptive routing with tractable gradient surrogates.

title: ProbMoE: Differentiable Probabilistic Routing for Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Geometric foundation models hold promise for unconstrained dense geometry prediction from uncalibrated images. However, current feed-forward designs often produce heuristic confidence scores that lack probabilistic interpretation and fail to indicate where and how much the predicted geometry can be trusted. To address this gap, we present Trust3R, a lightweight evidential uncertainty framework for feed-forward 3D reconstruction. Trust3R combines gated residual mean refinement with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart evidential head, yielding a closed-form multivariate Student-t distribution for per-point geometric uncertainty. This provides probabilistically grounded pointmap uncertainty estimates with moderate inference overhead. We evaluate on diverse indoor and outdoor benchmarks and compare against MASt3R’s built-in confidence map, single-pass heteroscedastic regression, MC dropout, and deep ensembles. Experimental results show that Trust3R consistently improves risk–coverage and sparsification, generally improves geometric accuracy, and strengthens uncertainty ranking across benchmarks. On ScanNet++, Trust3R achieves 25% lower AURC and 41% lower AUSE, providing a practical reliability signal for uncertainty-aware weighting in downstream geometry pipelines. Our project page and code are available at https://trust3r-z.github.io.

paragraphs: Trust3R adds probabilistically interpretable uncertainty to feed-forward 3D reconstruction from uncalibrated images. Existing confidence maps can indicate confidence heuristically without specifying how much geometric uncertainty a point carries. The paper aims to provide a more grounded reliability signal for deciding which predicted geometry deserves trust.

The framework combines gated residual refinement of the predicted mean with a Normal-Inverse-Wishart evidential head. This yields a closed-form multivariate Student-t distribution for each point’s geometry, expressing uncertainty through a probability distribution. The authors describe the framework as lightweight, with moderate additional inference cost.

Evaluations span indoor and outdoor benchmarks and compare against MASt3R confidence, heteroscedastic regression, MC dropout, and deep ensembles. Trust3R consistently improves risk–coverage and sparsification results, generally improves geometric accuracy, and strengthens uncertainty ranking. On ScanNet++, it reports 25% lower AURC and 41% lower AUSE. These findings support using its uncertainty estimates to weight geometry in downstream processing, with the accuracy improvement explicitly described as general rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Trust3R equips feed-forward 3D reconstruction with probabilistic per-point uncertainty that improves the ranking of unreliable geometry.

title: Trust It or Not: Evidential Uncertainty for Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction with Trust3R

abstract: As large language models continue to scale, fine-grained block-scaled low-precision formats such as NVFP4 are increasingly adopted for their substantial throughput and memory benefits. However, a single FP4 micro-format often mismatches heterogeneous block-level tensor statistics. To address this without changing the standard block-scaled MMA/GEMM execution path, we propose MixFP4, a mixed micro-format extension to NVFP4 that selects between two stored FP4 micro-formats (E2M1 and E1M2) per block. MixFP4 reuses NVFP4’s scale hierarchy and encodes the format choice with zero additional metadata by repurposing the sign bit of the FP8 E4M3 block scale. By decoding both micro-formats into a unified internal E2M2 compute representation, MixFP4 avoids datapath duplication. Across representative LLM families, MixFP4 improves FP4 quantization robustness and accuracy over NVFP4 baselines with modest tensor-core overhead (3.1% area, 1.5% power).

paragraphs: Four-bit representations reduce the memory and computation demands of large language models, but one numerical format may not suit every block of a tensor. MixFP4 addresses that mismatch by letting each block choose between two stored floating-point micro-formats, E2M1 and E1M2. The adaptation targets differences in the numerical statistics of individual blocks.

The design preserves NVFP4’s existing hierarchy of scales. It records the format choice by repurposing the sign bit of the FP8 E4M3 block scale, so the choice requires no additional metadata. Both stored formats are decoded into a common internal E2M2 representation for computation, avoiding the need for duplicated arithmetic datapaths.

This arrangement keeps the standard block-scaled matrix multiplication execution path while adding flexibility to storage. Across representative language-model families, the paper reports better quantization accuracy and robustness than NVFP4 baselines. Reported tensor-core costs are 3.1% additional area and 1.5% additional power. The contribution is an adaptive representation whose accuracy benefits come with modest stated hardware overhead.
summary.tldr: MixFP4 selects between two four-bit formats per tensor block, improving quantization accuracy with no extra metadata and modest tensor-core overhead.

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) aims to improve generalization performance by learning multiple related tasks simultaneously. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning shared structures from multiple related tasks. We present an improved formulation (iASO) for multi-task learning based on the non-convex alternating structure optimization (ASO) algorithm, in which all tasks are related by a shared feature representation. We convert iASO, a non-convex formulation, into a relaxed convex one, which is, however, not scalable to large data sets due to its complex constraints. We propose an alternating optimization (cASO) algorithm which solves the convex relaxation efficiently, and further show that cASO converges to a global optimum. In addition, we present a theoretical condition, under which cASO can find a globally optimal solution to iASO. Experiments on several benchmark data sets confirm our theoretical analysis.

In this paper, we consider the problem of learning shared structures from multiple related tasks. We present an improved formulation (iASO) for multi-task learning based on the non-convex alternating structure optimization (ASO) algorithm, in which all tasks are related by a shared feature representation. We convert iASO, a non-convex formulation, into a relaxed convex one, which is, however, not scalable to large data sets due to its complex constraints. We propose an alternating optimization (cASO) algorithm which solves the convex relaxation efficiently, and further show that cASO converges to a global optimum. paragraphs: Related prediction tasks can benefit from learning a common feature representation. This paper studies how to discover that shared structure while training the tasks together. It begins with alternating structure optimization, or ASO, and develops an improved formulation called iASO. The central challenge is that this formulation is nonconvex, making its optimization difficult.

The authors construct a convex relaxation of iASO. Although this changes the optimization problem into a more tractable mathematical form, its complicated constraints still make direct application unsuitable for large datasets. They therefore introduce cASO, an alternating optimization algorithm designed to solve the relaxation efficiently, and prove that it converges to a global optimum of that relaxed problem.

A separate theoretical condition establishes when cASO also recovers a globally optimal solution of the original iASO formulation. That distinction matters: solving the relaxation globally does not automatically settle the original problem. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support the theoretical analysis, connecting the proposed formulation and algorithm to practical multitask learning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops an efficient algorithm for a convex relaxation of shared multitask learning, with conditional guarantees for the original nonconvex formulation.

title: A convex formulation for learning shared structures from multiple tasks
